1248- Dept. of COMMIENCE LETTER OF TRANSMITTAL 

May 29, 1947. 

MY DEAR MR. CLARK: I transmit herewith a volume entitled "OPA

Bibliography, 1940-1947." It is Miscellaneous Publication No. 3 in the 

OPA series of Historical Reports on War Administration, and has been approved for publication. 

This work is unique in several respects. So far as I am aware no Federal agency of comparable size in the executive branch has previously made publicly available, or perhaps even compiled, so complete a guide to its printed and duplicated materials, including those intended for internal as well as external use. Certainly no such guide, embracing the entire life span of the agency in a single volume, has been issued so nearly contemporaneously with the documents it covers. This has made it possible to have the compilation and annotation done by persons familiar with the use of the documents in agency operations. 

The usefulness of this bibliography for study and reference should be greatly enhanced by the fact that the underlying collection of documents it describes is being deposited intact in the National Archives, arranged in the same order and with the items marked with the same identifying symbols used in this volume. The possibility that the entire collection may be microfilmed or put on microcards, and so become available in a number of libraries, adds to the potential value of this guide. 

Respectfully submitted.

EARL W. CLARK, HARVEY C. MANSFIELD, Chief, Policy Analysis Branch. 

Director, Division of Liquidation, Office of Temporary Controls.

INTRODUCTION 

In 1943 John W. Willis, commenting on the regulatory literature of the agency, could already say:

In sheer bulk the "delegated legislation" of OPA has probably never had a counterpart, at least in this country. To the uninitiated, too, the literature is at first a bewildering maze.

Disregarding the technical and promotional literature and concentrating solely on the official regulations and orders, he still found this "the most prolific agency in Washington." In contrast with prewar administrative bodies which commonly employed not more than three or four terms to describe their regulatory documents, OPA terminology already recognized 15 or 20. Charitably he added:

This semantic prodigality is not, however, based on any intent to confuse. The magnitude of the task has made it necessary to use ingenuity in designing new bottles for old and new wine, and on the whole the craftsmen of OPA have done an efficient job in pioneering a new field.¹ 

By 1945 the complexities of OPA literature had increased rather than diminished. It was in that year that the agency made its first effort to provide a bibliography of its publications.² This aimed to describe a representative selection of the materials that had appeared to the end of 1944. 

As a matter of practical expediency it deliberately excluded the official regulations and orders, the press releases, the progress reports, the transcripts of meetings, and several other types of duplicated or printed material. Even so there were 920 entries. In particular the serials were omitted. Of these some 200 had been started, though a considerable number had not persisted beyond the first few issues. 

The present bibliography is a successor to that of 1945. All of the earlier entries have been rechecked, and hundreds of them are incorporated in this later edition without essential change. There are, however, marked differences between the two works, particularly as to coverage and as to the treatment of items originally designated as confidential. 

The limited coverage of the earlier edition was explained in the introduction in the following terms:

Much of its inadequacy is due to gaps in the official file on which it is based. 

That file is of rather recent origin. In the early days the agency seems to have made no attempt to keep a central collection of its printed and processed publications. 

Various sets of such material were maintained at numerous points, and for about a year after its establishment the Historical Records Office proceeded on the assumption that each unit of the organization could be trusted to keep a file copy of whatever it had issued. Often this was true, but often, as experience showed, it was not. 'John W. Willis, "The Literature of OPA," Michigan Law Review, XLII (Oct. 1943), 235-256; revised and reprinted in OPA Service, Release No. 152 (Jan. 29, 1944), 700:204-221. 

'OPA Bibliography: Miscellaneous Publications to the End of 1944. Preliminary Edition (Records Management Section, OPA, Washington, D. C., May 1945), 229 pages (mimeographed). 

1

In 1944, therefore, the Director of the Office, Dr. Robert E. Stone, gave instructions that a collection of all OPA publications should be assembled. Partial sets from various sources were brought together and filed alphabetically by title in a comprehensive series.. Even [so], however, . . . the collection is known to be far from complete, especially for the early periods. ...

Subsequently the OPA Library and the Division of Research turned over practically their entire collections of OPA publications to the Policy Analysis Branch, and it was hoped for a time that the Editorial and Publications Section of the latter, which had undertaken to prepare the revised bibliography, would have a copy of every item therein described. 

This it has not been quite possible to achieve, although the OPA Records Branch has attempted to fill some gaps. When only one copy of a publication could be found, however, the Records Branch has decided, in general accordance with the archival principle of maintaining the integrity of files, that that copy should stay with the permanent files of the organizational unit which issued it. All OPA files remaining after some sorting and collation, except for a few relating to continuing functions transferred to other agencies, are being deposited with the National Archives. 

Any investigator seeking to examine works described in the present bibliography should therefore find them in one building, but must be reconciled to looking for some particular items in more than one place. He may need to consult especially the residual files not only of the Editorial and Publications Section but also of the Information Department, the Enforcement Department, and the Office of the OPA Secretary. 

With regard to regional office publications the present work has hardly been more successful than its predecessor. The previous introduction 

Conspicuously absent are most of the regional publications. The degree of autonomy permitted by the OPA to its regional offices has been very considerable, and they have issued many publications on their own authority and have revised not a few publications of the national office to suit their special needs. Only an inconsequential scattering of all these is to be found in the present bibliography. 

The regional materials available are still too sporadic to justify any systematic treatment of them in the present edition. However, selected categories of regional office materials were preserved and are now on deposit in the National Archives. These include copies of informational releases created within the regional offices, as well as procedural materials such as memoranda of instructions, manuals, and periodic reports. It should be noted, moreover, that the Library of Congress has made an earnest effort to assemble representative collections of the regional publications of the war agencies. From its holdings, therefore, as well as from the file materials which the OPA Records Branch has assembled from the regional offices for deposit in the National Archives, it should be possible to study a fair sample of the regional literature of OPA. 2

A further source for some elusive OPA publications exists at the University of California Library. Mr. Jerome K. Wilcox, while on the staff of that institution, indefatigably collected the publications of the wartime Government agencies and has issued an extensive bibliography of them. 

His lists contain numerous OPA items not found in the collections on which the present bibliography is based. For completeness it has seemed advisable to insert in each such case a copy of his entry and annotation, conforming it somewhat as to style wherever necessary, and adding in parentheses the letter "W" and the volume number and serial number of his reference. He included individual annotations for a good many of the 

OPA regulations and OPA press releases. These have not been taken over, since the present work does not aim to list such items separately but only by groups or types. 

The principles of selection on which the 1945 bibliography was based have been followed without essential change in Sections 3-6, which form the core of the present edition. To quote once more the earlier introduction : 

In addition to the accidental defects of the basic collections, the work has had certain limitations imposed upon it deliberately. In the first place, it is confined to material that has been printed or otherwise duplicated, by mimeograph, hectograph, multilith, etc. No typewritten studies have been included, though occasionally some of these may exceed certain of the included materials in intrinsic value. In general, however, that is not true.

On the other hand, not every piece of printed or duplicated matter which the agency has issued deserves to be called a publication. To take an extreme example, when someone desired to have copies of a certain portion of an article in Fortune Magazine, he had the extract mimeographed, but manifestly this is in no sense an OPA publication. There are also many casual memoranda that have poured from the mimeograph machines, as well as budget justifications, fiscal statements, progress reports, transcripts or proceedings of meetings, press releases, lists of prices, posters and flyers, pictures and maps, and items in the list of around 2,000 OPA forms or the list of over 36,000 official documents (price regulations, ration orders, etc.). 

All of these have been excluded from the present instalment of the bibliography, though a determined person could probably stretch the word "publication” to include every one of them.

To state the principles of selection in the most general terms, the bibliography aims to include the library type of material (books and pamphlets developing a definite subject) and to exclude the archival type of material (letters and memoranda addressed to a particular situation). Between these, as every librarian and archivist knows, there are many borderline cases. It is often necessary to look below the surface, since an item which calls itself a memorandum may actually have a title and be carefully organized around a specific topic. If so, it is included. We have also included internal directives, usually in series, of sufficient size and scope to reveal significant policies of the agency or to show the larger aspects of its organization. 

We have included practically everything which calls itself a manual, as well as periodic or special reports to Congress, and prepared statements presented to Congressional Committees. Some question might be raised as to the inclusion of many of the promotional items, since their economic content is often slight. To students of the art of conducting public relations, however, they should be of considerable interest. 3

So far as entries for individual items are concerned, these principles still hold. In some respects, however, the coverage has been considerably extended. An attempt is here made to give summary accounts of the serial literature of OPA together with the official regulations and orders, the press releases, the progress reports, the minutes or verbatim transcripts of meetings, the budget justifications, and the statistical forms. 

It was out of the question to try to list these great masses of literature item by item, but the main types are described with an indication where possible of the quantities issued and the location of accessible copies. 

Individual charts, maps, pictures and posters, separately printed, have been excluded.

Section 10 of the bibliography lists the very considerable number of unpublished studies, narratives and chronologies which have been prepared by or for the Policy Analysis Branch. Most of these focus on 

OPA actions in connection with a particular commodity or group of related commodities; most of the remainder on an organizational unit of the agency, in the national office or a field office. Some, however, are topical or analytical, and a considerable number represent the outlay of much thought and effort. Though they vary greatly in the degree of completeness and reliability which they have attained, these manuscripts cover a wide range of interests and will, if consulted, save future historical investigators a good deal of preliminary study. They have been put together in a separate file in the collection, arranged in the same order as they are listed herein. Each item has been put in a folder, marked for ready reference with the same identifying code number assigned to it in this bibliography. For example, Louis J. Kroeger's manuscript entitled "Administrative Experiences in Rationing," listed here on page 344, has been marked 10B.18 in the file.

Among the duplicated items in the collection on which this bibliography was based are a good many headed, or stamped across the face, "Confidential" or "Restricted" or "For Staff Use Only." Three types of security need to be distinguished here. In the first place, none of these materials were restricted for reasons of "business security." The statutes governing 

OPA gave a confidential status to individual company data on profits, costs and the like obtained by the agency, and criminal and other penalties were prescribed for their disclosure. The materials in question are not of that sort. In the second place, they were not restricted for reasons of "military security". Considerations of espionage and wartime secrecy were not involved. Rather, the materials were restricted at the time they were 3 

Emergency Price Control Act of 1942, as amended, secs. 4(c), 202(b), 205(b); Second War 

Powers Act, title III, par. 4, 56 Stat. 176; Executive Order 9125, 7 F.R. 2719; Federal Reports

Act of 1942, sec. 4(b), 56 Stat. 1078; Second Deficiency Appropriations Act of 1945, OPA 

item No. 4, Pub. Law 132, 79th Cong., 1st Sess.

duplicated to prevent the premature spreading abroad of matters thought to be not then ripe for public discussion, for any of a variety of reasons. 

This is a sort of "executive security." There is no discernible uniform. standard of selection in the items so marked, and personal preferences evidently played a substantial role in the decision in numerous instances. 

The considerations of administrative confidentiality appropriate to an operating agency fade rapidly with the passage of time, especially in the case of an agency that has ceased to exist. Accordingly the Director of the Division of Liquidation, in anticipation of the transfer of this special collection of publications to the National Archives, advised the Archivist of the United States, by letter of July 10, 1947, that "we do not now regard any of these items as confidential after the lapse of six months from the date of their issuance, or after the termination of the operating programs to which they relate. . . With this exception [of certain rent control materials still in effect] when your office takes custody the markings . . . need no longer be regarded as binding."

Users of the first edition were warned that only rarely could extra copies of the items there listed be obtained. This is still more true now, when the agency has been disbanded. It is likely, however, that the collection will be microfilmed. If so, copies of the film will be purchasable. 

A bibliography of this size and scope is inevitably a cooperative enterprise. The annotations taken over from the earlier edition represent the painstaking efforts of Harriet Batterton Osgood, who pioneered the way through a previously uncharted field. The new annotations are chiefly by 

George A. Wood, who has also reviewed the earlier entries and been able in not a few instances to correct them on some points of detail. 

Mabel Randolph has made a very considerable number of annotations herself, has controlled and directed the various parts of the undertaking, and has determined most of the questions, often quite difficult, of the proper classification of the materials. But for her steady persistence through the closing months of the agency's life, the project would not have been completed. Virgil B. Zimmermann has advised on questions of classification and furnished the introductory notes on periodic progress reports, agency policy and procedures, training, economic, technical and legal studies, press releases, and unpublished manuscripts. John H. 

Burchard assembled the budget justifications and key operating reports on personnel, and prepared the accompanying notes. Harvey C. Mansfield supplied the notes on opinions and interpretations, statistical and reporting forms, and transcripts of meetings; and William Jerome Wilson the description of official regulations and orders. The annotations for the unpublished histories and chronologies, many of which posed delicate and puzzling problems of their own, have been prepared by Laurence E. 

Tilley and Carol S. Piper. The general planning of the bibliography has 5

been done by William Jerome Wilson.

His article "Analysis of Govern ment Records: An Emerging Profession," The Library Quarterly, vol. 

xvi, p. 1 (January, 1946) may be profitably consulted by the researcher in OPA archival materials. 

In the listing of individual entries in this bibliography vacant parentheses following the title of the item have been used to indicate that the issuing unit is unknown. Matter in brackets has been supplied by the annotator. After the listings were first set in type a good many items were reclassified. In order to save the printing expense of a complete renumbering, only the items that were moved were renumbered. This accounts for the missing numbers in many sequences and the addition of the letters "a", "b", etc. where entries were inserted between those already consecutively numbered.

1. OFFICIAL REGULATIONS AND ORDERS 

The OPA regulations and orders, with all their justifications, amendments, supplements, and revisions, doubtless constitute the most extensive system of administrative law yet promulgated by any single agency of Government in this country, if not in the world. Though not the sole aim of the agency's existence, they were the means by which its economic purposes were translated into action, and as such they form its most important body of historical records. With these every serious student of OPA history will normally begin. Having familiarized himself with the official regulations and orders, he may then proceed to probe into the reasons and circumstances of their issuance, the economic principles which they exemplify, the organization which created and enforced them, and their results. 

A. OPA Document Series 

For control purposes the official issuances of the agency were numbered in a continuous series, beginning with the first price schedule on February 17, 1941, and closing with No. 59,191 on April 28, 1947. There are very rare gaps, doubtless due to accident or oversight. For example, Documents 26,046-26,049 are completely missing. They are not even recorded on the numerical card index which the agency maintained, from 1941 to 1943 in the office of its Federal Register Attorney and from 

1943 to 1947 in the Office of the OPA Secretary. 

1. Relation to the Federal Register. 

The series was sometimes referred to as the "Federal Register Documents," since the items in it of general interest and applicability were published in the Federal Register, while all other items were filed in certified copies with the Division of the Federal Register at the National Archives. For legal purposes this gave official notice to the parties affected. Most of the items not published in the Register were specific orders or opinions addressed to individual companies, telling them what they might legally charge under existing price regulations or what they might do under existing ration orders. 

After passage of the Emergency Price Control Act of 1942 each price or rent regulation and each amendment thereto was required to be accompanied by a statement of considerations. This statement at first. was given a separate number in the Document Series just after the regulation, order, or amendment to which it applied. Later the statement was included as part of its basic document without any separate number. 

In either case the statement of considerations was not published in the 

Federal Register until 1946 when the Administrative Procedure Act made the printing mandatory. It was regularly printed in the OPA 

Service and in its successor, the Desk Book, just after the basic document.

OPA Bibliography 1A. OPA Document Series (continued) 

For the documents which it published the Division of the Federal Register used its own system of control numbers, which it printed in small type at the end of the text along with the day, hour, and minute of filing. These numbers take the form: "F. R. Doc. 42-7305," in which the "42" indicates the year. The elaborate card index maintained in the Division of the Federal Register took no account of the numbers of the OPA Document Series, but was based on the Register's own numbering system. 

2. Legal Authority of the Series. 

Within the agency the numbers in the OPA Document Series were used merely as a means of keeping track of the endless procession of papers, but they give a significant indication as to the total workload in successive periods. In the table on pp. 12–13 the chronological periods are divided according to the basic legal authority under which OPA or one of its predecessor agencies was operating. At the points of transition there is some uncertainty as to members, since a few days commonly elapsed before the documents ceased to cite the old legal authority and began to cite the new. This will explain the differences between the dates in the second column and those in the fifth.

As might be expected, the beginning and the end of the series show some irregularity. The original organization, the National Defense 

Advisory Commission, was advisory and had only the slightest executive powers, but toward the end of the NDAC period its Price Stabilization Division, anticipating the authority which it had already asked for and which it was to receive in the next stage, issued five price schedules and three amendments. Just before the last period began there was a break of 25 days, July 1-25, 1946, in the legal authority. During that interval no new regulations were promulgated, though some special orders were issued for the purpose of adjusting existing regulations to the circumstances of particular businesses. Several weeks before the end of the final period the issuance of official documents stopped, and the few remaining OPA functions were assigned to other executive departments or agencies.

The continuity of the OPA Document Series was maintained by legal notices issued at the three main points of transition. (1) As soon as 

OPACS was set up, April 11, 1941, its first official action was to announce in the Federal Register that "all price schedules, instructions, announcements, forms and notices" issued by the Price Stabilization Division and Consumer Division of NDAC, as well as all committees, thereby appointed, were ratified and adopted by the new organization. (2) A still greater change the greatest, in fact, in the history of the agencywas marked by the passage of the Emergency Price Control Act on January 30, 1942. This act provided that all price schedules issued 10

OPA Document Series (continued) 14. 

previously by OPACS or by OPA should be effective under the new authority, if they were reprinted in the Federal Register, with all amendments to date, within ten days after the Administrator took office. Accordingly, on February 21, 1942, Price Schedules 1 to 105 were printed as amended, except Nos. 5, 14, 25, 27, 48 and 72, which had already been revoked. (3) During the 25-day break in July 1946 the 

Attorney General of the United States issued a formal opinion to the effect that, while price and rent control had lapsed, the remaining ration orders were still in effect and also that the enforcement activities of the agency might legally continue with respect to previous violations of price and rent regulations.

Ration orders, their amendments, and many specific orders and opinions based on them were inserted in the OPA Document Series along with the price and rent regulations, although they rested on an entirely different legal authority. It is the authority over prices and rents which always seemed basic in the agency and which has determined the successive periods as shown in the table. During the NDAC period there was no thought given to rationing except by a few of the most far-sighted. 

During the OPACS period the agency legally had the power to ration consumer goods but never had occasion to use it. The prestatutory OPA lost the rationing power but regained it in limited degree on December 

14, 1941, by informal delegation from the Office of Production Manage ment. The first ration order, the original Tire Rationing Regulations, was issued on December 30, 1941. On January 24, 1942, by WPB Directive

No. 1 (7 F. R. 562), OPA received from the War Production Board 

(successor to OPM) formal authority to administer consumer rationing, which promptly became the largest of its three major programs. Under the Second War Powers Act of March 27, 1942 (56 Stat. 176), the ṛation ing authority was maintained through all the succeeding periods, including the 25-day hiatus in price and rent control in July 1946. Shortly before the demise of OPA, however, that authority (sugar rationing was all that was left) was transferred by Presidential delegation to the newly created Office of Temporary Controls, and soon afterward, by Congressional directive, to the Department of Agriculture. 

For some details as to the successor agencies of OPA, see pp. 48, 50 and 77 below. The OPA-OTC interlude began on December 12, 1946, but ended differently for different programs. The Sugar Rationing Administration, which also exercised price control over sugar and rice, operated under the Department of Agriculture from March 31 to July 28, 1947. The Office of Rent Control was set up by the Housing 

Expediter on May 2, 1947, and is still continuing in 1948. These successor agencies overlap to such an extent that it does not seem feasible to present them at the end of the table. 11

OPA Bibliography 1B. Available Sources and Indexes B. Available Sources and Indexes 

Although there are abundant materials and excellent tools for the historical investigation of official OPA documents, no one source and no one index is at the same time complete, logically arranged, and readily available. It seems desirable, therefore, to indicate briefly what the main sources and indexes are, together with the scope, the utility, and the limitations of each. 

1. Certified Typewritten Copies. 

With the issuance of the first price schedule early in 1941, the basic system of records was established for controlling the documents of the agency. The first task was to keep track of the typewritten copies of the amendments and new regulations. When a regulation was put in final shape, after much drafting and redrafting and many timeconsuming "clearances" by the operating officials concerned with it, it then came up to the Administrator (or in his absence from the office, to an Acting Administrator designated for the purpose) for approval and promulgation. The initials or signatures of the officers who had passed upon it were shown on a covering "clearance sheet." If the 

Administrator agreed, he signed, either personally or by proxy, an official copy which then went to the Federal Register for record and publication. 

To handle the official documents a Federal Register Liaison Attorney was appointed, whose title was later shortened to Federal Register Attorney. He transmitted the certified typewritten copies to the Division of the Federal Register, and kept a set of duplicates in his own files. 

The Federal Register numbering has been described above. The duplicates retained by OPA were filed according to "document designation" in folders marked "Price Schedule No. 1," "Civilian Allocation Program 

No. 1," etc. Any amendment, correction, supplement, revision, or revocation was kept in the folder of the schedule or other document to which it pertained, or in a folder immediately adjoining. Thus the succession of folders beginning with Price Schedule 13, for example, showed the entire official development of that regulation through all its stages and all its amendments to its final appearance as a 3rd Revised MPR. 

In 1942, with the passage of the Price Control Act and the rapid expansion of the agency, an Office of the OPA Secretary was established and an additional set of duplicate copies of the documents was there maintained. Manifestly this meant some overlapping of effort, and in 

1943 the two offices were merged. For the combined office it seemed best to use the simpler term, OPA Secretary, but the functions performed and the records maintained were for the most part those originated by the Federal Register Liaison Attorney. The Office of the 

OPA Secretary was thereafter continued to the end of the agency, and 14

Available Sources and Indexes (continued) 1B. 

most of its records were finally deposited with the National Archives for safekeeping.

Two sets of certified typewritten copies of the official OPA documents, therefore, are now in the custody of the National Archives. The set deposited day after day with the Division of the Federal Register is there filed away in the order of receipt, the OPA documents being mixed in with documents received from other agencies on the same day. Such an arrangement is obviously not conducive to sustained researches in OPA history. The other set, begun by the Federal Register Liaison 

Attorney and continued by the OPA Secretary, is more suitably arranged for historical study. It is, in fact, a valuable source for investigators who can go to Washington to consult it. The copies of the documents, being usually on thin tissue, are a little difficult to read and to handle, but the information is there in its original official form for those who need it. 

2. Separate Printed Copies. 

Publication of a certified official document in the Federal Register was legal notice to all concerned that it had been put into effect. Nevertheless, for such documents as OPA promulgated, the Federal Register was not a sufficient medium of distribution. Lawyers are accustomed to using it, as are large manufacturing firms with legal staffs, but small businessmen, farmers, and housewives seldom see it and would hardly know how to use it if they did. OPA therefore took many other steps on its own initiative to disseminate knowledge of its issuances. For items of limited circulation it was enough to strike off copies by mimeograph. 

For items of very wide appeal, as the General Maximum Price Regulation or many of the ration orders, it was necessary to print thousands of copies. The multilith served for cases in between. Many copies were printed with a franked label on the back so that they could be folded mechanically and mailed without envelopes to prepared lists of those known to be interested in the matter treated. Even before the agency had developed a regular Information Department, it became the custom to issue a press release explaining the circumstances and significance of each important new regulation, order, or amendment. Usually, the press release and the new issuance were printed together, the release coming first on the page. It is this form of reprinting, with a press release prefixed, which made up most of the copies in the Document Series File. 

A difficult problem, and one never fully solved, was the prompt distribution of new regulations to the regional and district offices and the local boards. All too often the field received its first notification of such matters through the public press or by some other unofficial channels. 

One line of effort to remedy this was a preprinting of the material, after 15

OPA Bibliography IB. Available Sources and Indexes (continued) 

the Administrator had signed it but before the certified copy was filed with the Federal Register. These preprints-"hot copies" they were often called-were handled by the Secretary's Office. In the normal course they were supposed to reach field offices by the time of public release. 

In the early days the Federal Register Attorney's Office served as a central distribution point for copies of regulations, as well as of forms which the regulations prescribed for use. This was the origin of the 

Document Series File. In the course of time, as the production of mimeographs, multiliths, offsets, or reprints increased to enormous bulk, a special Public Distribution Section was set up to handle them. It also handled vast quantities of informational literature and of internal procedures and instructions. But the Public Distribution Section operated under great pressure and on a strictly current basis. It had to unload its racks and files frequently of obsolete and superseded materials and could make no effort to assemble record sets of the documents which it disseminated. It was first in the office of the Federal Register Attorney therefore, and later in the office of the OPA Secretary, also a lawyer, that a continuous file was maintained of the OPA documents in serial order. Here, despite the constant pressure of deadlines, there was more of that perspective and emphasis on orderly records which characterize the legal profession.

Thus the Document Series File, though originally a mere storage file for extra copies, became an important repository, even before the end of the agency, for historical materials. The copies which it contained were of all sorts-reprints, offsets, multiliths, mimeographs, or occasionally photostats or clippings from the Federal Register, but not typescripts. 

If a request was presented, either by mail or in person, for a copy of an early price schedule, it went to the office of the Federal Register Liaison Attorney. If only the title or the PS number was known, this was looked up in the appropriate card index, the official document number was determined, and in the corresponding folder of the Document Series File the desired copy was usually found. Naturally, in a series which rose ultimately to almost 60,000, there were some gaps. An occasional folder was empty. In such a case, if the request was really urgent, it was always possible to look up the document in the file of certified typewritten copies and have another copy made. 

In 1944 the Document Series File became so great, and at the same time the need of filing cabinets throughout the agency was so pressing, that a weeding-out process was undertaken. All regulations and orders of general applicability were retained in the file, but the letter orders and special authorizations addressed to individual firms were taken out, placed in cartons, and stored with the Historical Records Office. That 16

Available Sources and Indexes (continued) 1B. 

office began the assembling of a comprehensive file of the documents, to consist of a single copy of each, arranged in numerical order; but the task was not completed. For historical purposes the weeded-out file from the Secretary's Office may well be more useful than the original file would have been, though of course many of the folders were loaded with dozens of extra copies of the same document. The fate of the cartons of letter orders and special authorizations is not known. 

Still another set of copies of the printed regulations and orders was maintained in ring-binders in the Secretary's Office and is now in the National Archives. This contained only the items of general applicability; the letter orders and special authorizations were not included. In these binders the amendments, supplements, revisions, etc., of each regulation were kept together, so that a rapid historical survey of the material in each separate field is possible. Unfortunately, however, there are a good many gaps, and an investigator using these binders will frequently have to look elsewhere to complete his research. 

3. Loose-Leaf Compilations. 

Almost every operating official in the early days of OPA kept ringbinders with sets of the official documents that especially interested him. Such sets were costly of time and effort and became almost impossible to keep complete. In the summer of 1942 the agency therefore inaugurated the OPA Service, a loose-leaf compilation arranging the official documents in logical groups and indexing them for ready reference. To the lawyers and economists of the agency this proved an indispensable tool. The pages of the initial issue were all dated August 1, 1942, in the lower margin. While this mass of some 3,000 pages was going through the press, another 1,400 pages of amendments and new documents accumulated, and those were issued in what was referred to as the "Zero Release," since its pages carried no date or release number in the lower margin. Subsequent releases, which appeared every two weeks, were numbered serially from 1 up. Each new page carried in its lower margin the number and date of the release to which it belonged. Release No. 1 appeared August 15, 1942. A News Letter accom panying each release called attention to especially significant items. With it went instructions for filing. 

Every important OPA unit soon had a set of "The Service", and sets were also sold commercially by the publishers. Along with the releases containing official documents there were, in the early months, a number of Confidential Releases containing intra-agency instructions and procedures. This material was not included in the sets distributed outside of OPA. After the establishment of the OPA Manual the confidential releases of the OPA Service were discontinued. 17

OPA Bibliography 1B. Available Sources and Indexes (continued) 

Although the compilation of the material was largely done in the Office of the Secretary, OPA always insisted that it was not legally responsible for the work. A private firm did the publishing, and there was thus no infringement on the special prerogative of the Federal Register as the authoritative medium for the dissemination of governmental regulations. The title page of the original issue read: 

OPA Service: Price Control, Rationing, Rent, edited by James A. Pike and 

Henry G. Fischer.-Federal Regulations Publishers, Rochester, N. Y., 1942.

This title page was later revised by the addition of the words: "Managing editor, John W. Willis." The preface was signed by the

Editors at Washington, D. C., August 15, 1942. The News Letters for the original service were numbered from 1 to 223, and ranged in date from August 16, 1942, to December 2, 1944. These, taken as a group, give a valuable summary of the development of the OPA regulations and orders. In the words of the first in the series: 

A News Letter will accompany each semi-weekly release. The Editors have given a good deal of thought to the functions of this letter. It will try to do the following things: (1) Give an up-to-date picture of OPA controls; (2)

Summarize for you the latest important public pronouncements of officials and other responsible sources as to trends and matters under consideration which will affect business in the price, rationing, and rent fields; (3) Furnish helpful leads in the more effective use of your Service; (4) Outline the important developments contained in the current release.

By midsummer of 1944, after the accretions of two years, the work had grown to a bulk of more than 30,000 pages. By reason of its monumental size the number of outside subscribers declined, though agency officials relied on it more and more. The number of volumes varied according to the amount which the filer had seen fit to crowd into a binder, but normally there were about 16. Some effort had been made to subdivide the releases into groups labelled "General," "Price," "Rationing," and "Rent," with the intention that a Price Department official should receive the "General" and the "Price," a Rationing Department official the "General" and the "Rationing," and so on. The effort was only partly successful, but it pointed the way to a radical later change in the construction of the loose-leaf service. On August 10, 1944, the OPA Secretary announced the plans for a complete revision. There was to be a new publication known as the Desk Book. Each user was to be provided with the General Desk Book, which ultimately grew to 4 volumes. He also received the appropriate set of the following 7 

Commodity Desk Books: Building Materials and Paper, which came to fill 2 volumes; Chemicals and Rubber, 2 volumes; Consumer Goods, 3 volumes; Food, 5 volumes; Fuel, 1 volume; Lumber, 2 volumes; 

Metals and Machinery, 3 volumes. These 7 sets were confined to the 18

operations of the Price Department.

In the words of the announcement 

(Press Release OPA-4650): 

The Commodity Desk Books will replace those volumes of the present service containing price and general material. The present volumes dealing with rent control will be continued. It is planned to consolidate the present four volumes containing rationing material into one volume, and to use this volume in conjunction with the loose-leaf rationing service now used by local War Price and Rationing Boards. 

The Commodity Desk Books will not include the former text of regulations now in the present 16-volume service. For reference to this material, which will be more or less of a historical nature, a set will be kept available in each division of the OPA National Office and in each of OPA's Regional and 

District Offices. 

In addition to the general orders, administrative notices, and the like, the General Desk Book gave the successive statutes and Executive orders under which OPA had operated, the State and local laws designed to help enforce its regulations, and Rules 1-30 of the Emergency Court of Appeals. The title page read: 

Pike and Fischer OPA Price Service. General Desk Book, Containing All Material of a General Nature in the Field of OPA Price Control.-Edited by James A. Pike, Henry G. Fischer, and John W. Willis.-Federal Regulations 

Publications, Rochester, N. Y., 1944.

In addition to the General Desk Book, the 7 Price Commodity Desk Books, and the retained sets of the old OPA Service, there was also printed, chiefly for the benefit of the lawyers, a 2314-page bound volume (see below, p. 59) with the following title page:

Opinions and Decisions. Opinions of the Price Administrator and Decisions of the Federal and State Courts on Price Control, Rent Control, Rationing.-OPA, 

Chester Bowles, Administrator.-Prepared under the general direction of

Ervin H. Pollack, Secretary, Office of Price Administration.--Copyright 1944 by Federal Regulations Publishers. 

This bound first volume of the Opinions and Decisions contained all pertinent materials up to date. It was supplemented thereafter by weekly releases in loose-leaf form. These came to fill some 5 volumes, depending on the user's preference in binding. The releases for the Desk Book were numbered from 1 to 100 and ranged in date from January 9, 1945, to February 4, 1947. The accompanying News Letters, however, stopped with No. 97 on December 10, 1946.

The OPA Service, with its continuation in the Desk Books and the Opinions and Decisions, probably forms the most convenient single source for the official documents of the agency. Designed originally as a reference tool for lawyers and operating officials, it is now an historical tool of the highest importance. Its advantages may be summarized as follows: 

19

OPA Bibliography IB. Available Sources and Indexes (continued) 

(1) The materials are grouped topically. This is an extraordinary help. The OPA regulations and orders grew so rapidly that a given industry or commodity group, as a perusal of the subjoined summaries will show, was likely to be covered first by a Maximum Price Regulation, presently by a succession of amendments thereto, then perhaps by a Supplementary Regulation, a Supplementary Order, a General 

Order, a Licensing Order, or some other special rulings. It is helpful to have these brought together in logical groups. (2) There are superb indexes. These also are a great convenience. 

The actual arrangement of the books serves to show the larger groupings of the various regulations, but only by indexes and cross reference can the finer points of interrelationship be brought out. (3) The editors of the work have been particularly careful to give footnote references to the volume and page in the Federal Register at which the original official publication of each item can be found. (4) The footnotes specifically call attention to changes introduced into any regulation or order by means of an amendment. In fact, the editors regularly give both the new wording in the text and the old wording in the footnote. The value of such information to the historian is obvious. (5) When one of the major regulations or orders is revised, the OPA Service adds after the new text a complete reprint of the old text. 

Running titles carefully mark this as "Former Text of the Regulation" (or some equivalent term) to prevent misunderstanding as to its significance. To the present-day investigator the new text and the old are equally historical, but it is a manifest convenience to have them both in juxtaposition. (6) The justifying statements are printed in full. In general OPA officials were anxious to comply with the statutory requirement of statements of considerations, as a means of gaining public support and understanding, and at least until the latter stages tended to err rather on the side of over-full explanations. Hence not only every price regulation but also every amendment thereto was accompanied by a statement of considerations. Some few of these were valueless, being a merely formal compliance with a requirement, but most of them were informative and the best of them were economic briefs of great skill and cogency. The statement of consideration accompanying the General 

Maximum Price Regulation is an outstanding example. Rent regulations were frequently though not always accompanied by a Statement of Reasons. Ration orders were not required by law to carry any supporting statement, but the agency nevertheless usually issued one for each ration 20

Available Sources and Indexes (continued) 1B. 

order and each amendment thereto, naming it a Rationale. All of these justifying statements were printed in the OPA Service and the Desk Book. All orders-general, special etc., except only the ration orders, which really had the status of regulations-carried a justifying "Opinion," though in the case of letter orders this opinion was embodied in the opening paragraphs of the communication. Letter orders were not included in the loose-leaf services. 

The drawbacks of these compilations result mainly from their looseleaf form. The operating utility of this kind of compilation was that it presented the regulations in their current aspect. The filing instructions accompanying each release gave directions as to what pages should be inserted and what pages should be taken out and thrown away. Footnotes might give the former reading of a phrase or sentence, but this would carry the matter back only one stage. Previous changes at that point were shown on pages that had by this time been thrown away. The same was true of revised texts and former texts; if there had been several revisions, the record of the earliest forms would already have been discarded. Such practices were perfectly adjusted to the current needs of a rapidly moving agency. For the later historian they leave something to be desired.

The Historical Records Office at one time undertook to compile a comprehensive or historical set of the OPA Service, but the task was perforce abandoned when about half done. The intention was to file in, as they were issued, all new pages from the distributed releases, while not throwing away any of the old pages. Such a set, if completed, would have filled between 50 and 75 volumes. Its sheer bulk would have made it difficult to use, but it would have assembled in topical order and chronological succession a record of each change made in every regulation and order of general applicability. The partly completed set is now at the Harvard Law Library. 

In addition to "the black service," as it was frequently called from the color of its binding, there was also in OPA "the green service," the proper title of which was War Price and Rationing Board Loose-Leaf Service. This, despite the word "price" in its name, was at first confined to rationing operations, though in 1943, with the establishment of the price panels in the local boards, some material on price control was also included. The Local Board Service, as it was commonly but unofficially known, is entered in section 3 below because it was primarily an instrument of intra-agency instruction. It is also a possible source for the official rationing documents, but these are just as readily available in the appropriate volumes of the OPA Service. It is well to note, however, that for the history of any particular rationing program the Local Board Service has the peculiar advantage of presenting together 21

OPA Bibliography 1B. Available Sources and Indexes (continued) 

both the official documents and the related procedures, forms, and intraagency instructions.

At the desk at which the semi-weekly releases for the Local Board Service were numbered and controlled, a file was meticulously kept of the superseded printed pages. These were arranged in the chronological order of their removal from active status. If the file has been preserved at the moment of present writing its fate has not been determinedit should be of unique value as an historical source. 

In addition to the quasi-official OPA Service, Desk Books, Opinions and Decisions, and Local Board Service there were also a number of purely commercial loose-leaf publications which distributed to their subscribers the up-to-date texts of OPA regulations. The "C.C.H." or

Commerce Clearing House series, for example, gave the price schedules and maximum price regulations in their numerical order. For historical study that arrangement is less convenient than the arrangement by commodity groups. It is doubtful if any of the commercial loose-leaf publications is as useful historically as the OPA Service. 

4. Bound Volumes. 

For the official OPA documents the two sources most commonly available in libraries are the Federal Register and the Code of Federal Regulations. The Register, though issued daily (except Sunday and 

Monday) in pamphlet form, is intended to be bound and is provided with monthly, quarterly, and annual indexes. OPA documents are found from volume 6 (1941) to volume 11 (1946), inclusive. There are two very numerous types, however, that are usually left out of the Register. 

One is the supporting or justifying statement of considerations, or its counterparts, the statement of reasons, the rationale, and the opinion (see above in the discussion of loose-leaf compilations). Until the 

Administrative Procedure Act in 1946 required their publication the Register considered these as outside its intended scope. In 1941, however, when OPA's authority to issue regulations was still a little dubious, its price schedules were introduced with preambles explaining their cause and purpose. These preambles, manifest forerunners of the statement of considerations, were published in full in the Register. With the passage of the price control law, the Register drew the line against publication of the separate statements. Thereafter, until 1946, OPA could only file certified copies with the Division of the Federal Register. 

Another type of document not usually printed was the special order or letter order. Publication in the Register is mandatory for official Federal documents of "general applicability and legal effect." A regulatory agency like OPA had also to deal with thousands of individual cases, but when its decisions or directives were applicable only to individually 22

Available Sources and Indexes (continued) 1B. 

named concerns, notice could be given them directly by mail, making it unnecessary and wasteful to set the whole matter forth in the pages of the Federal Register. As is indicated below in the entries on special orders, on suspension orders, and on adjustment and authorization of prices, OPA started out by printing such specific matters in full, but soon gave it up. Instead, it deposited an official copy of each individual order with the Division of the Federal Register, in the National Archives building, and contented itself thereafter with publishing lists in the Register giving the dates and the names of the recipients of such orders. 

Later, letter orders were merely deposited with the OPA Secretary, where they were open to public inspection. In a twilight zone-between such orders, which had the force of law, and official interpretations (see below under Interpretations; see also Problems in Price Control: Legal 

Phases, pp. 66-72, 104), which were provided for in Procedural Regulation 1, though also not published in the Register-were a class of unrecorded interpretative letters of doubtful legal standing. Some price branches, operating under general regulations stipulating "in-line" prices for new models, were understaffed and impatient of the delays in preparing formal documents for clearance. They developed the practice of writing letters over the signature of the price executive or section chief, simply informing an inquirer that the office construed an in-line price for his new model to be so much. Presumably such letters usually served the substantive purposes of both parties, but they were binding on no one and could be acutely embarrassing in later litigation. Instances of this sort led to a tightening of procedures requiring that all documents purporting to authorize specific prices be cleared and recorded. 

The Code of Federal Regulations and its supplements codify under 50 titles the regulations issued by Federal agencies. The Cumulative 

Supplement covered the regulations promulgated from June 2, 1938, to June 1, 1943. What was known as the 1943 Supplement covered the remainder of 1943. Later Supplements covered, respectively, the issuances of the calendar years 1944, 1945, and 1946. 

There was an earlier Supplement, covering the publications of the year 1941 but not itself published until 1943. This showed what the Code of 

Federal Regulations might conceivably have done for OPA in less strenuous times. Omitting the preambles, it reprinted the text of the first 

63 price schedules, the 30 civilian allocation programs, and the original 

Tire Rationing Regulations of December 30, 1941 (1941 Supplement, Book 3, pp. 3102-3336). It also provided tables which served as a topical index to the reprinted material (Book 4, pp. 4756-4759). Any price schedules or civilian allocation programs, however, that by December 31, 1941, had already expired or been revoked were not reprinted. They were 23

OPA Bibliography 1B. Available Sources and Indexes (continued) 

merely listed, with page references to the Federal Register publication and with mention of the terminal date. The documents that were reprinted were arranged topically according to the predetermined scheme of codification by parts and sections, as indicated by numbers in the 

Register. The OPA material began with Part 1301 on Machine Tools and closed with Part 1358 on Tobaccos.

The 1941 Supplement shows several of the basic ideas that went into the construction of the loose-leaf OPA Service. The material is arranged topically. There is a subject index. Superseded material is recorded but not reprinted. Only what is current at the end of 1941 is actually presented, so that the picture is accurate only as of December 31, 1941, though the added references make possible a survey of the history of the agency's official actions throughout the whole year. In leisurely times this might have served the lawyers and businessmen as a means of ready reference to OPA material, but it could not meet the pace and pressure of the war emergency. It was not sufficient to have an annual presentation issued more than a year after the events. By its loose-leaf arrangement the 

OPA Service gave a picture of the changing conditions at intervals of two weeks.

Later Supplements took account of the realities of the war years. 

They gave up the effort to reprint everything issued by the Board of Economic Warfare, the War Production Board, and the dozens of other agencies. From the OPA output the Code thereafter picked out for republication only the procedural regulations. These were chiefly concerned with telling how an aggrieved businessman should go about it if he desired to lodge a formal protest against the controls to which he was subjected, or if he wished to ask that they be amended or adjusted in his favor. They dealt also with suspension of the right to do business and with the conduct of hearings on such matters. Each later Supplement also provided valuable and extraordinarily reliable tabulations of the titles of the price regulations, rent regulations, ration orders, etc., issued in its assigned period, together with all amendments, supplements, revisions, and the like for each regulation or order listed (32 C.F.R., Cum. Supp., Book 6, pp. 9371-9405; 1943 Supp., Book 3, pp. 15241544; 1944 Supp., Book 2, pp. 2808-2833; 1945 Supp., Book 3, pp. 

3400-3425; 1946 Supp., Book 4, pp. 4951-4974). For every item are also given the date of issuance and the Federal Register citation. Thus, with the Code, a set of the Register, and a good supply of patience one can trace the full development of almost any important OPA regulation or order.

As a rule the special orders and letter orders are not treated in the Code, which, in the words of its subtitle, is "a codification of documents 24

Price Control Documents 1C. 

of general applicability and legal effect issued by Federal agencies and filed with the Division of the Federal Register." As is noted below, however, in the entry on Adjustment or Authorization of Prices, the 

Code (1943 Supp., pp. 2406, 2430-2436) made some attempt to tabulate special orders but did not carry this on after 1943. See also the entry on 

Regional, State, and District Office Orders for the beginnings of a tabulation of those documents (1943 Supp., pp. 2407-2429). Anyone desiring to study the great mass of letter orders may consult at the National Archives the official files of the typewritten duplicates of these documents as they were preserved for record in the Secretary's Office. 

These are filed numerically by the regulation, order, or section thereof under which they were issued. The following are the basic documents: 

MPR (or RPS) 1–611; GO 68; FPR 1-2 and 6; GMPR; SR 1-15 (with gaps, since some of the supplementary regulations did not lend themselves to the issuance of letter orders); Supplementary Storage 

Regulations; Restaurant MPR 2; MIPR.

The Code gave no heed to such supporting documents as the statements of considerations, rationales, and the like. These, at least for documents of general applicability, may be found in the loose-leaf services, unless in any given case the regulation desired has already been superseded and the pages in question have been thrown out. They may also be found in the Document Series File, except for the opinions accompanying individual orders that were weeded out in 1944. Any systematic and thorough investigator of all the supporting documents will evidently be thrown back upon the certified typewritten copies deposited at the National Archives. 

1. Price Schedule.

C. Price Control Documents Series, Nos. 1-105. February 17, 1941-February 10, 1942. 

Under this title the Price Stabilization Division of NDAC inaugurated the series later known as Maximum Price Regulations. For notes on the price schedules see the introductory part of the next entry. No. 105, February 10, 1942 (7 F.R. 954), was the last price schedule to be issued by the prestatutory OPA under the President's authority as delegated by Executive orders. 

2. Maximum Price Regulation.

Series, Nos. 1-615. February 17, 1941-September 23, 1946. 

This monumental series, the most significant among the OPA official documents, was also the oldest in point of time. It originated as a succession of price schedules, 105 in number, antedating the Price Control Act of 1942, the first 5 even antedating OPA itself. American business firms had frequently called their published lists of prices "price schedules," and early in 1941 the Price Stabilization Division of NDAC adopted the term for its own use. Finding second-hand machine tools to be selling for as much as double the price of new ones, it issued Price Schedule 

No. 1 (6 F.R. 1021) with a list of what it declared to be "reasonable limitations on prices for second-hand machine tools." Each limitation, adjusted for the age and condition of the tool, was stated in terms of a percentage of the current list price of an equivalent new tool. Weekly reports of inventory and monthly reports of purchases and sales were required of dealers in second-hand tools, and the Price Stabilization Division promised to use the weapon of publicity against any seller who exceeded the prescribed limitations. 25

Under existing authority no penalty except publicity seemed to be available, since the National Defense Advisory Commission was by definition a consultative body with only a few and very limited executive powers. Toward the end of 1940, however, there was considerable agitation to give some of the divisions of NDAC an active responsibility for directing parts of the rearmament program. The 

Divisions of Industrial Production and of Industrial Materials led the way. By 

Executive order they were reconstituted as an independent Office of Production Management on January 7, 1941. About the same time an Executive order was drafted to reconstitute the Divisions of Price Stabilization and of Consumer Protection as an Office of Price Administration. But the order was not issued until April. Price Schedule No. 1, therefore, on February 17, 1941, anticipated by nearly two months the formal authority on which it should have rested. (See 

The Beginnings of OPA, in this series.) 

Nevertheless, with such authority as it could muster, the Price Stabilization Division of NDAC issued a total of 8 official documents. Five were price schedules, numbered 1-5. The rest were amendments, not separately numbered. The serial numbering of OPA amendments began much later, with Amendment 2 to PS 19, on November 19, 1941 (6 F.R. 5876). Before that time amendments had been referred to, often awkwardly, by their subject and their date of issuance. 

OPACS was responsible for 20 additional schedules, Nos. 6-25, with 21 amendments, supplements, corrections, and revocations. There was also a special notice on April 15, 1941 (6 F.R. 1965), stating that OPACS was adopting as its own the schedules of its predecessor, the Price Stabilization Division. This notice is what OPA later chose to regard as its Administrative Order A and still later as General Order No. 1 (see below). No. 25, it may be noted, was not designated as a price schedule, but merely as "Schedule 25" (6 F.R. 4491). It dealt with a commodity group, namely, fats and oils and their products, but it did not directly concern itself with their prices. It forbade certain speculative practices in the trade, including forward sales for delivery at a date more than 45 days in the future. 

Subsequent direct regulation of the prices of fats and oils made Schedule 25 unnecessary and it was revoked February 23, 1942 (7 F.R. 1496). Until the Margin

Requirement Regulation in 1946, no other OPA regulation was aimed primarily at speculative practices, as distinguished from prices. 

The period of the prestatutory OPA saw the issuance of 80 further price schedules, Nos. 26-105, with 158 amendments, corrections, and revocations. The

Emergency Price Control Act, signed January 30, 1942, provided that the existing price schedules of OPACS or OPA should be effective under the new authority if reprinted in the Federal Register, with all amendments to date, within 10 days after the Administrator officially took office. Accordingly, on February 21, 1942 (7 

F.R. 1202-1342) Price Schedules 1-105 were printed as amended, except Nos. 5, 14, 27, and 48, which had been revoked, and No. 25, which was on the point of being revoked (7 F.R. 1496). When reprinted, they were all designated as "Revised

Price Schedules" (commonly abbreviated to RPS). The order for the reprinting (7 F.R. 1201) was later regarded as Administrative Order B and still later as 

General Order 2 (see below). Though all the reprints bore the heading of "Revised 

Price Schedule," about a third of them, including Nos. 22, 23, 34, 54, 61, 67, 68, 71–74, 76, 78, 82, 85, 89, 91, 92, 96, and 98–105, had not up to that time had any amendment, and the agency subsequently saw fit to refer to them merely as "price schedules" unless and until a revision became necessary. A few were never revised at all, but carried their original designations and numbers until revoked. 

After this mass reprinting, in recognition of the terminology used in the new act, additions to the series were called Maximum Price Regulations. The numbers were continuous. The first of the reconstituted series, MPR 106, regulating domestic shorn wool, was issued February 28, 1942 (7 F.R. 1648). After this any PS or RPS, if it needed more extensive changes than an amendment or a supplement could conveniently carry, was issued in revised form as an MPR, but still with the original number. For any numbers from 1 to 105, therefore, an MPR designation really indicates a revision. A subsequent revision, if required, became a Revised 

Maximum Price Regulation (RMPŘ). There were also cases of a Second and in very rare instances even a Third Revised MPR.

The best example is PS 13, regulating prices of Douglas fir logs and plywood. 

This ran through the whole gamut from PS to 3d RMPR, as indicated below. 

Amendments to any stage of the progression were numbered separately from 1 up. 26

In outline the history of the regulation, with the successive titles, is as follows: 

PS 13, "Douglas Fir Peeler Logs and Douglas Fir Plywood." August 1, 1941 (6 F.R. 3865) 

RPS 13, "Douglas Fir Plywood," February 21, 1942 (7 F.R. 1235) 

MPR 13, "Douglas Fir Plywood," July 20, 1942 (7 F.R. 5567) 

RMPR 13, "Douglas Fir Plywood," November 30, 1942 (7 F.R. 10017) 

2d RMPR 13, "Douglas Fir Plywood," September 21, 1943 (8 F.R. 12887) 

3d RMPR 13, "Douglas Fir and Other Softwood Plywood," July 30, 1945 (10 F.R. 9460)

On the other hand, PS 6, one of the most important schedules ever devised and the first official issuance of OPACS, had a simpler career. It was promulgated on 

April 16, 1941 (6 F.R. 1767), "to stem a threatened general increase in steel prices."

It was included in the mass reprinting of February 21, 1942 (7 F.R. 1215) and continued thereafter as RPS 6 to the end of the price control program. It was amended 18 times, but never so drastically as to need redesignation as an MPR. Even the 

RPS rewriting was designed merely "to eliminate certain ambiguities and minor errors." PS 6 from the start had accepted implicitly the steel industry's own system of price determination, including the multiple basing points, price leadership, and "extras.' Its long and relatively uneventful career illustrates one of the basic lessons which OPA learned, namely, that governmental price controls fitted most easily in an industry already highly organized, with prices customarily uniform. 

In this regard, steel and lumber stood at opposite ends of the scale, and the difference is reflected in the vicissitudes of PS 13 as compared with PS 6. 

In addition to the formal revisions it was a regular practice, after a considerable number of amendments, say 10 or 20, to reprint an MPR or RMPR, codifying all amendments to date. This was called a collation. It and the practice of revision were conveniences to the field offices and the trade, saving them the necessity of searching files of documents, not always complete, to make sure of the up-to-date language of a regulation when an inquiry arose. 

Nos. 1-119 in the PS-MPR series, down to April 23, 1942, were based on the selective principle of price control. (See Problems of Price Control: Pricing 

Techniques, in this series.) Each regulation dealt, that is to say, with a separate commodity or commodity group_in which prices were rising or threatening to rise in an inflationary manner. For the most part the early schedules sought to control raw materials prices, partly on the theory that if the charges of manufacturers and other producers could be stabilized, wholesalers' and retailers' prices would more or less stay in line, and partly because the office had no effective means of reaching the distributive trades at that time. But before the act of January 

30, 1942, became law, it was already apparent that the selective method of control would not long suffice. Inflation was imminent on a wide scale. Within three months after the passage of the act, therefore, the agency imposed an "over-all price ceiling" on April 28, 1942 (6 F.R. 3153). This froze a large part of the price structure throughout the Nation, including especially the prices of retailers, at the highest rates which had been charged during March 1942. There were a few specific exceptions, but in general it aimed to take in every price and pricing practice, not yet controlled, which was subject to the agency's authority. The regulation might with entire propriety have been entered in the numbered series as MPR 120, but actually it was set somewhat apart, out of deference to its vast scope and critical significance. It carried no number but was simply called the 

General Maximum Price Regulation. 

GMPR, or "General Max" as it was familiarly known, received 67 amendments. 

It also developed an important subsidiary series of Supplementary Regulations, and these became a model for modifications of the same sort attached to other sweeping regulations. On June 23, 1942, when the regulation of the service trades was segregated from the rest of the GMPR operation, a numbered regulation, MPR 165, was issued for the purpose (7 F.R. 4734). This developed a subsidiary series of its own, the Supplementary Service Regulations. As the GMPR base-period of March 1942 receded into the past, it became increasingly difficult, especially in commodity areas where items and styles changed frequently, to apply or enforce ceilings based on that norm. On March 20, 1945, therefore, MPR 580 was issued (10 F.R. 3015), taking March 19, 1945, as a new "base date" and requiring dealers in many categories of apparel and home furnishings to file "pricing charts" showing their invoice costs and prices at that time. This led to a subsidiary series of General 27

OPA Bibliography 

Retail Orders. A little later, on May 21, 1945, MPR 586 was issued (10 F.R. 

5797), gathering together out of GMPR, MPR 165, and elsewhere the regulations covering charges for storage and terminal facilities. From this developed the 

Supplementary Storage Regulations. See the separate entries below for these various subsidiary series.

GMPR was not the only regulation judged important enough to stand without a number. A few days earlier the agency issued an unnumbered Maximum Export 

Price Regulation (MEPR), which GMPR promptly incorporated by reference. 

Goods entering the country from abroad also furnished special pricing_problems. 

For more than a year import prices were controlled under Supplementary Regulation 12 to GMPR, but on August 20, 1943, a separate Maximum Import Price Regulation (MIPR) was issued. Hawaii was still another special case. For some months after the attack on Pearl Harbor the Military Governor of the Territory enforced his own system of price control and rationing, but by April 20, 1943, the situation had become sufficiently stable to permit the extension of the General Maximum 

Price Regulation to the Islands (8 F.R. 5307). On the MEPR, the MIPR, and the GMPR for Hawaii, see the separate entries below.

For various reasons the General Maximum Price Regulation, in spite of its name, was not universal in scope. The basic reason was the belief, nearly though not quite unanimously held, that any attempt at a complete economic freeze such as Bernard Baruch advocated would prove politically and administratively unworkable. Thus, GMPR did not cover wages. When the price bill was under discussion, the agency's representatives consistently asked that the control of wages be entrusted to other hands. At the same time the farm interests succeeded in writing into the bill, against the agency's protest, pricing standards for agricultural commodities which practically excluded them from effective price control. During the hearings on the bill the fishing industry successfully argued that its problems were enough like those of farming to receive a similar exemption. It was also decided by Congress, and not contested by OPA, that public utility and transportation charges, rates for insurance, and fees for professional services should be exempted. Further statutory exemptions included publications, broadcasting, theatres, and advertising. The exemption of these mass media of public information no doubt facilitated passage of the bill. 

The text of GMPR, in sections 1499.9, and 1499.10, presents two long and at times intricately worded lists of exemptions to the operation. Many are a simple repetition of the statutory exemptions. Others, such as postage stamps and coins, art objects, antiques, and the like, were excepted on the agency's own responsibility, as not amenable to that form of control or not worth the effort of regulation. One excepted item consisted of the single word "Securities," italicized for emphasis. 

The exclusion of used automobiles was the result of a last-minute plea to the Administrator. Wages, though not mentioned by that name, were entered in the list of exceptions as "services of an employee to his employer." Rents were excluded by the basic definition of GMPR, which was limited to the prices of commodities and services. Rent regulation was explicitly authorized by the price control act, but it was handled separately. The maximum rent regulations (see below) were never regarded as a part of the PS-MPR series. 

In general these and other exceptions, however they may have originated, were intended to pare the GMPR down to manageable proportions. But the food exemptions stood on a different footing. Here the agency wanted more authority than it was given, arguing that all food prices needed regulating, since they enter so significantly into the daily cost of living. GMPR in this area accepted such restrictions as it had to, but no more. It made an exception for "any raw and unprocessed agricultural commodity," but immediately limited the exception by adding, "while it remains in substantially its original state." In the face of rising prices at the farm, OPA hoped that the control of processed food prices would cause the processors and middlemen to exert a restraining influence on their costs. In the case of restaurant prices, however, no immediate attempt to secure the absorption of increased cost seemed feasible, and these were therefore explicitly excluded from the operation of GMPR. Not until after the Stabilization Act on Octber 2, 1942, amended the original statute, did the agency make an effective start toward controlling most food prices.

Selective price control did not stop, then, with the promulgation of GMPR. It went on with as much speed as circumstances, administrative, legal and political, permitted. The "over-all ceiling" was not viewed as a permanent substitute for 28

selective controls, but as a huge temporary fortification behind which more refined and specialized operations could be made ready. By April 1942 the existing PS- 

MPR series covered a little less than half of the dollar value of all commodities at wholesale. In the next five months 112 additional MPR's were issued, about 20 of them appearing simultaneously with GMPR itself. Relatively few dealt with raw materials, the prices of which had already been fairly well covered in previous periods. Down to October 2, 1942, the greatest new advances were in the field of manufactured goods, of foods beyond the farm stage, and of such retail services as laundries and automobile repair. There were also special regulations for Puerto 

Rico (MPR 183), Alaska (MPR 194), and the Virgin Islands (MPR 201). 

The process of refinement and extension of GMPR was nowhere better illustrated than in the case of MPR 188, issued July 30, 1942 (7 F.R. 5872), covering manufacturers' prices of consumers durable goods and, until a late stage, building materials an array of hundreds of industries and thousands of commodities. MPR 

188 replaced section 3 (b) of GMPR, a catch-all which recognized the impracticality of applying the GMPR pricing rules to producers in areas where, as with apparel and restaurants, the problems of new and changed types of goods were crucial. Starting with a succession of pricing rules to be used in turn if applicable, MPR 188 itself wound up with a catch-all (section 158) requiring that individual orders specifying prices, sometimes including resale prices, should be issued for particular articles in cases otherwise unprovided for; and it also later authorized (section 159b) general orders modifying the pricing rules for particular commodities. Orders of the former type, unless they set resale prices, were ordinarily "Letter-orders," not printed in the Federal Register; and authority to issue them was later delegated to field offices as well. (See A. Moore Lifter, "Pricing by 

Specific Authorization," in Problems in Price Control: Pricing Techniques.) 

Under the broad aegis of MPR 188, consequently, thousands of orders were issued, mostly to individual firms and covering the ephemeral output of transient new producers. A few of them established cost-plus pricing formulas for named firms. Some, e. g., Order 1509 under MPR 188, on upholstered sofa beds, issued 

April 17, 1944 (9 F.R. 4262), set up entire structures of dollars-and-cents prices for manufacturers of a commodity, including resale prices that would, if changes in manufacturers' prices had not been involved, have appeared as an amendment of SR 14 to GMPR. Such an order might in turn authorize a new series of subsidiary orders making individual modifications in the prices so fixed and be for all practical purposes the equivalent of a new MPR.
