Again, some orders made industry-wide price adjustments in response to rising costs, like Order 1052 under 

MPR 188 on furniture, issued December 17, 1943 (8 F.R. 17012). Others stated the conditions under which individual adjustments would be made (2nd Rev. Order 

A-3, 9 F.R. 4038, and orders thereunder), or relaxed the pricing methods for new small manufacturers (Order 4332, 10 F.R. 11017). In a real sense MPR 188 was an omnibus of price control techniques.

After the passage of the Stabilization Act there was a great outburst of activity on agricultural prices at all stages of production and distribution. From October 2, 1942 to June 30, 1943, about 40% of the new MPR's (67 out of a total of 166) dealt with food, beverages, feeds, and tobacco; from June 30 to December 31, 1943, about 21% (43 out of 204); during all of 1944, about 23% (19 out of 81); during 

1945, about 28% (10 out of 36); and during 1946, about 36% (4 out of 11). But these figures are far from indicating the intense preoccupation of OPA with food problems, especially in 1943. That year saw the development of the restaurant maximum price regulations, issued partly by the national office and partly by the regions, and the community ceiling price lists, issued by State or district offices on food items sold at retail. Among the many other regional, State, and district orders setting maximum prices by areas, the commonest subjects, aside from fuel, were fluid milk and vegetables. By 1944 a codification of some of the food pricing rules was attempted, resulting in the food products regulations. On these various series see the separate entries below.

It would be mistakenly naive to think of the price regulations as needing only to be placed on the books and allowed thereafter to operate unchanged. Tremendous shifts were taking place in the industrial activities of the country, and businessmen found their costs, volume, and profits often changing week by week if not day by day. 

Under such circumstances only a flexible system of controls could hope to succeed. 

The perennial problem was to adjust and adapt without yielding on the funda- 29

mental principles of stabilization. (See Problems in Price Control: Pricing 

Standards, in this series.)

There were two principal methods by which OPA sought to conform its price regulations to the demands of a war economy and to the needs of the business community. One was to alter the rules themselves by means of general amendments. 

The other was to grant special "adjustments" to individual companies. (See Problems in Price Control: Legal Phases, Pt. II, in this series). The individual adjustments of allowable maximum prices naturally were almost always upward. No case is known in which an individual firm asked to have its legal maximum reduced, and OPA had only limited facilities for the investigation and follow-up needed to compel individual reductions. In the series of procedural regulations (see the separate entry below) No. 1 provided a systematic procedure by which either an amendment or an adjustment to an MPR might be formally requested. 

Hundreds of both were issued, the adjustments proving an especially burdensome task in the months immediately following the issuance of GMPR and again after the middle of 1945. The amendments were all published in full in the Federal 

Register (for the most convenient listing see 32 C.F.R., Cum. Supp., pp. 93739397; 1943 Supp., pp. 1525–1538; 1944 Supp., pp. 2809–2827; 1945 Supp., pp. 34023418; 1946 Supp., pp. 4952–4967).

A requested adjustment was granted or denied by means of a special order, and at first_these also were published in full, but the quantity soon became overwhelming. The annual index of the Federal Register for 1942, under "Special authorizations, exceptions, etc.," gives approximately 1200 separate items. In July 

1943 it was decided merely to file certified copies of them with the Division of the Federal Register and publish a list of the titles (8 F.R. 9310, beginning with a list filed July 5 of the orders filed July 2). For a table of 77 of the lists, see 32 C.F.R., 1943 Supp., pp. 2406-2407, covering the period from July to December 1943 (this tabulation not continued in later supplements). In addition to the lists, many of the more important orders were still published in full. The adjustment orders were numbered serially under the MPR on the authority of which they were issued. 

Under many regulations the special orders ran into the hundreds, but in such cases as GMPR or MPR 188 they ran into the thousands. The end of price control on all commodities except sugar and rice halted the flow. The last "Adjustment of Maximum Prices," not published until November 28 but effective November 8, 1946, was designated as "Region II Order G-11 Under MPR 592, Amdt. 1" (11 F.R. 

13937). The only practical effect of such retroactive individual adjustments was usually to quash pending enforcement proceedings.

GMPR recognized several different situations in which special prices might be allowed. When therefore an order was issued under that regulation, it was necessary to specify the exact section on which it rested. The references were often abbreviated. Since all sections of GMPR, according to the official codification, had numbers beginning with "1499," it was easy and common to omit the "1499" altogether. Thus, "Order 324 under 18 (a)" meant the 324th special order issued under the authority of section 1499.18 (a) of GMPR. This was a section allowing a retailer, on a showing of hardship, to seek an upward adjustment in case his maximum price, as determined by what he had charged in the base-period, was "abnormally low in relation to the maximum prices of the same or similar commodities or services established for other sellers at retail." Closely related in technique to the adjustment of prices was the approval by the agency, on application, of prices requested by a seller under a regulation forbidding sales of new goods until ceilings had been so established. When the regulation itself prescribed a formula for the determination, a simple notice of approval, or the waiting of a stated period, usually 15 days, without notice of disapproval, was enough. Where no formula was given in the regulation a formal order was required, but this was presently simplified to a "letter-order" if it did not purport to fix a ceiling for anyone but the addressee; otherwise a formal order in the Federal Register was legally necessary. For example, section 1499.3 (b) provided for orders determining maximum prices for manufacturers of articles that had not been sold during the base-period. The manufacturer was required before selling to apply to 

OPA for a specific price authorization. In the parlance of the agency, this was "3 (b) pricing." Most of the special orders under GMPR, MPR 165 and MPR 

188 were called "Adjustment of Maximum Prices" or "Authorization of Maximum

Prices." Under section 3 (a) a retail dealer in similar circumstances was given a pricing formula and merely required to file the price he so determined. 30

Price Control Documents (continued) 1C. 

After the issuance of GMPR, it was the avowed policy of the agency to take the commodity and service areas, one after another, out from under that regulation and subject them if possible to straight dollars-and-cents pricing. If that was impossible, some formula was sought, usually in the nature of a percentage or fixed mark-up. The rate at which new areas were brought under these more definite types of control may be roughly gauged by the new MPR's that were issued: 

175 from April 28 to the end of 1942; 310 in 1943; 81 in 1944; 36 in 1945; 11 in 

1946. Only two new MPR's were issued after the hiatus in price control in July 

1946. By that time the vast majority of the country's transactions in goods and services had been brought at least formally under price control. 

After this hiatus_various relaxations in pricing standards were enforced upon the agency by the Price Control Extension Act of 1946, and these were put into effect chiefly by amendment to existing MPR's. For such purposes the device of the Supplementary Order was especially useful. For notes on this closing stage in the price program, and on its virtual termination by SO 193 on November 12, 1946, (11 F.R. 13464) see the separate entry for Supplementary Orders below. 

Although MPR 615 on specified candy items, issued September 23, 1946 (11 F.R. 

10758), was the last of its series, the agency had prepared No. 616 and was on the point of issuing it when the program of price control ceased. 

3. Temporary Maximum Price Regulation. 

Series, Nos. 1-37. February 21, 1942-February 19, 1945. 

The Emergency Price Control Act of 1942 authorized OPA to issue a temporary maximum price regulation, without warning and without an accompanying statement of considerations, when circumstances called for immediate imposition of some sort of control. This authority recognized, what the agency's experience in 

1941 had shown, that considerable time might be required for the surveys and consultations needed to formulate a satisfactory regulation not of the "freeze" type. According to the statute, a TMPR might remain in effect for only 60 days. 

By that time if it had not already been replaced by a regulation in permanent form, it lapsed. Its technique was to freeze prices at the levels prevailing during the 5 days preceding its issuance. Ordinarily it was frankly a stop-gap measure. 

TMPR 1, covering the prices of mixed fertilizer, was issued on the day of the mass reprinting of the Revised Price Schedules, February 21, 1942 (7 F.R. 1496).

It was replaced on April 28, 1942, by MPR 135 (7 F.R. 3187). It was the first of a group issued that spring in anticipation of full-fledged regulations then being worked on. Others were shortly added to the list. For example, on March 

12, 1942, used typewriters were put under rationing by means of Rationing Order 4, and maximum prices for used typewriters were fixed the same day by TMPR 9 (7 F.R. 2002). On June 11, 1942, the temporary regulation was replaced by 

MPR 162 (7 F.R. 4484); this was a case where more than 60 days were required to develop the detailed dollars-and-cents ceilings it contained. GMPR, issued 

April 28, 1942, brought under its control the commodities covered by 7 existing TMPR's, and on that date was therefore issued a revocation of those 7 by means of SO 4 (see the entry below on supplementary orders). The President's directive under the Stabilization Act of 1942, approved on October 2, was the signal for the issuance of another group of TMPR's extending food price controls. 

The TMPR's naturally became rarer as the agency developed. There were 24 in 1942, 10 in 1943, 2 in 1944, 1 in 1945, and none in 1946. TMPR 37, the last of its line, covering the prices of hogs and pork in Puerto Rico, was issued February 19, 

4. General Maximum Price Regulation. 

April 28, 1942.

This, the most important and far-reaching price document ever issued by OPA (6 F.R. 3153), was not numbered in the MPR series, though it logically might have been. For notes on its form and significance, see above in the entry for maximum price regulations. 

5. Maximum Export Price Regulation. 

April 25, 1942.

The Export Control Schedules issued in 1941 by the the Administrator of Export Control (6 F.R. 1536, etc.) were more concerned with the flow of goods than with their price. But on April 25, 1942, a Maximum Export Price Regulation (often known as MEPR) was formally issued by OPA (7 F.R. 3096). For a 31

manufacturer or producer this fixed the export ceiling price as his maximum domestic price plus premiums for certain services and functions if performed and further premiums for war risk insurance, shipping charges, and the like. For a wholesaler, jobber, or other middleman it fixed the export ceiling as his cost of acquisition plus a similar set of premiums. The penalties, suits for treble damage, and other enforcement procedures authorized by the recently passed Emergency Price Control Act of 1942 were made applicable to exporters violating MEPR. 

Exceptions to its operation were to be made in special cases certified by the 

Board of Economic Warfare. (See unpublished Ms., S. E. Harris, Price Control of

International Commodities, item 10S.5 in this bibliography). 

The provisions of MEPR were incorporated by reference in the General Maximum 

Price Regulation on April 28, 1942 (7 F.R. 3154, sec. 1499.6). MEPR was amended 

3 times, the revision of July 2, 1942 (7 F.R. 5059) 5 times, the second revision of 

March 30, 1943 (8 F.R. 4132) 23 times, and the third revision of August 20, 1946 (11 F.R. 9069) 3 times, the last being on October 21, 1946 (11 F.R. 12356). 

6. Maximum Import Price Regulation. 

Aug. 20, 1943.

Although the General Maximum Price Regulation was of nearly universal applicability, some exceptions were made from the start and by Amendment 1 to Supplementary Regulation 4, on May 25, 1942 (7 F.R. 3942), imported commodities were added to the excepted list. By June 19, 1942, SR 12 to GMPR (7 F.R. 4661) had been prepared, establishing controls over the prices of imports. On August 20, 1943, the revised and amended SR 12 was revoked as such and was redesignated as the Maximum Import Price Regulation (8 F.R. 11681). MIPR was amended 

9 times, and the revision of March 18, 1946 (11 F.R. 2827) was amended 3 times, the last being on July 31, 1946 (11 F.R. 8360). 

7. General Maximum Price Regulation For Hawaii. 

April 20, 1943. 

The original General Maximum Price Regulation of April 28, 1942, was declared applicable to the territories and possessions of the United States, but 

Supplementary Regulation 5, issued May 16, 1942 (7 F.R. 3723), postponed the effective date in Hawaii to June 18, 1942. On May 29, 1942, the Military

Governor of Hawaii issued his General Maximum Price Regulation No. 1, to become effective June 18, 1942. For nearly a year thereafter_OPA_exercised no jurisdiction in that territory. On June 25, 1942, by Supplementary Regulation 

13 (7 F.R. 4798), the operation of GMPR was extended to Puerto Rico and the 

Virgin Islands, though the base-period was changed from the month of March to the period of April 10-May 10, 1942. On the same day was issued PR 7 (7 F.R. 

4779) prescribing rules for applications for adjustment of maximum prices in any of the territories or possessions. 

The following spring, when OPA's General Maximum Price Regulation was extended to Hawaii, it was not regarded as in substance a new control, but merely as a formalization of what was already in effect under the Office of the Military Governor. He relinquished to OPA his authority over prices on 

March 10, 1943, and OPA on the same date issued its General Order 49 (8 F.R. 

3076) adopting all of his price and rationing regulations and orders. The way was now clear to apply GMPR to Hawaii by means of a supplementary regulation, as had been done for Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands, but in the circumstances this seemed inadequate. Instead there was issued a separate General Maximum 

Price Regulation for the Territory of Hawaii (8 F.R. 5307). This was modeled on the original GMPR, but established as a base-period the month of April instead of March 1942. There were the same lists of exceptions and the same provisions for amendment, adjustment, and "Section 3 pricing." On the same date was issued 

SO 44 (8 F.R. 5305) with a list of 10 RPS's and 36 MPR's applicable in Hawaii, all other price regulations being declared inapplicable.

The Hawaii GMPR received 7 amendments and 2 supplements, and also developed a small series of supplementary regulations (see the separate entry below). 

8. Supplementary Regulation Under GMPR. 

Series, Nos. 1–15. April 28,-November 2, 1942. 

When the two lists of exceptions to the General Maximum Price Regulation were printed in sections 1499.9 and 1499.10, it was forecast at the end of 32

Price Control Documents (continued) 1C. 

both that further exceptions might be announced in supplementary regulations. 

These were not long in appearing. SR 1 (7 F.R. 3158), issued on the same day as GMPR (see entry above for the Maximum Price Regulations) excepted certain commodities, including military items, requiring rather technical descriptions and not of enough general interest to justify including them in the exempt lists of the main regulation. SR 1 was destined to become one of the important items in its series. 

Others were more ephemeral. For example, SR 2 and SR 5, on May 11 and 13, 1942 (7 F.R. 3489 and 3723), postponed the effective date of GMPR respecting goods sold under Government contracts, respecting machinery presently to be covered by MPR 136, and respecting the Territory of Hawaii. The postponement for Hawaii helped to prepare the way for the Military Governor's controls and ultimately for the GMPR for Hawaii; see the separate entry above. 

With SR 3, on May 11, 1942, (7 F.R. 3522) the characteristic pattern of many of these regulations began to appear. Certain sales of woolen fabrics to the U. S. 

Navy were exempted from GMPR, but only on condition that the prices charged should not exceed those set forth in a subjoined table. This was more than a simple exception. It was an attempt to replace, for a particular set of commodities, the freeze prices of GMPR with the dollars-and-cents ceilings which were so much more definite and easy to enforce. 

SR 4, on May 13, 1942, made an out-and-out exception for certain military goods, including assembled aircraft, when sold to any agency of the U. S. Government (7 F.R. 3724). Similarly, SR 7, on May 27, 1942 (7 F.R. 3990), excepted certain contracts for making army field jackets. SR 4 and SR 7 were revoked on April 16, 1943 (8 F.R. 4986), the same day SR 1 was revised. With that revision the exceptions from GMPR were concentrated in SR 1. The regulation received 59 amendments before revision and 112 after revision, the last occurring on October 29, 1946 (11 F.R. 12793).

Another item of lasting signifigance was SR 11, issued June 16, 1942 (7 F.R. 

4543). It began in a modest way by excepting from GMPR the charges for transportation, storage, dry cleaning, and a few other services. Subsequent amendments added many others. A week later the so-called Service Regulation, MPR 165, was issued. This employed the freeze technique and specified in great detail which services were covered and which were not. Nevertheless, SR 11 continued in effect to the end of the price control program. After 5 amendments it was revised on August 13, 1942 (7 F.R. 6426), and subsequently received 104 amendments to 

October 21, 1946 (11 F.R. 12362). 

SR 12, June 19, 1942 (7 F.R. 4661), was again something more than a list of exceptions, being a substantive regulation of the prices of imported commodities. 

After one revision on December 14, 1942 (7 F.R. 10532), it was transformed into the Maximum Import Price Regulation, August 20, 1943 (8 F.R. 11681); see the separate entry for MIPR above.

Many-one might perhaps say most of the supplementary regulations under GMPR were of relatively minor importance and might have been issued as simple amendments, but for the desire to keep the text of that document simple enough to be read by retailers. Such were Nos. 6,8,9,10, and 13, issued in May or June of 1942, and covering, respectively, the addition of increased shipping charges to the prices of goods entering Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands, the calculation of maximum prices for certain washing machine models, the exemption from GMPR of brooms made by the blind in New Orleans, the exemption of rice and lard entering Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands, and a general exemption for territories and outlying possessions (7 F.R. 3905, 4117, 5427, 4231, and 4798). Even SR 1 and SR 11, in which the exceptions for commodities and the exceptions for services were respectively concentrated, were in the nature of very large and complicated amendments to GMPR's two lists. 

SR 14, on the contrary, was a substantive regulation, a catch-all for retail ceilings not worth writing up as separate MPR's. It followed the pattern of SR 3. 

SR 14 began very modestly on July 16, 1942 (7 F.R. 5486) by setting a maximum price of 12 cents a quart (in glass) or 13 cents a quart (in carton) for fluid milk in the New York metropolitan area, except for sellers with high base-period prices. Subsequent amendments set dollars-and-cents prices for dozens of other commodities. For still other dozens the amendments provided formulas for calculating costs or fixed mark-ups for determining prices. Thus SR 14 became "the repository for modifications of maximum prices for miscellaneous commodities and services otherwise governed by GMPR." By July 13, 1943, it needed revision 33

(F.R. 9787-9835). The commodities that had been taken up in the 194 previous amendments were now grouped logically for convenience except for a few that had become obsolete. Exception was also made for milk and milk products, and the method by which this was done seems a little intricate. On the same day, July 13, 1943, on which SR 14 was revised, amendment 195 to SR 14 was also issued (8 F.R. 9835). Amendment 195 transformed SR 14 into SR 14A, while at the same time restricting it to the provisions, not themselves altered, regarding milk and milk products. Here then begins the compartmentalization of the SR 14 modifications of GMPR pricing. On December 13, 1943 (8 F.R. 16794) was issued

SR 14B on bread and bakery products. By January 29, 1945 another revision was necessary in order to codify the matters that had been introduced by no less than 207 amendments. At this time also were issued SR 14C, SR 14D, etc., up to and including SR 14K, each containing "Modifications of Maximum Prices Established by GMPR" for a particular industrial group (10 F.R. 1154-1236). 

SR 15 was issued November 2, 1942 (7 F.R. 8959), and was the vehicle for authorizing field office adjustments in prices for certain essential_commodities or services subject to wide local variations in cost or supply factors. The first section of SR 15 authorized any OPA state director to raise the local prices on firewood if he found that GMPR prices were preventing the production of a sufficient supply. 

The second section authorized any OPA regional office to raise or lower the GMPR price for fluid milk or butter if it seemed that the production or distribution of those commodities was being seriously disturbed. The third section of SR 15 provided rules for hardship adjustments for truckers (not common carriers), and for persons supplying storage or terminal services. In both the firewood and trucking cases the ceilings involved applied to labor and the use of equipment by small operators, peculiarly sensitive to rising demand. 

9. Supplementary Service Regulation Under MPR 165. 

Series, Nos. 1-73. September 12, 1942-September 4, 1946. 

Although the General Maximum Price Regulation of April 28, 1942, was originally designed to cover both commodities and services, experience soon showed the administrative advisability of separating these two fields. On June 23, 1942, therefore, MPR 165 was issued (7 F.R. 4734). It was in effect a "GMPR for 

Services." Its emphasis was on retail services to consumers, like laundries, though some commercial and industrial services were included. As in the original GMPR, the base-period was the month of March 1942, with special rules for the prices of services not actually supplied in that month or supplied only seasonally. 

Incorporated by reference was Amendment 1 to SR 11 under GMPR, issued the same day (7 F.R. 4738), giving a list of 74 services excepted from the operation of MPR 165; some of these were statutory exemptions, and others, like the rental of typewriters, were covered under the appropriate commodity regulations. 

Most of the supplementary service regulations followed the basic principle of SR 14 under GMPR. That is to say, they placed some kind of restriction, usually by dollar-and-cents pricing or by fixed mark-up, on the charges for a service, superseding the general pricing rules of MPR 165. Thus, Supp. Service Reg. 

1 (7 F.R. 7249) permitted laundry contracts with any Government agency, if they had been entered into before March 1, 1942, and were expiring on or after April 1, 1942, to be renewed at the old price, but with a percentage increase to take account of the intervening rise in the cost of living. No. 2 (7 F.R. 7539) allowed the packers of apples or pears to insert in their contracts an "adjustable pricing" clause. This permitted shipments to be made at prices to be adjusted upward according to future OPA decisions in cases in which applications for increases had been made and were still pending; otherwise shipments would have been withheld until the cases were settled. No. 4 (7 F.R. 10619) regulated bowling by setting September 1941 as a base-period and allowing a fixed increase over the price then charged. For example, on each game of ten pins in open (i.e., nonleague) bowling there could be an addition of 3 cents to the old price. 

The service industries of laundering (hand or power), dry cleaning, and linen supply figured in a great many of these regulations, including Nos. 1, 5, 8-15, 17, 18, 20, 23, 29, 31, 33, 34, 36, 39, 40, 45, 51, 53, 54-56, 58, 59, 61, 65, 67, and 69. 

No. 17 (8 F.R. 12633) attempted to handle realistically the problem of reduced quality in these services. It specifically named certain economies of operation that might be instituted without reduction in the price of the service. No. 18 (8 F.R. 

12887) faced a particularly hard type of problem in retail price control, namely, 34

Price Control Documents (continued) 1C. 

the inclination of a laundry or dry cleaning establishment to discontinue a service offered during the base-period and offer in its place a similar but higher-priced service. This was declared to be a violation of MPR 165 unless certain conditions were shown to exist, such as the present lack of special equipment to perform the cheaper service, the willingness of other suppliers in the community to provide adequately the cheaper service, etc.

A few items in the series concerned themselves with the delegation of authority to regional or district offices to issue regulations in some particular field. Examples are No. 43 (9 F.R. 14853), No. 48 (10 F.R. 2811), and No. 50 (10 F.R. 3224), authorizing a decentralized operation of this sort with respect to certain agricultural services, to certain establishments repairing automobiles and farm machinery, and to the cleaning of septic tanks. In the larger decentralized operations of OPA, such as restaurant price control and community ceiling price lists, this type of delegation of authority was usually promulgated by means of a general order. 

Supp. Service Reg. 73, the last in its series, gave a table of maximum charges, in cents per pound, for processing the various kinds of meat in frozen food lockers in the State of Vermont (11 F.R. 9798). 

10. General Retail Order Under MPR 580. 

Series, Nos. 1–3. April 18–October 4, 1945. 

MPR 580 (10 F.R. 3015) was issued on March 20, 1945, at a comparatively late stage in OPA's life, to replace GMPR as the basic retail control over clothing, textile, and home furnishings prices not already brought under some other specific regulation; it covered perhaps half the merchandise of that description. 

The rapid changes in styles and fabrics long customary in this field, and accelerated by war influences, were fatal to the simple freeze technique of GMPR. The extreme variations, ranging from 30 to 60 percent or more, in the gross profit margins characteristic of store-wide operations, of separate departments within stores, and of particular articles sold in the same deparment, also ruled out any general application of such other control techniques as uniform dollars-and-cents or flat margin pricing. MPR 580 was therefore a complicated effort to apply the individually experienced gross margin of each of some half million retailers, for each different "cost-line" in each of several scores of specified categories of goods he might handle, to his pricing of goods in those categories thereafter. The regulation substituted for the March 1942 base-period a current base date, March 19, 1945, the day before MPR 580 was issued, and for the general freeze a new "pricing chart" method of control. 

Prices charged on the base date were unchanged, but ceilings for all new goods were readily and definitely ascertainable from the pricing chart without the subjective comparisons of "similarity" that made GMPR hardly more than a polite fiction as a control in that field. Each retailer was required to file with his OPA district office two copies of a chart showing in detail, by categories of merchandise, his net invoice cost, his selling price, and his percentage mark-up, for every article in his store on March 19. Rules were provided for applying these mark-ups to the pricing of all goods subsequently received. The commodities covered were carefully listed in the regulation in separately numbered categories. Time was allowed for filing and checking the charts before the new ceilings took effect. 

The regulation was amended 18 times to October 8, 1946. 

Plans for something along these lines, but less elaborate, had been discussed with a group of leading retailers beginning in 1943, and reached the stage of a mimeographed "Draft VIII” which was circulated for comment and then abandoned because of inherent complications and trade resistance. But the steady advances in clothing prices led to a revised effort to improve controls under a new Director of the Consumer Goods Division, Jerome M. Ney, late in 1944. MPR 580 was the result. It was prepared and issued in complete secrecy and under the tightest practicable mechanical deadlines, an imperative necessity because of the use of a current base date; any retailer with advance knowledge could have played havoc with the scheme by raising his price tags for that day. In the printed text the actual day was therefore mentioned only once, on the outside cover, in a space left blank for the purpose and filled in manually according to telephoned instructions relayed from the national office through the regional and district offices to local board price clerks a few hours before the copies were delivered by them simultaneously to retailers all over the country.

MPR 580 as issued left two general problems unsettled. One was what to do about stores newly opened for business after March 19. Synthetic pricing charts were established for them by OPA district offices as the occasions arose, in 35

several hundred separate orders for the individual stores concerned. The other was what to do about mail-order and chain stores which usually bought and sometimes priced their merchandise centrally, adding a service charge to the net invoice cost before transferring the goods to their retail outlets. In such cases the retail outlet might not know the net invoice cost, nor the central office the final selling price, which the pricing chart called for. There were numerous variations in practice, which could only be dealt with in individual orders. 

Some common problems, however, were treated in a small series of general retail orders. No. 1, issued April 18, 1945 (10 F.R. 4238), froze central office service charges to base-date levels. No. 2, issued the same day, modified the rules for identifying on a pricing chart the invoices relied upon as supporting evidence for the net cost of goods. It also dealt with cases in which invoices were lost or non-existent; as well as with certain additional problems of central purchasing for chains. An amendment to Order No. 2 (10 F.R. 4983) permitted chains to apply to OPA for adjustment of the rules if the nature of their business made the existing rules inapplicable.

General Retail Order No. 3 (10 F.R. 12603) illustrates again the use of subsid iary orders in the steady but piecemeal process of substituting_uniform prices or margins for individual freeze techniques. It was entitled, "Bed Linens: Modification of Ceiling Prices." Instead of using their experienced mark-ups as of March 

19, 1945, sellers of specified types of bed linens were now required to confine themselves to a fixed mark-up of 35%. Chain stores doing as much as $100,000 worth of business a year were limited to their "1942 mark-up" if this was less than 35%. Several of the later amendments to No. 3 placed similar fixed mark-ups on other types of apparel, cotton goods, etc. The last amendment, No. 11, dated 

September 11, 1946 (11 F.R. 10340), altered the effective date for applying this type of control to anklets and hosiery. 

11. Supplementary Storage Regulation Under MPR 586. 

Series, Nos. 1-4. May 21-December 28, 1945. 

It was the intention of GMPR to freeze at the March 1942 levels the prices of most goods and services, but for administrative purposes it was soon recognized that goods and services should be divided. On June 23, 1942, the "GMPR for 

Services,' numbered as MPR 165, was issued (7 F.R. 4734). This left the original GMPR applicable only to commodities. Some ambiguity existed as to whether a charge for handling and storing a commodity should go under the service regulation or the commodity regulation. There were portions of MPR 165 which dealt with storage and terminal facilities in particular. On the other hand, when SR 14 under GMPR systematically developed dollars-and-cents prices or fixed mark-ups to replace the freeze regulation in various fields, storage and terminal facilities came in for some share of attention. By May 21, 1945, the time seemed ripe for assembling these separate provisions in one place. MPR 586 was "issued for the purpose of gathering together and publishing in more convenient form all regulation of the maximum charges for storage and terminal services" (10 F.R. 5797). The statement was added, however, that it was "not the purpose of this new regulation to change the maximum prices previously established." In other words, MPR 586, despite its size and importance, was more in the nature of a collation than a revision. 

On the same day two supplementary storage regulations were issued. MPR 586 was couched in general terms, listing the services covered or not covered, naming the month of March 1942 as the base-period, and giving rules for the determination or the adjustments of maximum charges in special cases. Obviously, this was a typical "freeze" regulation. It was the function of Supp. Storage Reg. 1 (10 F.R. 

5802) to except certain storage and terminal services from the freeze and put them either under dollars-and-cents pricing or under fixed mark-ups. For example, warehousers storing fruits in Oregon or Washington were allowed to increase their 1941-42 charges by 3 cents a box or, for cannery storage, by $1.00 a ton. 

On the other hand, a flat price was set on the storing of grain in Utah. Warehouses in that State were allowed to charge 15 cents per ton per month, with 30 days' free storage but with a handling charge of $1.00 per ton. 

No. 2 in the series (10 F.R. 5804) placed similar detailed restrictions on cotton warehousing and cotton compressing. No. 3, on July 31, 1945 (10 F.R. 9589), covered in great detail the charges for cotton warehousing in the southeastern States, differentiating carefully between such types as producer loan cotton, 36

Price Control Documents (continued) 1C. 

Government pooled cotton, Government owned cotton, Government purchase cotton, and shipper cotton. No. 4 (10 F.R. 15468) gave tables of allowable charges for storage and for handling of merchandise for certain Government agencies in designated cities.

The supplementary storage regulations received several amendments. The latest was amendment 11 to No. 1 on October 28, 1946 (11 F.R. 12712), deleting the provisions as to storage and handling of soy beans. This had the effect of removing that service from price control. 

12. Supplementary Regulation Under the GMPR for Hawaii. 

Series, Nos. 1-2. December 14, 1943-March 27, 1946. 

Following the usual pattern of supplementary regulations, SR 1 under GMPR for Hawaii (8 F.R. 16835) made an exception for certain commodities. Sales of any waste, scrap, or damaged materials by Government agencies were excluded from the restrictions of the GMPR for Hawaii. 

No. 2 in the series (11 F.R. 3258) dealt with cane sugar in the territory. 

Maximum prices were raised by .455 cent per pound over the maximum prices established by the GMPR for Hawaii, but provisions were made to prevent speculators and others from profiting to this extent on sugar already in their possession on February 9, 1946. SR 2 was amended 9 times, the last on November 22, 1946, but effective September 18, 1946 (11 F.R. 13792). This again raised maximum prices for sugar and again included a clause for the recapture of windfall profits on inventory. 

In 32 C.F.R., 1946 Supp., p. 4952, there is an erroneous entry for what appears to be No. 2 in a series of GMPR's for Hawaii. The F.R. references there given, both for "No. 2" and its 9 amendments, all apply to SR 2 under the GMPR for 

Hawaii. There was never a "GMPR No. 2 for Hawaii." 

13. Territorial Consumer Goods Regulation. 

Series, No. 1 (no more issued). May 2, 1945.

No. 1 (10 F.R. 4911) assembled in a single document the more generalized provisions commonly used in fixing maximum prices of certain consumer goods sold in the Territory of Hawaii. It did not itself set any maximum prices, but explained how a seller might apply to OPA for a maximum price if he could not determine it under existing regulations, how he should handle an article having a manufacturer's established and maintained price higher than existing OPA regulations would allow, how he should treat Federal and State taxes in computing a maximum price, etc. Specific maximum prices for particular classes of goods were set forth in a succession of 5 supplements, and any previous order establishing or adjusting the maximum prices of articles covered by such a supplement was declared revoked as of the day on which the supplement became effective. 

Supp. 1 (10 F.R. 4915) dealt with jewelry, new watches and clocks, binoculars, and similar articles; Supp. 2 (10 F.R. 4921) with certain imported Swiss watches; 

Supp. 3 (10 F.R. 4925) with second-hand watches; Supp. 4 (10 F.R. 4918) with certain china, glassware, wallets, toys, etc; and Supp. 5 (11 F.R. 7084) with radio receivers and phonographs. 

Both this regulation and its supplements received a few amendments as to details. 

14. Order of OPA and WFA on Live Cattle Prices. 

On December 18, 1943, was published a "Certification of Live Cattle Prices at 

Points Other Than Chicago and in Line with Chicago Prices" (8 F.R. 17014). This "Joint Order," as it was often called, was signed by Chester Bowles as OPA 

Administrator and Marvin Jones as Administrator of the War Food Administra tion. It established 24 numbered and 9 unnumbered zones for the determination of price ranges for live cattle and gave a table of conversion factors, in order that the Defense Supplies Corporation might be able to calculate subsidy payments for slaughterers in various parts of the country. The Joint Order was once amended, January 14, 1944 (9 F.R. 709), in order to redefine certain of the zone boundaries. 

15. Restaurant Maximum Price Regulation. 

Series, Nos. 1 and 2, with Nation-wide applicability; also 9 separate regional series with hyphenated numbers ranging from 1-1 to 9-2. June 26, 1943-July 9, 1945. 

General Order 50, April 12, 1943 (8 F.R. 4808), authorized regional offices, 37

OPA Bibliography and such State or district offices as the regions might designate, to regulate the prices of food and drink sold by restaurants and similar establishments in given areas. On January 7, 1943, by Amendment 40 to GMPR (8 F.R. 371; see also 1317, 2110, and 3099) such prices had already been exempted from the operation of the General Maximum Price Regulation. GO 50 prepared the way for their control on a “base-period freeze” principle by requiring every proprietor of a restaurant, cafe, or similar eating place throughout the country to file with the appropriate war price and rationing board a copy of the menus or price lists which he had used during the week of April 4-10, 1943. It then remained for the regional administrators and district managers of OPA to decide whether, when, and where a restaurant maximum price regulation should be issued, and what form it should take. In practice the filed prices were usually made the legal ceilings, subject to later modification. There was a good deal of variation and experiment during the first year, and some offices took no action at all. 

Railroad dining cars obviously presented a special case. GO 50 had required the proprietors of such cars to file their base-period prices with the Services and 

Consumer Durable Goods Division of OPA in Washington, D.C. Rest. MPR 1, 

June 26, 1943 (8 F.R. 8845), was entitled "Food and Drink Sold for Immediate

Consumption by Dining Cars." It established as a base period the time from 

February 1 to April 10, 1943, and provided special formulas for the calculation of legal maximum prices on items not sold during that period. 

Most of the Rest. MPR's bore hyphenated numbers, the digit before the hyphen representing the number of the OPA region concerned. For example, the 4 Rest. 

MPR's for parts of Region I (the New England States) were as follows: No. 

1-1, issued April 29, 1943 (8 F.R. 7345), signed by Christopher Del Sesto as "State Director," and covering restaurant prices in Rhode Island; No. 1-2, issued 

April 30, 1943 (8 F.R. 6850), signed by L. J. Bresnahan, as "State Director,

Massachusetts State Office," and covering the Boston District; No. 1-3, issued 

May 17, 1943 (8 F.R. 7009), signed by Chester Bowles as "District Director," and covering the State of Connecticut; No. 1-4, issued May 18, 1943 (8 F.R. 

7347), signed by F. L. H. Sjostrom as "Acting District Director, Springfield

District Office," and covering 4 counties of Massachusetts. The variations in the titles of the signatory officers reflect the transitional period in which some of the State offices of OPA had accepted their redesignation as district offices, while others were resisting the change. 

As New Year's Eve of 1943 approached, it was felt that restaurant prices for that date needed special control. This was applied by means of Supplementary 

Order 79, December 10, 1943 (8 F.R. 16738; amendment on 17277), declaring that in all districts covered by a Rest. MPR the high prices for meals on New Year's 

Eve of 1943 should not exceed those charged for equivalent meals on New Year's 

Eve of 1942. 

The great year for the imposition of price control on restaurants was 1943, though amendments to the existing regulations continued as late as 1946. Most of the OPA regions contented themselves each with a single regulation for the whole region. But region I issued 4 Rest. MPR's, Region III, 15, and Region V, 13. Region VI at first issued No. 6-1, November 12, 1943 (8 F.R. 16695), to cover only the Chicago Metropolitan District, and later issued No. 6-2, February 15, 1944 (8 F.R. 1878), to cover the rest of the region. Region IX, which had charge of the territories and outlying possessions, issued 2 Rest. MPR's: No. 9-1 for 

Hawaii, March 2, 1944 (9 F.R. 2478), and No. 9-2, much later, for Puerto Rico, July 9, 1945 (10 F.R. 8613). Rest. MPR 7-1, covering all of the Denver Region, was issued in some haste on April 24, 1943 (8 F.R. 6059), and had to be revised on May 11, 1943 (8 F.R. 6623). By August 16, 1943 (8 F.R. 11948) it required a second revision.

In substance the various Rest. MPR's, with the exception of No. 1 for dining cars, differed very little. It was easy and natural therefore that they should be consolidated, much as the various maximum rent regulations had been consolidated, into a Nation-wide regulation. Rest. MPR 2, June 29, 1944 (9 F.R. 7263), was such a consolidation. It standardized the controls, making the week of April 410, 1943, the base period and giving rules for calculating and adjusting prices. 

New Year's Eve 1942 was made the norm for all subsequent New Year's Eves, and SO 79 was revoked by Rest. MPR 2. SO 80, March 24, 1944 (9 F.R. 3338, 3581, 4010), on the pricing of distilled spirits, wines, etc., was continued in force, as was Rest. MPR 1 on meals sold in dining cars. Licensing Order No. 1 38

Price Control Documents (continued) 1C. 

was made automatically applicable to all restaurants, and the suspension of licenses was authorized in case of violations. Using the device commonly called the "highest price-line limitation," Rest. MPR 2 sought to prevent restaurants from elminating the lower-priced meals or items from their base-period menus and introducing instead higher-priced meals or items. 

An experiment in dollars-and-cents pricing of beer and other malt beverages was tried for certain counties in the Dallas district by Dallas Orders 1 and 2 under 

Rest. MPR 5-4, October 1 and 7, 1943 (F.R. 14363 and 14364). This was before the issuance of the general Restaurant MPR 2. After that event, on September 25, 1944, similar authority for a flat-pricing beer order was delegated to Region III (the Cleveland Region) and its subordinate districts by means of Order 1 under 

Rest. MPR 2 (9 F.R. 11817). By Order 4 under Rest. MPR 2 (10 F.R. 5487), the OPA Administrator of Region VIII (in San Francisco) was authorized to set dollars-and-cents prices on wine sold for immediate consumption in the State of Washington, and he did so on May 16, 1945, by "Region VIII Order G-1 under 

Restaurant MPR 2" (10 F.R. 6282). Flat pricing was extended to coffee sold by the cup; see Rest. MPR 1, amendment 3 (10 F.R. 2435).

Some of the late amendments to Rest. MPR's 1 and 2 reflected the stresses of the post-war period of reconversion. Amendment 5 to Rest. MPR 1 and 

Amendment 11 to Rest. MPR 2, both issued on March 22, 1946 (11 F.R. 3089), were designed to help in the saving of salad oils and wheat in cooperation_with the Famine Emergency Committee. The last amendment, No. 18, to Rest. MPR 

2 was issued October 8, 1946 (11 F.R. 11701) and was accompanied by a published statement of considerations. In accordance with the requirements of the Price 

Control Extension Act of 1946, Amendment 18 eliminated the concept of the highest price-line limitation. It also permitted restaurants to use a 'cost-plusfixed-margin" principle in setting their prices for items on which they were being forced to pay increased prices themselves. The last amendment of all was No. 6 to Rest. MPR 1, issued on October 11, 1946 (11 F.R. 11928). This decontrolled food prices in dining cars entirely, but sought to impose a customary mark-up on prices charged by train butchers and peddlers. As thus amended, the two general 

MPR's for restaurants bore little resemblance to the base-period type of regulation in force from 1943 to 1945. 

16. Community Ceiling Price Order. 

Various series, named for the State or district office issuing them, the earliest being Rhode Island Order 1, May 8, 1943, and the latest Omaha

Order 53, December 11, 1946. 

General Order 51, May 6, 1943 (8 F.R. 6008) authorized regional offices, and such other offices (district or State) as the regions might designate, to issue maximum dollars-and-cents price lists on food items sold at retail. Each list applied to a convenient trading area within which uniform ceilings could be equitably applied-a city and its environs, a county, or sometimes most of a State. These "community ceiling prices," as they were called, were calculated from prevailing wholesale prices in the area, with the addition of markups prescribed for various categories of foods and adjusted to provide differentials for four types of stores. The prices were recomputed monthly and printed on large sheets. Retail stores were required to post the latest lists supplied to them by OPA. At the beginning these lists were incorporated in formal orders published in the Federal Register. The first 16 of them, each signed by a district director, were issued on May 8 and 10, 1943 (8 F.R. 6496-6526). They included for Region 

I the Rhode Island Order 1, (for the whole State except Newport County) and the 

New Hampshire Order 1 (for Concord); for Region II the Camden Order 1, the Trenton Order 1, and the Buffalo Order 1; for Region IV the Raleigh Order 1 (for Wake County, N.C.) and the Savannah Order 1 (for Chatham County, Ga.); for Region V the Kansas City Order 1, the Tulsa Order 1, the Fort Worth 

Order 1, the Arkansas Order 1 (for Pulaski County, Ark.) and the Shreveport

Order 1 (for Caddo Parish and Boissier Parish, La.); for Region VI the Springfield Order 1 (for Sangamon County, Ill.), the Springfield Order 2 (for Franklin County, Ill.) and the Peoria Order 1; and for Region VII the Colorado Order 

1 (for Denver).

Other large groups of such orders were published in full during May, but by June 3, 1943, it was deemed expedient merely to file the certified copies with the Division of the Federal Register and publish a list of the titles. See 39

F.R. 7407 for a list of 47 “State and District Orders Under Gen. Order 51," each with the F.R. Doc. number by means of which any item could promptly be produced on request at the National Archives. Long lists of this sort continued to appear during 1944, 1945, 1946; see "Community ceiling prices, lists of orders filed," under "Price regulations, commodities and services," in the annual indexes of the Federal Register, under the main heading "Price Administration, Office of." The last list appeared December 11, 1946 (11 F.R. 14256), comprising mere ly Omaha Orders 52 and 53 from Region VI. By means of Amendment 2 to SO 193, 

January 28, 1947 (12 F.R. 663) all commodities except sugar and rice were exempted from price control, and the community ceiling price lists and orders were accordingly discontinued. 

See also 32 C.F.R., 1943 Supp., p. 2407, for a table giving the dates and the

F.R. references for 71 "Lists of Community Ceiling Price Orders Under General 

Order No. 51." The dates range from July 5 to December 11, 1943. Later supplements to C.F.R. did not continue this tabulation. 

17. Food Products Regulation. 

Series, Nos. 1-5. June 16, 1944-April 18, 1945. 

FPR 1 (9 F.R. 6711) gathered into a single document the provisions most commonly used in fixing maximum food prices in sales by processors, repackers, and the like (but not by wholesalers or retailers). Actual prices were indicated in a series of 20 supplements to FPR 1 (June 16, 1944-October 18, 1946), the first 4 of them carrying notes as to the previous maximum price regulation which the supplement in question superseded. FPR 2, July 21, 1944 (9 F.R. 8304), organized in a similar manner the general provisions used in pricing certain grains, and 6 supplements (July 21, 1944-June 25, 1945) set the actual prices. 

FPR 3, September 16, 1944 (9 F.R. 11504), organized the general pricing provisions for certain feeds (10 supplements to June 14, 1946). FPR 4, April 16, 1945 (10

F.R. 4103), put into one document the provisions common to all retail community pricing orders on dry groceries, fresh fruits and vegetables, and fish, but left the actual prices to be announced in Adopting Orders issued by district offices of OPA. 

FPR 5 (April 18, 1945) gave the general provisions for the retail pricing of malt beverages. The various supplements and Adopting Orders were frequently amended. 

Certain provisions in the Price Control Extension Act of 1946 required OPA to modify FPR 1 by Amendment 4 (August 23, 1946), thereby revoking section 

3.1, which had restricted the amount that a processor might sell to a primary distributor. The 1946 act also necessitated Amendment 5 (September 30, 1946), which permitted primary distributors to recover their current costs of acquisition plus the average percentage mark-up in effect on March 31, 1946. 

18. Supplementary Order. 

Series, Nos. 1–194. March 10, 1942-December 20, 1946. 

The Supplementary Order (SÓ) was a device by which several maximum price regulations (or price schedules) could all be amended simultaneously, just as several maximum rent regulations were dealt with simultaneously by means of a supplementary amendment. The first three were not originally numbered (7 F.R. 

1836, 2000, and 2132) but were entitled, respectively, "Order Amending Modification Provision in Certain Revised Price Schedules," "Order Revoking Affirmations of Compliance in Certain Revised Price Schedules," and "Order Amending Enforcement Sections of Certain Revised Price Schedules." The numbering began with SO 4 (7 F.R. 3159), which was issued April 28, 1942. On that day was promulgated the General Maximum Price Regulation, which covered by its sweeping provisions the prices of certain goods previously controlled by 7 of the Temporary 

Maximum Price Regulations, namely, Nos. 12-15 and 17-19. SO 4 revoked those 

7 TMPR's and so helped to prepare the way for the GMPR. 

The licensing of buyers and sellers-with, or more frequently without any actual physical registration of their names and businesses-was provided for in the GMPR covering retail prices (7 F.R. 3153), in MPR 165 covering services (7 F.R. 4734), in MPR 183 for Puerto Rico (7 F.R. 5620), in MPR 194 for

Alaska (7 F.R. 5909), in MPR 201 for the Virgin Islands (7 F.R. 6269), in GO 

41 (7 F.R. 4734), and in several amendments to the foregoing. Provisions for licensing, with or without registration, were partly standardized in a succession of supplementary orders, including Nos. 5 (7 F.R. 3403), 11 (6167), 14 (7033), 17 (7239), 18 (7240), 19 (7434), 20 (7490), 33 (10535), and 36 (8′ F.R. 1798). 40

The clauses on registration were usually provisional, merely stating that dealers in a given business might be required to register when and as the OPA should subsequently determine. But SO 5, issued May 5, 1942, imposed actual registration on licensed sellers of waste, scrap, and salvage material. Similarly, SO 20, issued 

September 21, 1942, imposed registration on dealers in secondhand machine tools.

A year later these matters were standardized still further by means of the 

3 licensing orders, all issued September 27, 1943. LO 1 made the automatic licensing system applicable to any person making any sale under price control, and LO 2 and LO 3, respectively, continued the registration requirements of SO 5 and SO 20. 

The supplementary orders covered a great variety of other matters. Thus SO 

9 was the principal vehicle for individual adjustments to high-cost suppliers under war contracts; it cut across all but a very few price regulations. SO 94 covered sales of Government surplus goods; and SO 108, SO 110, and SO 113 applied the "maximum average price" (MAP) plan to apparel and to rayon and wool fabrics, respectively. SO 118 and SO 119 embodied the "reconversion formula" adjustments for durable goods manufacturers when the restrictions on production were lifted. Toward the end of the life of the agency certain relaxations of control required by Congressional enactment were promulgated in supplementary orders. One of the earliest of these appeared in SO 93, issued July 5, 1944 (9 F.R. 

7574), eliminating the "highest price line limitation" on sellers of garments at retail. Such limitation had been forbidden by an amendment of June 30, 1944, to the Emergency Price Control Act and Stabilization Act. Similarly, in the fall of 1946 the supplementary order was often used to revoke or relax certain standard or recurrent provisions in the MPR's and so bring them in line with the Price Control Extension Act or with other governmental regulations or decisions. Thus, SO 179, on August 23, raised the maximum prices for lime, cement, tile, and similar materials because the Interstate Commerce Commission had raised freight rates on these commodities by an order of June 20, 1946. On 

September 14, by Amendment 33 to SO 131, the prices were revised upward on certain cotton textiles for producers who had been authorized to pay increased wages in accordance with Executive Order 9697. On October 2, by SO_185, the prices were revised upward on certain part-cotton textiles because the Price Control Extension Act prevented OPA from putting a ceiling on raw cotton and so caused a considerable increase in the price of cotton yarns. On November 12, by SO 

193 (11 F.R. 13464), all commodities except sugar and rice were exempted from price control, in accordance with a Presidential directive. On December 

20, by SO 194 (11 F.R. 14597), which was the last of its series, prices on sales within the Virgin Islands (but not prices on imports from continental United States into the Virgin Islands) were removed from control. 

SO 193 was signed by the OPA Administrator, but SO 194 by the Temporary Controls Administrator, to whose jurisdiction the OPA had by that time been transferred. One of the last constructive efforts on the part of the Administrator before the transfer was Amendment 1 to SO 40, issued on December 4, 1946 (11 F.R. 

14103). This declared that repeal or revocation of a price regulation, or exemption or suspension of commodities from price control, did not extinguish any right, obligation, liability, or penalty incurred prior to such repeal, revocation, exemption, or suspension, and that any legal action initiated under the price regulations might continue to be prosecuted as if they were still in force. 

Apparently the last official issuance bearing on the OPA price program was an unnumbered amendment of November 6, 1947, to SO 189. That order (11 F.R. 

12568) had declared that records which the price regulations had required to be kept as to any commodity which might thereafter be exempted from price control must be preserved for a year from the date of the exemption. By the amendment dated 

November 6, 1947, the period of preservation was now extended to 3 years. The amendment was accomplished by means of a joint order signed by the Secretary of Agriculture, the Secretary of the Reconstruction Finance Corporation, and the Director of the Division of Liquidation in the Department of Commerce, and was approved by the Attorney General (12 F.R. 7327). The joint order was sent to the Federal Register by the Sugar Rationing Administration, to which, in addition to its main function, had been entrusted a limited function of price control as to sugar and rice. 

19. Supplementary Order to Regional Orders. 

The device of the supplementary order was also used to modify or amend 41

simultaneously several regional orders regarding prices. An example is the order of December 1, 1943 (9 F.R. 361) raising bituminous coal prices by a specified amount above the prices previously set for certain counties in North and South Carolina, Georgia, Tennessee, and Virginia. The previous prices had been set by OPA 

Region IV in Regional Orders G-3 to G-11, inclusive, under Rev. MPR 122. The new order was headed: "Region IV Orders G-3-G-11 under RMPR 122, Supp. 

Order 1." 

20. Adjustment or Authorization of Prices. 

Hundreds of OPA orders were printed in the Federal Register with an added descriptive title of "Adjustment of Maximum Prices" or "Authorization of 

Maximum Prices." These were types merely. Neither of them formed a numbered series, though imaginably they might have done so. Practically it was not feasible to keep track of thousands of price adjustments or thousands of special authorizations in a single numerical succession. Rather, since the operating branch which originated a maximum price regulation had also to pass on individual cases in its particular field, it was natural to let that branch number serially the special orders under each regulation which it had sponsored. A somewhat similar descriptive_title was "Establishment of Maximum Prices;" see, e.g., Order 1509 under MPR 188, issued April 17, 1944 (9 F.R. 4262). Still another was Simplified 

Pricing," Order 4332 under MPR 188 (10 F.R. 11017). For the function of amendments and individual adjustments in keeping controls flexible, and also for the significance of the special authorizations, see the entry above on maximum price regulations. For the systems of numbering see the entry below on special orders, section 1F. 11. 

See also Table 5, "Notices Relating to Adjustment of Maximum Prices, by Companies," and Table 6, "Notices Relating to Adjustment and Authorization of Prices by Commodities," in 32 C.F.R., 1943 Supp., pp. 2431-2435, giving in each case the name of the company or commodity, the number of the order (including the MPR, RPS, or section of GMPR under which it was issued), the date, and the F.R. citation. These tabulations were not continued in later supplements.

D. Rationing Documents 1. Civilian Allocation Program. 

Series, Nos. 1-30. May 29-August 28, 1941. 

The Office of Price Administration and Civilian Supply (OPACS, the immediate predecessor of OPA) was designed not only to control inflationary prices but also to regulate the distribution of scarce commodities and services. 

While therefore its Price Division was issuing 20 price schedules with 32 amendments, its Civilian Allocation Division issued 30 Civilian Allocation Programs with 8 amendments. In the Federal Register, as also in the Code of Federal 

Regulations, the programs are not numbered, but in the OPA Secretary's Document 

Series File (now in the National Archives) the folders are marked CA 1, CA 2, etc. CA 1 (6 F.R. 2681) dealt with copper, already in excessive demand, and CA 

30 (6 F.R. 4536) with tungsten. Of special interest in the light of later developments was No. 6 (June 20, 6 F.R. 3066), which aimed to build up "a reserve stock of rubber sufficient to provide for future military and essential civilian needs." Processors of rubber were instructed to reduce their quotas month by month until by December 1941 they were using only 80% of what their monthly average had been during the year April 1940 to March 1941. At the same time consumers were instructed not to overstock but to buy rubber goods only for immediate need. There were, of course, no penalties for noncompliance. Each 

CA was issued by OPACS in conjunction with one of OPM's General Preference Orders, in order that both military and civilian use of the product might be rationally, controlled. With the transfer of the "Civilian Supply" portion of OPACS to the Office of Production Management, the entire CA program was divorced from OPA. 

The list in 32 C.F.R., Cum. Supp. p. 9371, is alphabetically rather than numerically arranged. It has omitted No. 10, July 5 (6 F.R. 3286), on railroad cars. 

2. Ration Order. 

Series, Nos. 1-21 (omitting Nos. 15 and 18) December 30, 1941–April 30, 

What was subsequently regarded as Ration Order No.

1 was originally issued 42

Rationing Documents (continued) 1D. 

without number as the Tire Rationing Regulations (7 F.R. 72). It provided for the appointment of State tire rationing administrators, local tire rationing administrators, and local tire rationing boards; for the announcement of monthly quotas of tires to be made available in each State; and for the eligibility rules and the applications, certificates, and other forms to be used by the boards in granting permission to purchase tires. The regulations were amended once (7 F.R. 257) and on February 11, 1942, they were reissued as Revised Tire Rationing Regulations (7 F.R. 1027), with the addition of rules to govern the retreading and recapping of worn tires and the sale of "camelback," the uncured rubber compound used in such repairs. 

The Revised Tire Rationing Regulations were amended 40 times before they were again reissued on November 6, 1942, as Ration Order 1A (7 F.R. 9160), with the comprehensive title, "Tires, Tubes, Recapping, and Camelback." This greatly expanded and tightened the tire rationing program, and coordinated it with the Ration Order No. 5C designed to restrict the use of gasoline, in accordance with recommendations of the President's Special Committee to Study the Rubber 

Situation, September 10, 1942. RO 1A received 111 amendments to Otctober 26, 1945 (10 F.R. 13403), and was finally revoked December 26, 1945 (10 F.R. 15348).

Tire rationing was extended in 1943 by separate orders to the territories and outlying possessions: to Puerto Rico by RO 1B on July 10, (8 F.R. 9551; revoked December 28, 1945, 11 F.R. 298); to the Virgin Islands by RO 1C on July

The revocations of RO 1B-1F, despite the different dates of issue, all became effective January 1, 1946.

Rationing Order No. 2, on New Passenger Automobiles (7 F.R. 667), was issued 

January 30, 1942, and was followed the next day by Price Schedule No. 85, fixing ceiling prices on the same commodity. PS 85 states the cause in its opening sentence: "The complete diversion of automobile manufacturing facilities to war work has brought the production of passenger automobiles to an end." Administration of RO 2 was entrusted to the local tire rationing boards, which were therewith redesignated as local rationing boards. Forms and eligibility rules were provided. On February 21, 1942, an improved program for automobile rationing was set up by Rationing Order No. 2A (7 F.R. 1542), which stipulated that the new rules should supplement the earlier RO 2 and that in cases of conflict RO 2A should prevail. There were numerous amendments to RO 2A. With Amendment 21 on December 30, 1942 (8 F.R. 18), the term "Rationing Order 2A" was shortened to "Ration Order 2A," to correspond to what had by that time become the prevailing usage. On February 25, 1943 (8 F.R. 2843), the program was again revised. 

The original RO 2 was revoked and RO 2A was superseded by RO 2B, except that RO 2A continued to apply to the territories and possessions. RO 2A was finally revoked August 23, 1945 (10 F.R. 10431). RO 2C, to cover used automobiles in Hawaii, was issued July 28, 1944 (9 F.R. 9164; terminated by Amendment 3, 10 F.R. 12848, which fixed the expiration date as October 8, 1945).

A new type of rationing, affecting not selected individuals but practically every citizen, had to do with sugar. Rationing Order No. 3, issued April 21, 1942 (7

F.R. 2966), assigned this program also to the local rationing boards and arranged for the Nation-wide distribution of War Ration Book One with numbered stamps. 

To provide a system for the circulation of these stamps through wholesale and retail stores a ration banking plan later was set up by General Ration Order 3A (8 F.R. 1130, erroneously using "Ration Order 3A" in the title, but "General 

Ration Order 3A" in the text; actually there was no "Ration Order 3A").

Revisions of RO 3 were issued as follows: 1st revision, February 2, 1944 (9 F.R. 

1433); 2nd revision, November 14, 1944 (9 F.R. 13641); 3rd revision December 29, 1945 (11 F.R. 134). RO 3 received 112 amendments, the first revision 52, the 2nd 54, and the 3rd 42. Final revocation, under authority of the Sugar Rationing Administration in the Agriculture Department, occurred July 28, 1947 (12 F.R. 5280).

Under RO 3 were also set up 9 zones (later increased to 14) in order to permit certain restrictions on the shipment of sugar; see below under Zoning Order 1. 

Rationing Order No. 4, issued March 12, 1942 (7 F.R. 2003), dealt with used typewriters, assigning this program to the local rationing boards and providing forms and eligibility rules. 1942 (7 F.R. 2317), to include some new as well as used typewriters. The revised order was superseded on December 22, 1942 by RO 4A (7 F.R. 10806)—the legal practice of the office at the time frowned on terminology involving "second" or "third" revisions. RO 4A extended the certificate requirements to cover rentals as well as sales of non-portable machines, and to cover new portables. The order was designed to channel the more desirable models to fill Government procurement needs, and otherwise, by encouraging rentals rather than sales, to keep in dealers' hands a stock of usable machines for the more essential needs. RO 4A was also something of a guinea pig for drafting efforts then being made to simplify the language of regulations. RO 4A was terminated by Amendment 9, April 22, 1944 (9 F.R. 4350).

Gasoline was originally rationed only in the East Coast shortage area, and later throughout the country for its indirect effect on the conservation of rubber tires. 

On May 11, 1942, by Ration Order 5, were promulgated the Emergency Gasoline Rationing Regulations (7 F.R. 3482), setting up what was commonly known as the "Interim Program." This rationed the use of gasoline in the States along the Atlantic seaboard, by means of cards to be punched by gasoline dealers. The program was administered by the local rationing boards, with the use of 3 classes of cards, A,B, and C. RO 5 was supplemented but not wholly superseded on 

July 7, 1942, by RO 5A (7 F.R. 5225), which set up an improved coupon system for the entire eastern part of the continental United States. RO 5A was administered by the local boards which by now had been redesignated as War Price and Rationing Boards. It provided Basic Ration Books in Classes A,B,C and D. On July 20, 1942, by RO 5B (7 F.R. 5607) the program was instituted in Puerto Rico, with the same 4 classes of Basic Ration Books. On August 28, 1942, by RO 8 (7 F.R. 6871) the program was extended to the Virgin Islands, with provision for books in Classes A,B and C. Under RO 8 were issued three 

Gasoline Rationing Emergency Orders (see below). On October 21, 1942, by RO 5D 

(7 F.R. 8551) it was extended to the Canal Zone, using books in Classes A,B and E, and being administered by the Governor of the Panama Canal through the Canal Zone Gasoline Rationing Board and the Chief of the License Bureau. 

On September 10, 1942, the President's Special Committee to Study the Rubber 

Situation, after considering alternatives recommended Nation-wide gasoline rationing as a means of saving tires. It advised a reduction of the national average automobile mileage to 5,000 miles a year. With this in view, and concurrently with RO 1A on automobiles (see above), RO 5C was issued on November 6, 1942 (7 F.R. 9135). This restricted the basic business use of passenger automobiles to 

470 miles a month, but it also provided, under rigid restrictions, for various supplemental and other rations. The relation of RO 5C was carefully defined in respect to RO 5A, which in effect it superseded. Both RO 1A on automobiles and 

RO 5C on gasoline were designated as parts of a program of mileage rationing, for the dual purpose of saving rubber and conserving gasoline. A further element in mileage rationing was RO 5E, issued July 16, 1943 (8 F.R. 9975), extending similar controls to Puerto Rico. The relation of RO 5E was carefully defined in respect to RO 5B, also for Puerto Rico, which in effect it superseded. 

Within a few days after the attack on Pearl Harbor gasoline rationing had been imposed on Hawaii by the Military Governor of the Islands. The first compelling motive was the conservation of supplies of gasoline but in 1943 the existing rules were modified to produce a more equitable distribution and to conserve rub ber as well. On March 5 by GO 48 the OPA Director for the Territory of Hawaii received general authority to ration food and other materials (F.R. 2898), and on March 10 by GO 49 the OPA ratified and adopted all rationing actions and documents of the Military Governor. Thus the way was prepared for the issuance, on June 30, of RO 5F (8 F.R. 10742) with the title of "Mileage Rationing: 

Gasoline Regulations for the Territory of Hawaii." Ration Books included classes 

A, B, C, and D. The order applied only to the islands of Kauai and Maui.

3. Restriction Order. 

Series, Nos. 1-18. October 1, 1942-May 15, 1946. 

The restriction orders were used in various ways to prepare for or to supplement the rationing programs, usually with a view to preserving to a reasonable degree the normal distribution of the commodities in question. Thus, RSO 1 (7 F.R. 

7839) set quotas for certain types of meat and provided for the issuance of administrative suspension orders (see below) in case of violations. After receiving 19 amendments, RSO 1 was transferred to the jurisdiction of the Department of Agriculture on April 1, 1943 (8 F.R. 4151, signed by the Secretary of 

Agriculture and the OPA Administrator). RSO 2, on December 8, 1942, attempted to regulate the distribution in Puerto Rico of the highly important commodity of rice (7 F.R. 10536; revoked March 8, 1943, 8 F.R. 3714). Applicable also to 

Puerto Rico were RSO 4, 6-8 and 10-18. RSO 3, on February 18, 1943 (8 F.R. 

2214), in anticipation of the issuance of RO 16, forbade, with some exceptions, the sale of canned meat and canned fish in the continental United States, and required wholesalers to report their inventory as of February 17, 1943. Similarly, RSO 5, on March 21, 1943 (8 F.R. 3615), halted the sale of edible fats and oils 45

for one week prior to their being rationed on March 29, 1943, by RO 16. RSO 9, on November 13, 1944 (9 F.R. 13994) placed restrictions on the sale of laundry soap in the Virgin Islands in anticipation of RO 20 on November 16, 1944 (9 F.R. 14229). 

4. Control Order. 

Series, Nos. 1-2. April 25, 1945-April 25, 1946. 

The original Control Order was designed to regulate livestock slaughter and correct the geographic maldistribution of meat which had resulted from lowered meat production and continued high military requirements. Since the great centers of population obtain most of their meat from other States, and since only meat slaughtered in Federally inspected plants is allowed to cross State lines, Control Order 1 sought to increase the livestock going to Federally inspected plants by imposing production quotas on other plants (designated as "class 2 slaughterers"). The latter were required to register and were given slaughtering quotas corresponding to the livestock weight which they had slaughtered during the base period of 1944. This year was made the norm because by 1944 most of the population shifts induced by the war had taken place. The "class 3 slaughterers" (farmers selling up to 6,000 pounds of meat a year) were given quotas not for their production but for their sales of meat. 

Control Order 1, after being amended 22 times, was suspended September 8, 1945 (10 F.R. 11578) and finally revoked December 17, 1945 (10 F.R. 15115). But the cessation of active war and the return of many veterans to civilian life failed to put the demand for meat into normal relation to the supply. On March 27, 1946, by Amendment 69 to Revised Maximum Price Regulation 169, a partial attempt was made to restore the limitations on slaughter and sale of beef and veal. By 

April 25, 1946, the Secretary of Agriculture and the OPA Administrator agreed that general controls must be reimposed, though with somewhat altered provisions as to details. The former issued War Food Order 75-7 (11 F.R. 4644) and the latter issued Control Order 2 (11 F.R. 4657). There were five amendments and one supplement, itself amended five times, to Control Order 2. On October 15, 1946, in view of the extreme shortage of supplies coming to market, President Truman directed the revocation of Control Order 2 (11 F.R. 12054; see also 12865 for an amendment to the order of revocation).
