10. General Ration Order. 

Series, Nos. 1-20 October 24, 1942-June 16, 1947. 

The ordinary ration order (or rationing order) covered the program for rationing a particular commodity or group of commodities, but the general ration order (GRO) dealt with matters common to several or all of the separate rationing programs. Typical subjects were the requesting of administrative exceptions, the issuance of the War Ration Books, the system of ration banking, and the special provisions for institutions and industrial concerns, which had need of rationed goods but could not be treated quite in the manner in which individuals were treated. In connection with each general ration order, instead of filing a rationale with the Division of the Federal Register, OPA usually printed in the Federal Register a preamble explaining the reasons for its issuance. 

The great year for general ration orders was 1943, which saw the issuance of Nos. 

3-16. Many were heavily amended. GRO 5, for example, between February 18, 1943, and November 28, 1945, received 122 amendments; it was revised December 29, 1945, and received 19 more amendments to March 21, 1947. 

GRO 1 (7 F.R. 8653) defined the procedure for requesting administrative exceptions to any ration order which did not itself provide for such requests; but the warning was added that no administrative exception would be permitted to modify the eligibility rules for securing a rationed commodity. GRO 2 (7 F.R. 

10070) specified what records an institutional user must keep as to rationed foods, and subsequently GRO 5 (8 F.R. 2195) divided institutional users of rationed foods into three groups, required them to register accordingly, and gave rules for making allotments to each group. Industrial users had been required to register for sugar in accordance with Rationing Order No. 3 (7 F.R. 2966) and for processed foods in accordance with Ration Order 13 (8 F.R. 1840), for the purpose of securing their proper allotments; but by December 14, 1943, it was felt necessary to issue GRO 16 (8 F.R. 16840), which laid down rules for their reregistration and required reports from them as to their use of rationed commodities in quarterly periods. 

GRO 3 (8 F.R. 865) first set up the system of ration banking, using the existing banks of the country for the purpose and providing a schedule of reimbursements to them for the expense of carrying ration accounts. GRO 3 47

OPA Bibliography 1E. Rent Control Documents was supplemented by GRO 3A (erroneously entered in 8 F.R. 1130 as Ration 

Order 3A and so listed in the monthly index_but corrected in the annual index) prescribing rules for ration bank depositors. It was also supplemented by GRO 

3B (8 F.R. 2665) prescribing rules for accounts maintained by “exempt agencies," i.e., those permitted in particular ration orders to obtain the rationed commodities without restriction as to quantity. 

GRO 6 (February 17, 1943; 8 F.R. 2190), GRO 12 (June 2, 1943; 8 F.R. 7453), and GRO 14 (October 18, 1943; 8 F.R. 14211) laid down rules for the issuance of War Ration Books Two, Three, and Four, respectively. GRO 6 was revoked as early as November 1, 1943, since Book Two was by that time completely superseded. Since Books Three and Four were to some degree interdependent, GRO 12 and GRO 14 were continued in effect until December 29, 1945, at which time they were revoked together (11 F.R. 166 and 174).

GRO 17, (issued March 31, 1944; 9 F.R. 3508) dealt with the export of rationed foods. GRO 18 (issued March 22, 1945; 10 F.R. 3086) accorded returning veterans the right to set up new businesses in which they would handle rationed foods; it was revised as late as July 8, 1946. 

At the turn of the year 1946-1947 separate revocations were published for GRO 1, 3A, 3B, 7, 9-12, 14, 16, and 17. On January 20, 1947, the Director of the Bureau of Priorities (12 F.R. 408) revoked WPB Directive No. 1 (originally issued Jan uary 24, 1942; 7 F.R.

562), thus removing from OPA the basic delegation of au thority to conduct consumer rationing. By authority of the Sugar Control Extension 

Act of 1947, however, the Secretary of Agriculture on March 31, 1947, set up in the 

Department of Agriculture a Sugar Rationing Administration (see General Sugar 

Order No. 1 and No. 5, below) and on May 15, 1947, issued GRO 19 (12 F.R. 

3398), allowing some rationed sugar to go to other new businesses aside from those of veterans. On June 16, 1947, he issued GRO 20 (12 F.R. 3998), removing individual consumers and institutional users from sugar rationing restrictions, but continuing the restrictions on industrial users. By July 28, 1947, the sugar shortage was so far relieved that not only the 3d Rev. RO 3 but also GRO 18, 19, and 

20 were all revoked at one time (12 F.R. 5280). 

11. General (Sugar) Order. 

Series, Nos. 1-9. March 31-July 30, 1947 By authority of the Sugar Control Extension Act of 1947 the Secretary of 

Agriculture issued his General Order No. 1 (12 F.R. 2807), establishing under his jurisdiction a Sugar Rationing Administration. This carried on also the price control of sugar and of rice until the expiration of the Emergency Price Control 

Act on June 30, 1947. By his General Order No. 5, March 31, 1947 (12 F.R. 3829), the Secretary of Agriculture adopted and continued in force the rationing regulations and orders of OPA (then in the Office of Temporary Controls) relating to sugar. No. 9, the last traced (12 F.R. 5279), gave directions for the keeping of records as to price control of sugar until October 31, 1948. 

The items in this series were generally known by the simple term "General Order." On August 5, 1945 however, when No. 2 in the series was being revoked (12 F.R. 5386), the heading in the Federal Register was "Gen. Order 2, Revocation," but the document itself used the term "General Sugar Order." If this term had been used throughout, it would have distinguished this series from the older 

OPA series of general orders. 

An "Opinion Accompanying Revocation of General [Sugar] Order 2" was pub lished (12 F.R. 5386) along with the revocation.

E. Rent Control Documents 1. Designation and Rent Declaration. 

Series, Nos. 1-32. March 2, 1942-July 22, 1943. Originally unnumbered. 

No. 27, June 3, 1942 (7 F.R. 4232) was the first to carry a number in the

Federal Register. 

The Emergency Price Control Act of 1942 made a sharp break administratively with the Fair Rent Committees, which had attempted in the prestatutory periods to stabilize rents on a local basis. The fundamental idea was continued, however, of naming a previous date on which rents in a given area were judged to have been normal, and of declaring such rents to be the legal maximum after 48

a specified effective date. The new act prescribed that after a given area had been marked out as one in which inflationary rise in rents had already occurred or were threatening, the local governmental authorities should have 60 days in which to take effective countermeasures. 

Defense-Rental Area Designation and Rent Declaration No. 1 (7 F.R. 1675) 

designated three townships in their entirety and a specified portion of a fourth township in the County of San Diego, California, as a defense-rental area and declared, with certain adjustments for special cases, that the rents which had prevailed on Janurary 1, 1941, ought to be the maximum legal rents within the meaning of the Price Control Act. It recommended that if within 60 days the State or local authorities had not established effective control, the OPA Administrator should promulgate a maximum rent regulation. This was actually done for the 

San Diego Area on May 27, 1942 (see below). The first 21 Designations and

Rent Declarations as they soon came to be called, dealt each with a separate defense-rental area. Beginning with No. 22 (7 F.R. 3192) it was found convenient to deal with 8 areas at one time. No. 25 (7 F.R. 3195) dealt with 259 areas. The last, No. 32 (8 F.R. 10365), dealt with the Oahu Defense-Rental Area. There were numerous amendments issued for the purpose of changing the boundaries of the areas for administrative convenience. No. 31 received 49 amendments, the last on November 7, 1946 (11 F.R. 13305).

The items in this series were always understood to be preparatory, their chief purpose being to mark off the area, to name the date from which the 60-day warning period was to be calculated, and to give an intimation as to the maximum rent date which might ultimately be specified. The final determination of the maximum rent date, the effective date on which Federal control should be applied, and the date for registration of rental properties within the area was left to the maximum rent regulation (see below). 

2. Maximum Rent Regulation. 

Series, Nos. 1-67A. May 27, 1942-April 30, 1943. 

For items in this series the abbreviation MRR was at first employed, but these letters were found to be too easily confused with MPR, which stood for maximum price regulation. Hence the designation “Max. Rent Reg." came to be used instead. 

The first 20 items were numbered to correspond to the 20 (originally unnumbered) 

Designations and Rent Declarations issued March 2, 1942 (7 F.R. 1675-1695). 

Thus, Max. Rent Reg. No. 1 (8 F.R. 4038) was entitled "Housing Accommodations Other Than Hotels and Rooming Houses in a Portion of the San Diego 

Defense-Rental Area," corresponding to Defense-Rental Area Designation and Rent Declaration No. 1, which marked off the San Diego Area. Beyond No. 20 

another system was adopted. Max. Rent Reg. 21A was issued June 25, 1942 (7 F.R. 4783) to cover the other main_type of rents, those for hotels and rooming houses, in the same 20 areas. From this time onward the two types were distinguished in the numbering system. That is to say, the rent regulations for hotels and rooming houses carried the letter A after the number, whereas those for other housing accommodations (ie., for apartments and houses) carried plain numbers only. The addition of the letter A was an extra precaution, since the numbers for the two types were not duplicated. 

For example, Nos. 21A, 22A, and 23A all were for hotels and rooming houses, whereas 24,25,26,27, and 28 were for other accommodations. (Nos. 21-23 were not used, nor Nos. 24A-28A.) Often there was a pair of regulations for the same area, as No. 39 for housing and No. 40A for hotels and rooming houses, both at Vallejo. The last pair of the series, No. 66 and No. 67A (8 F.R. 5728 

and 5733; April 30, 1943) covered, respectively, the housing accommodations and the accommodations in hotels and rooming houses in 14 designated areas. 

Most of the maximum rent regulations received amendments, and when it was necessary to amend a standard provision simultaneously in a large number of the maximum rent regulations, a Supplementary Amendment was issued (see below).

The series of numbered maximum rent regulations was highly standardized and offered an obvious opportunity for simplification through consolidation. 

They applied, of course, to different geographical areas, but each had an effective date, a "base period" or "maximum rent date" chosen as the norm, and a date on which the registration of dwellings or rooms was required to be filed. On 

May 31, 1943, therefore, the entire numbered series was superseded by two master regulations, one a Rent Regulation for Housing (8 F.R. 7322), the other 49

OPA Bibliography 

a Rent Regulation for Hotels and Rooming Houses (8 F.R. 7334). Technically these were presented as amendments. In the words of the Rent Regulation for 

Housing, each of the Maximum Rent Regulations Nos. 1-20, and the others from 

24 to 66 not carrying a suffixed letter A, "is redesignated Rent Regulation for Housing and is amended to read as set forth herein." In the words of the other master document, each of the Maximum Rent Regulations carrying in its number the suffixed A "is redesignated Rent Regulation for Hotels and Rooming Houses and is amended to read as set forth herein." Both of the master regulations included a table of 370 defense-rental areas, giving in each case the name of the area, the State, the counties covered, the maximum rent date, the effective date of regulation, and the date (inclusive) by which the registration statement was to be filed. 

The administrative simplification thus achieved was considerable. 

Both the housing regulation and the hotel regulation, as they came for simplicity to be known, were amended. They were also supplemented by 5 additional regulations. Four of these, issued in 1943, were for the control of hotels and of housing in New York City (8 F.R. 13910 and 13914) and in Miami, Florida (8 F.R. 13118, 14043, 14047, and 14048; see also Eviction Regulation 2, 8 F.R. 

12622). In 1944 the area centering in Atlantic City, New Jersey, was withdrawn by 

Amendment 27 (9 F.R. 6819) from the general Rent Regulation for Housing, and a separate unnumbered Rent Regulation for Housing in the Atlantic County Area was promulgated (9 F.R. 6819). All 7 of these unnumbered rent regulations were considerably amended. 

By Executive Order 9806, on December 12, 1946 (11 F.R. 14281), the functions of 

OPA, along with those of certain other emergency agencies, were transferred to the Office of Temporary Controls, and on December 19, 1946, OTC Regulation 

2 (11 F.R. 14704) declared all official issuances of OPA, insofar as they were in effect on December 12, 1946, to be adopted, ratified and confirmed by the new agency. The rent control program continued to operate without very great change under the OTC-OPA set-up. But on May 2, 1947, by Housing Expediter Rent Control Order 1 (12 F.R. 2986), the "regulations, orders, delegations of authority and organization of the Office of Temporary Controls (Office of Price Administration) 

relating to rent control" were transferred to the Housing Expediter, under whose authority an Office of Rental Control was established. The existing state of the 

7 unnumbered rent regulations and their amendments at the moment of the final removal of the program from OPA jurisdiction is conveniently indicated by the table in 12 F.R. 2986. A table on the following page summarizes the then existing state of the procedural regulations, general orders, and the like which bore on rent control. For a summary of the organizational structure of the Rent Department as it existed on March 31, 1947, see 12 F.R. 3708.

The Housing Expediter, under the authority of the Housing and Rent Act of 1947 (PL 129, 80th Cong.), has maintained the rent control program longer than any other element of OPA, but not without considerable modification and relaxation. On May 29, 1947, Amendment 116 to the Rent Regulation for

Housing, Amendment 108 to the Rent Regulation for Transient Hotels, Residential 

Hotels, Rooming Houses, and Motor Courts (as it was by that time called), and 

Amendment 43 to Designation and Rent Declaration No. 25 were issued (12 F.R. 

3509-3511). These curtailed the scope of rent control appreciably by dropping the program in several areas and by consolidating certain areas. Along with these 

3 amendments the Federal Register published a statement of the reasons for their issuance. On June 30, 1947, which happened to be the date on which the last traces of the OPA organization were obliged to be terminated according to Congressional decision, the Expediter issued in somewhat revised form all 7 of the unnumbered rent regulations. These included a Rent Regulation for Controlled Rooms in Rooming 

Houses and Other Establishments (12 F.R. 4302) and a Controlled Housing 

Rent Regulation (12 F.R. 4331), each with a table of 371 areas; also both types of rent regulation for Miami (4325 and 4374) and for New York City (4295 and 

4318) and a regulation for controlled housing for Atlantic City (4381). For the Rent Procedural Regulation No. 1, see below under "Procedural Regulation." 

3. Eviction Regulation.

Series, Nos. 1-2. November 6, 1942–September 13, 1943. 

The designation of certain defense-rental areas and declaration that rents therein must be stabilized led in many cases to a sharp increase in the number of tenants removed from possession by means of evictions, actions to evict, and notices to quit or vacate the premises. It was evident that these practices were in 50

Rent Control Documents (continued) 1E. 

an indirect manner causing or contributing to an inflationary rise in rents. The 

Nebraska Defense-Rental Area was therefore selected as a typical case and Eviction Regulation 1 (7 F.R. 9132) was issued in an attempt to halt such practices, in accordance with the provisions of the Price Control Act of 1942. The attempt proved for the most part workable and effective and the substance of Eviction Regulation 1 was therefore embodied with little change in the general 

Rent Regulation for Housing and the general Rent Regulation for Hotels and 

Rooming Houses on May 31, 1943 (8 F.R. 7322 and 7334).

The schedule of rent areas embodied in these two general regulations did not include Miami, but it became increasingly evident that the rents in Miami needed to be controlled. Eviction Regulation 2 (8 F.R. 12622) was therefore issued as a temporary measure on September 13, 1943. It fixed September 1, 1943, as the maximum rent date. It was announced that Eviction Regulation 2 would subsequently be replaced by a Rent Regulation for the Miami Defense-Rental Area, and that appropriate adjustment_provisions would therein be provided. This was done on 

September 24, 1943 (8 F.R. 13118), and on the same day Eviction Regulation 2 was revoked (8 F.R. 13124). It had been for rent what a TMPR was for price. 

4. Rent Regulation. 

The 7 unnumbered rent regulations are treated in connection with the numbered series of maximum rent regulations, to which they form a natural sequel. They covered, respectively, the following: (1) hotels and rooming houses, generally; (2) housing, generally; (3) hotels and rooming houses in New York City; (4) housing in New York City; (5) hotels and rooming houses in Miami; (6) housing in Miami; and (7) housing in Atlantic City. 

5. Supplementary Amendment. 

A double series, Nos. 1-18 and Nos. 1 [A]-10A. The inclusive dates, July 

21, 1942-April 23, 1943, were the same for both parts of the series. 

Most of the separately numbered maximum rent regulations (distinct from and earlier than the two consolidated rent regulations issued May 31, 1943) received a few amendments, these being numbered serially for each maximum rent regulation concerned. But the rent regulations were of the so-called "freeze" type and tended therefore from the start to be highly standardized. The substantive part of the rules followed a fairly consistent pattern, though the effective dates, the maximum rent dates, and the registration dates varied from area to area. As developing experience with rent control suggested the need of improvements in the rules, it became evident that standard provisions occurring in a number of maximum rent regulations might conveniently be amended all at one time. For this the device of the supplementary amendment was used. 

The numbering system applied to the supplementary amendments was modeled generally on the system used for the maximum rent regulations themselves. These, after some initial confusion, had been numbered in a single consecutive series from 1 to 67, with a letter A added to those which concerned hotels and rooming houses, the plain numbers being reserved for those concerned with other types of housing (i.e., houses and apartments). The supplementary amendments were numbered, however, in double rather than single series; they might even be thought of as two series, with the same title. Those bearing on the housing regulations used plain numbers, 1-18, whereas those bearing on the hotel regulations used numbers with the suffixed A, i.e., 1A-10A. At the very beginning, however, there was a slight slip. On July 21, 1942 (in 7 F.R. 5645) were issued "Supplementary 

Amendment No. 1 of Maximum Rent Regulations for Housing Accommodations Other Than Hotels and Rooming Houses" and "Supplementary Amendment No 1 

of Maximum Rent Regulations for Hotels and Rooming Houses." Manifestly the latter should have been No. 1A.

On July 30, 1942, the system was regularized. Supplementary Amendment 2 (7 

F.R. 5912) was made applicable to maximum rent regulations bearing plain numbers, and Supplementary Amendment 2A to maximum rent regulations bearing numbers with a suffixed A. The last to be issued were Supplementary Amendment 

18 and Supplementary Amendment 10A, both on the same day (8 F.R. 5480). 

6. Rent Procedural Regulation. 

Series, No. 1 (no more traced). September 4, 1947.

See the description of this item below, at the end of the series of procedural regulations. It was issued by the Housing Expediter, who had taken over the rent control program from OPA. 51

OPA Bibliography 1F. Other Documents F. Other Documents 1. Compensatory Adjustment Regulation. 

Series, No. 1 (no more issued). May 18, 1942.

CAR 1 (7 F.R. 3749) was designed to provide compensation for the increased cost of transporting Southern bituminous coal by rail instead of by tidewater transshipment from Hampton Roads to New York and points north. The Government, through the Reconstruction Finance Corporation and the War Shipping Administration, paid the extra costs on a monthly basis to qualified applicants supplying the necessary data. CAR 1 was amended 8 times down to May 31, 1943, was revised on October 11, 1943 (8 F.R. 13980) to take in some anthracite dealers and some dealers in northern Maine and northern New Hampshire and received 9 further amendments to November 20, 1946. The last amendment (11 

F.R. 13695) provided that no further subsidies under CAR 1 should be paid on coal received at business establishments after November 9, 1946. 

2. Commodity, Practices Regulation. 

Series, No. 1 (no more issued). July 17, 1942. 

CPR 1 (7 F.R. 5564) attempted to stabilize the weight, size, and quality of bars or packages of soap or cleansers, on the ground that changes in weight, size and quality were manipulative practices under the terms of the Emergency Price Control Act of 1942 and might be used as methods of evading the General Maximum Price Regulation. There were 2 amendments, the second of which (October 20, 1943; 8 F.R. 14348) permitted certain limited changes of formula with respect to the anhydrous content. Its provisions having been largely incorporated in MPR 391, CPR 1 was revoked on December 28, 1944 (9 F.R. 15106). 

3. Margin Requirement Regulation. 

Series, No. 1 (no more issued). April 3, 1946.

Although the Emergency Price Control Act of 1942 authorized the regulation of speculative and manipulative practices in the commodity markets, such authority was not exercised until the issuance of MRR 1 (11 F.R. 3602). By this time the Office of Economic Stabilization had been set up with coordinating authority over the wartime economic agencies. MRR 1 was issued under an OES directive with a view to checking the current speculation in cotton by setting minimum margin requirements for trading in cotton futures contracts. The regulation was signed by the Acting Administrator of OPA and by the Secretary of 

Agriculture, with a note above the second signature reading: "Approved: (By direction of the Director of Economic Stabilization April 2, 1946)." The Price Control Extension Act of 1946 expressly forbade OPA to issue any regulation or order as to any agricultural commodity unless a maximum price regulation or order as to that commodity had been established by OPA before April 1, 1946. Since OPA, under the parity restrictions of its 1942 act, had never set a maximum price for cotton, it was now obliged to revoke MRR 1. This was done on August 15, 1946 (11 F.R. 8962). 

4. Procedural Regulation. 

Series, Nos. 1-18 (including in the same numbering several designated as temporary). May 14, 1942-November 14, 1946.

The procedural regulations were not concerned with the internal procedures of the organization, but with the steps which the public needed to follow in certain formal dealings with OPA. They aimed, in the first instance, to give general rules and orderly processes by which business firms objecting to certain price regulations and claiming to suffer hardship under them might seek relief of one kind or another. PR 1, on February 12, 1942 (7 F.R. 971), gave rules for filing a protest against the existence of a regulation alleged to be invalid, for petitioning that it be amended in certain particulars, or for requesting that an adjustment or exception to it be made for an individual firm. The filing of a protest was an indispensable prerequisite to an appeal in the Emergency Court of Appeals. 

Experience soon showed that practically no price regulations were revoked because of protests, that a few might be amended on petition, but that very great numbers of adjustments might be expected as a result of applications therefor. 

PR 1 stood almost to the end of the agency as the basic statement on adjustments. 

Subsequent regulations in the series took up special cases. A temporary regulation, TPR 2 (7 F.R. 3522 and 3664) dealt in a preliminary way with adjustments 52

for retailers of commodities under the GMPR, while TPR 5 (7 F.R. 4730) dealt with adjustments for the service trades (MPR 165). These two were combined later as PR 2 September 1, 1942 (7 F.R. 6962). PR 3, May 25, 1942 (7 F.R. 3936), set up procedures for protest, amendment, or adjustment with respect to rent regulations. PR 6, July 1, 1942 (7 F.R. 5087), covered the special case of adjustments asked for respecting commodities or services under Government contracts, while PR 7, June 25, 1942 (7 F.R. 4779), dealt with adjustment of prices in the territories and outlying possessions of the United States. The last of the special cases had to do with carriers other than common carriers and with suppliers of storage or terminal services. Their adjustment rules were given in TPR 8, September 29, 1942 (7 F.R. 7746).

With a view to securing industry cooperation and technical advice, OPA had established even in the prestatutory period a system of advisory committees representing the various industries affected. PR 13 issued June 7, 1943 (8 F.R. 

7658; revised 9 F.R. 13133) formalized the system. It gave rules for the appointment of such committees in industries which as yet had none. Safeguards were instituted to make each committee truly representative, and rules were established for its meetings, its officers and subcommittees, its consultation with OPA when necessary, and the filing of its reports and recommendations. A protest or a request for amendment of a regulation naturally had more weight from such a committee than from an individual firm.

The Rationing Department did not have the same need to set up rules for protesting its orders or for requesting their amendment, since it operated under no such system of judicial review as the price control law set up; but it dealt quite extensively with appeals by individuals from the decisions of the local boards and of the hearing commissioners. TPR 4, June 5, 1942 (7 F.R. 4296), followed on February 6, 1943, by the permanent PR 4 (8 F.R. 1744), described the procedure by which OPA might suspend rationing violators from further dealings in rationed commodities, but allowed them the right to be heard by a regularly constituted hearing commisioner. PR 9, October 28, 1942 (7 F.R. 8796), offered uniform rules for appeals and petitions for review under ration orders. Appeals from the rulings of war price and rationing boards were to go first to the state director and thence to the regional administrator, with the Washington office reserving the right to hear a final appeal. PR 10, October 12, 1942 (7 F.R. 8281), dealt with disqualification of board members in certain cases and with the review of board action.

The remaining procedural regulations were somewhat miscellaneous in character. 

PR 11, November 12, 1942 (7 F.R. 9390), directed common carriers and public utilities to file advance notice with OPA before instituting general increases in rates, so as to give the agency time to intervene before the appropriate regulatory commissions. PR 12, March 1943 (8 F.R. 3171), told the public what to do about lost, stolen, or mutilated ration books. PR 14, February 9, 1944 (9 F.R. 1594), forbade any former full-time official of OPA to represent a client in any OPA administrative proceeding within a year from the termination of his service (within six months in the case of a board member). PR 15 and 16, August 13 and 20, 1945 (10 F.R. 

9957 and 10226), covered the applications for certain subsidy payments to meat slaughterers.

Like the supplementary orders, the procedural regulations were used toward the end of the life of the agency in modifying the price regulations to accord with certain Congressional requirements. In an effort to make the decontrol process rational and orderly, PR 17, August 23, 1946 (11 F.R. 9345), prescribed the form and content of petitions to the Decontrol Division of OPA for the removal of nonagricultural commodities from price control. It also provided for appeals to the 

Administrator or his deputy and for the hearing of evidence from the Consumers Advisory Committee and the Labor Advisory Committee, and allowed a final appeal to the Price Decontrol Board of three members which had been set up out side OPA by the Price Control Extension Act of 1946. Under the same act the manufacturers of apparel were granted special rights, which PR 18 (11 F.R. 

13485) sought to put into effect, providing for standard forms of application, for hearings and the taking of evidence, and for boards of review. Finally, after the demise of OPA, the Office of Rent Control, which the Housing Expediter had set up to administer the provisions of the Housing and Rent Act of 1947, found it necessary to issue Rent Procedural Regulation No. 1, September 4, 1947 (12

F.R. 5918). This was concerned with landlords' petitions for adjustment, with tenants' applications for decreases in maximum rents, with applications for de- 53

OPA Bibliography control, and with appeals, suspensions, and review. Rent PR 1 was in substance a continuation of the long line of OPA Procedural Regulations, which were a perennial testimony to the efforts of the agency to assure even-handed treatment and to its anxiety to relieve any genuine hardship suffered under its regulations. 

5. Administrative Notice. 

Series, Nos. 1–25. April 16, 1942-March 25, 1946 

No. 1 (7 F.R. 2984) granted to about 60 manufacturers of machinery certain specified exceptions to the general prohibition against raising their prices above a given level, usually the level of October 1, 1941. No. 2 (7 F.R. 3341) conveyed the Administrator's approval of the use of the Accounting Division's Form A 

(Annual Financial Report) and Form B (Interim Financial Report). But most of the items in the series are notices given in advance to growers of particular agricultural products, advising them that a regulation of their prices is in contemplation. Usually the name and number of the proposed maximum price regulation is stated, or the number of the proposed amendment to an existing regulation. 

The notices are signed by the OPA Administrator and approved by the Stabilization Director or by the War Food Administrator. Occasionally an announcement of this sort was not incorporated in the numbered series, as, for example, the one issued July 14, 1944 (9 F.R. 7996) proposing an amendment to MPR 426. The last in the series, as preserved in the OPA Secretary's Office and deposited with the National Archives, is No. 25, issued March 25, 1946. 

6. Licensing Order. 

Series, Nos. 1-3. September 27, 1943. 

The three Licensing Orders were issued the same day (8 F.R. 13240-1). The licensing of business firms took two forms under OPA. The first was a sort of automatic licensing of anyone engaged in the business in question. The second involved an actual registration of the individual firm or dealer. In either case, the licensing was an enforcement device. The object was to have something to revoke as a penalty for violation of price regulations if such violation occurred. In 

1942 the General Maximum Price Regulation and MPR 165, regulating the prices of services, carried provisions for the automatic type of licensing. To supplement this, a Nation-wide plan for registration of retailers was strongly urged and elaborately prepared for, but finally abandoned (see p. 325). About a dozen of the supplementary orders (see above) granted licenses to various groups of dealers, and in some of the highly competitive and poorly organized lines of business an actual registration was required (see SO 5 and SO 20, above) or was mentioned as something which might be required (see SO 36 and SO 39).

LO 1 broadened the automatic licensing, making it applicable to any "sale under price control." It authorized suspension of the license in case of violations, but said nothing about licensing through registration. LO 2 continued and emphasized the provision of SO 5 that dealers in waste, scrap, and salvage should register. 

LO 3 similarly continued the requirement of SO 20 that second-hand machine tool dealers should register. Amendment 4 to SO 5 and Amendment 2 to SO 20 were issued on the same day as LO 1-3. 

7. Suspension Order. 

Various series, each series being numbered separately for the particular ration order or other regulation on which the authority for the suspensions rested.

The first item in the first series was issued March 13, 1942 (7 F.R. 2106), under the Revised Tire Rationing Regulations (later regarded as RO 1). This original Suspension Order (abbreviated as SSO 1) prohibited a firm in Albany, N.Y., from dealing in rubber tires and tubes for about 3½ months from date, on the ground that it had violated the tire regulations. SSO 7 under the same regulations was more severe, prohibiting a firm in Charlottesville, Va., from dealing in the commodity for a year from date. 

Suspensions under the Emergency Gasoline Rationing Regulations (RO 5) 

also began early. SSO 1-14 in this series were all issued on June 15, 1942 (7 

F.R. 4550-4556). Some of these led to further administrative action. On June 17, in accordance with TPR 4, a petition for reconsideration of SSO 11 was filed; on June 30 the order was affirmed (7 F.R. 5032). On June 24 a similar petition respecting SSO 12 was filed, setting forth certain facts not presented at the 54

original hearing on June 11, and on June 29 this order was therefore declared to be stayed until July 7, 1942 (7 F.R. 5033). A similar petition as to SSO 14 led to a stay and the setting of a date for a new hearing (7 F.R. 5033). 

Not only did most of the ration orders provide for suspensions, but so also did the restriction orders, which were a related part of the rationing program. 

RSO 1, issued October 1, 1942 (7 F.R. 7839), established certain meat quotas and specifically provided for the issuance of suspension orders in case the quotas were violated. Many, though not all, of the later restriction orders and control orders carried a similar provision. In the case of Control Order 1 the provision for suspensions was not added until Amendment 20 on August 31, 1945 (10 F.R. 11249).

When the operation of Control Order 1 was terminated on September 8, 1945 (10 F.R. 11578), it was specified that the suspension orders issued under its authority were themselves suspended. 

At the end of February 1943 it was considered no longer feasible to print in the Federal Register all of the separate suspension orders with their reconsiderations, stays, confirmations, etc., though certified copies were still filed for record with the 

Division of the Federal Register at the National Archives. SSO 230 under 

RO 5A, February 26, 1943 (8 F.R. 2517), was the last of the ordinary suspension orders to be printed in full. 

On May 10, 1944, SSO 249 under RO 16 (on meats, fats, fish, and cheese) was printed in full (9 F.R. 5019), but this was a general modification of all the suspension orders under RO 16 that were then in force. It permitted the suspended firms to deal, despite the suspension, in any foods which might be declared to have a zero point value. 

Since suspension orders were always for a specified period of time, it was not necessary to revoke them individually when a particular ration order under which they had been issued was revoked or terminated. 

8. Administrative Order (Lettered). 

Series, [Nos. A and B]. April 15, 1941 and February 17, 1942. 

Originally issued without any indication that they formed part of a series. 

Subsequently they were regarded as A and B, prefatory to the public-official series of Adminstrative Orders 1-30 (see below), and still later were incorporated by reference as Nos. 1 and 2 in the reconstituted series of general orders, according to General Order No. 38 (7 F.R. 9909). 

No. A, as it was later called (published in 6 F.R. 1965), carried merely the title "Adoption of Schedules, Etc., of Price Stabilization and Consumer Divisions" and declared that all price schedules, notices, etc., promulgated by those divisions of the NDAC, as well as all committees formed by them, were to be continued in full effect under the new authority of OPACS. No. B, as it was later called (published in 7 F.R. 1201), carried merely the title "Order for Reprinting of 

Price Schedules in the Federal Register" and ordered the publication, as authorized by the Emergency Price Control Act of 1942, of Price Schedules 1-105 previously issued by OPACS and by the prestatutory OPA. Exception was made of a few items already revoked. According to section 206 of the act, this reprinting continued the validity of the price schedules under the new authority. 

9. Administrative Order (Numbered). 

Series, Nos. 1–30. June 27, 1942-November 11, 1942. 

Subsequently this series was incorporated by reference into the series of general orders (see below) in accordance with General Order No. 38 (7 F.R. 

9909). According to this, the two prefatory Administrative Orders A and B (see above) were redesignated as GO 1-2, AO 1-21 as GO 3-23, AO 22 (though already revoked) as GO 26, AO 23 as GO 28, AO 24-26 as GO 31-33,

AO 27 as GO 36, AO 28-29 as GO 34-35, and AO 30 as GO 37. This series forms a part of the official regulations and orders of OPA, as is evidenced by the publication of the material in the Federal Register. It is not to be confused with the series of internal procedures known as Administrative Orders (see below, No. 3A.10). It was to obviate such confusion that this public-official series was reconstituted under the name of general orders. 

These orders for the most part were issued by the Administrator for the purpose of delegating certain parts of his authority to his regional administrators, to his deputy administrators, to his General Counsel, and to other lawyers and administrative officials, with the stipulation that they in turn might, when necessary, redelegate such authority. By this means a great deal of the administrative and 55

OPA Bibliography enforcement activity and a restricted amount of the policy-making authority were decentralized in OPA. 

10. General Order. 

Series, Nos. 1-76. July 8, 1942–January 13, 1947. 

Nos. 1-3 in this series delegated to the regional administrators the authority to issue subpoenas in rationing investigations, to administer and conduct hearings in connection with rationing, and to send warning notices to licensed dealers thought to have violated the provisions of their licenses. No. 4 delegated to OPA inspectors the authority to procure sworn written statements. No. 5 delegated to local board clerks and OPA distribution officers the authority to administer oaths. 

These 5 general orders were obviously similar to the series of public-official administrative orders. Hence, after a period of some confusion, it was decided to reconstitute these 5 general orders, the 2 administrative orders designated as A and B, and the numbered administrative orders, which by that time had increased in number to 30, as a comprehensive series of 37 general orders. Accordingly, GO 38 was issued November 26, 1942 (7 F.R. 9909) giving a table of correspondences between the old numbers and the new (see also the Federal Register Annual Index for 1942, pp. 151-152) and citing the Federal Register reference for the original publications. For the sake of definiteness GO 1-5, of which the content has been indicated above, were reprinted (7 F.R. 9908) as GO 24, 25, 27, 29, and 30, of the new series.

Many general orders were concerned with delegation of authority to the heads of Territorial Offices in Puerto Rico, the Virgin Islands, the Panama Canal 

Zone, Alaska, and Hawaii, either directly or through the Regional Administrator of Region IX, who operated in Washington, but had oversight of OPA activities in the Territories and outlying possessions. GO 41, December 10, 1942, went so far as to authorize the OPA Director for Puerto Rico to require registration of sellers, thus providing a special method of checking on compliance and enforcement a method which had been considered for the United States as a whole, but had for various reasons been postponed and finally rejected. GO 34 (originally issued as AO 28, October 24, 1942) and GO 37 (issued as AO 30, November 11, 1942) delegated to the Secretary of Agriculture the authority to ration farm machinery and fluid milk. Two of the most important general orders were No. 50 (April 12, 1943) and No. 51 (May 5, 1943), which set up, respectively, the framework for the control of restaurant prices and the system of establishing periodically the community ceiling prices in dollars and cents for foods and other staple commodities at retail. 

The series closed with GO 76 (12 F.R. 213) by which the Administrator of

OPA (then a part of the Office of Temporary Controls) delegated to the Hearing 

Administrator and Hearing Commissioners the authority to hold hearings, administer oaths, issue supoenas and consider appeals with regard to alleged violations, by subsidy applicants, of meat or livestock regulations. Though published later 

(12 F.R. 456), the Region IV Sugar Rationing Delegation Order 1 under General 

Order 75 was issued earlier (December 31, 1946). 

11. Special Order. 

There was no inclusive series of special orders, nor was that term commonly employed in the official designations. Agency employees in conversation constantly referred to actions affecting only individually named firms as "special orders,' but the official designations took such form as "Order 1 under MPR 165" or "Order 954 under MPR 188." In this way, under such of the price regulations as authorized this type of action, dozens of series were developed. There was also at least one special order under the Commodity Practices Regulation, April 10, 1943 (8 F.R. 4808). Some of the MPR's were so complex that certain sections of their texts were taken separately as the authority for distinct series of special orders. This produced such designations as "Order 1 under section 3 (b) of GMPR." If the national office of OPA was issuing the order, this was not specifically indicated in the numerical designation, but was left to be understood. 

On the other hand, if a regional or district office was issuing it under delegated authority, then the number of the region (in Roman numerals from I to VIII) or the name of the district (as Dallas District, Springfield District, etc.) was given first, followed by the serial number of the order and the designation of the MPR furnishing the authority for its promulgation. 56

No useful purpose would be served here by attempting to list separately all the dozens or even hundreds of series of special orders. For certain of the main types see the entries above for adjustment or authorization of prices and below for regional, State, and district office orders. For the function of these and other orders in keeping the controls flexible, see the entry for maximum price regulation. 

12. Regional, State, and District Orders. 

The size and complexity of the OPA operation made decentralization a necessity, as is evident from the large number of orders issued by regional, State, and district offices. In cases of this sort two general types of delegation may be distinguished, with intervening gradations. The one is a delegation to a field organization of the power to set policies and institute programs. The other is a delegation merely of the task of administering and enforcing what has already been decided upon by the central authority. Since commodity movements were Nation-wide, and sensitive to local price variations, the major price control policies and programs, as well as many of their details, had to be formulated centrally for the Nation as a whole. It was therefore natural that the maximum price regulations, maximum rent regulations, supplementary regulations and basic ration orders should be issued by the national office. But the field offices were allowed to issue a great many special orders making exceptions, adjustments, authorizations, suspensions, and the like, with a view to adapting the Nation-wide regulations to local conditions without the necessity of referral to Washington. 

They did so, however, only by express delegation of authority, and usually the authority was carefully defined. In some instances it rose to the program-making level, as when the regional offices were authorized to write restaurant maximum price regulations (see the separate entry above), but even here some fundamental conditions-the "freeze" technique, the filing of records, the base-period, etc.—were prescribed by the national office.

The field offices received their delegations of authority through a variety of documents. Often the chosen instrument was a general order (see the separate entry above). The most notable of these were GO 50, which transferred to the regional offices the responsibility for restaurant pricing, and GO 51, which made the district offices responsible for the community ceiling price program. Supplementary 

Regulation 15 to GMPR authorized State directors to raise the price of firewood and regional offices to raise or lower the prices for fluid milk and butter, in specified circumstances. At least three of the supplementary service regulations to MPR 165 delegated authority to regional or district offices to institute controls over certain service charges. Various MPR's especially those dealing with food and with fuel, as well as various sections of GMPR and a great many of the supplements issued under the food products regulations, delegated particular forms of authority to the field offices. 

For a survey of the early stages of this decentralized activity see table 3, "Regional, State, and District Office Orders," in 32 C.F.R., 1943 Supp., pp. 24072430, giving the commodity, area, date, and Federal Register citation of some 1,100 orders. The numbers of the orders all carry a prefixed "G". Some of them rest on the authority of more than one regulation, since the delegations at times overlapped, especially in the case of fluid milk. For example, Region VI issued on November 29, 1943 (8 F.R. 16572), its Regional Order G-13 dealing with the prices for fluid milk in Paris, Illinois, and citing three delegations of authority: 

SR 15, which in its second section permitted the raising or lowering of the GMPR price for milk or butter if production or distribution seemed to be seriously upset; 

MPR 280, on "Maximum Prices for Specific Food Products"; and MPR 329, on "Purchase of Milk from Producers for Resale as Fluid Milk." 

These tabulations were not continued in later C.F.R. Supplements, but the trend toward decentralization went on throughout the life of the agency. The vast scale on which it was operating in the final stage of OPA may be vividly discerned in 32 C.F.R., 1946 Supp., pp. 4904-4949. Here are given in tabular form nearly 700 regulations, orders, or separate sections thereof under which some specific authority was delegated to the regional offices, with a notation as to whether redelegation was possible, and if So, which district offices received it. These, it should be noted, are not 700 separate regional or district orders, but 700 separate delegations, under each of which a large number of such orders could be and usually were issued. The tabulation was made at a time when the already much reduced OPA program was being placed in the Office of 57

OPA Bibliography 

Temporary Controls. The rationing activities had almost all been terminated. 

In this tabulation the only ration orders remaining are RO 3 and GRO 18. 

State offices issued many orders under delegated authority in the early stage. 

But the State offices proved to be a passing development in the OPA organization. 

They originated with the system of local rationing boards, were later reconstituted as district offices more fully under regional office supervision, and after a certain period of resistance finally accepted the redesignation (see above in the entry on restaurant maximum price regulations). Hence the table of delegations in the 1946 

Supplement takes no cognizance of State offices. 58

2. OPINIONS, DECISIONS, AND INTERPRETATIONS A. Opinions and Decisions 

The need for the texts of current court decisions, selected for their possible bearing on OPA's legal problems, and available promptly in a convenient form for general reference, was first felt in the Court Review, Research and Opinion Branch of the Legal Division; its responsibilities included preparations to meet any anticipated legal challenges of the agency's actions. That branch, with the support of Enforcement, therefore began in March 1942 to mimeograph a fortnightly (later monthly) series of Current Decisions. Since actual litigation lagged well behind the regulatory actions taken, the decisions reprinted in this series for the most part did not involve OPA directly. Perhaps for this reason, and because most OPA lawyers were preoccupied with more pressing concerns than reading background materials, the series was discontinued after a little over a year.

By the fall of 1943, however, with the disestablishment of the Legal Department, the Enforcement Department (newly elevated to departmental status) was carrying a heavy load of litigation. Because of the novelty of many of the questions presented, and because of the decentralization of its activities to over a hundred field offices with changing personnel, a medium was needed for keeping its staff abreast of court developments in OPA cases and their significance. Accordingly the Litigation Division commenced in November to circulate a Weekly News Letter, reprinting significant decisions and commenting on their bearing on enforcement policies and activities. 

In the ensuing months the consolidation in the Secretary's office of the custody of all official actions of the Administrator with the editorial work of preparing regulations, amendments and orders for publication in the Federal Register, and of these and other materials in the OPA Service, provided the facilities for a more ambitious undertaking. As an outgrowth of the private contract for the OPA Service, a collection of Opinions and Decisions was put together and published under the direction of the Secretary in a single substantial volume in July 1944. It included decisions of Federal and State Courts and also adjudicative opinions of the Administrator issued in connection with disposing of protests and petitions. The immediate utility of this volume led to arrangements for its continuation in a loose-leaf series; it was extended down through June 1947 in four additional volumes and an index digest, and became the standard source of office reference to the materials it contained.

Opinions of an altogether different type, not ordinarily published, were those of the General Counsel and his assistants in the Research and 59

OPA Bibliography 2A. Opinions and Decisions (continued) 

Opinion Branch. As a sort of family lawyer to the Administrator and the operating deputies he was constantly called upon to advise on matters beyond the immediate ken of the price, rationing and rent lawyers who were busy drafting and interpreting regulations. These matters included questions of more than departmental scope within OPA, and interagency and Congressional problems, among others. The General Counsel's rulings were binding within the agency. Those reduced to writing filled many file cabinets over the course of five years; they are included in the records of the Research and Opinion Branch. One notable exception to the general rule of confidentiality for these opinions was the General 

Counsel's advice to the Administrator on July 1, 1946, after President

Truman vetoed the price control extension bill, that the agency's employees were authorized to continue working on limited functions while the Congress deliberated on a substitute bill; this opinion was duplicated and circulated to all employees.

Opinions of still another type, already discussed above in the section on Official Regulations and Orders, were those issued to accompany and support OPA's quasi-legislative price orders. What the statement of considerations was to a maximum price regulation, this type of opinion was to a general order, supplementary order, special order—in fact to any of the OPA orders except a ration order. The distinction between statement and opinion here was purely verbal.

B. Interpretations 

OPA's official interpretations of its regulations, amendments and orders told firms or individuals subject to them what the published language would be taken to mean in cases of doubt or apparent conflict, and in cases unprovided for. Because the Emergency Price Control Act gave immunity to those who acted in good faith pursuant to any regulatory 61

OPA Bibliography 2B. Interpretations (continued) provision or requirement, Procedural Regulation No. 1 early erected safeguards to control the issuance of official interpretations, reliance on which was declared to constitute action "in good faith." They had to be in writing, in response to written request stating actual not hypothetical situations, and they had to be signed by one of a designated list of officials. 

They had the same legal force as the regulations themselves, so far as OPA and the parties addressed were concerned; and they were given great weight by the courts.

Because of this, and because the more significant rulings might equally apply to many other parties, interpretations were also of interest to operating officials, trade associations, the trade press, and in the case of rationing, to local boards and consumers as well. Because of the time element in changing regulations, and in some cases because of rights vested under existing language, it was important alike to those who regulated and those who were regulated to know what could and what could not be done without formal amendments. Because of the use of common terms in the General Maximum Price Regulation and other price regulations applicable to many different economic contexts, and in the several rationing orders, coordination of interpretations as well as publicity was imperative. For these reasons a Price Coordination Unit under Joseph A.

Forer was established in the Legal Division even before the GMPR, and by March 1942 Jacob H. Beuscher headed a staff performing a similar function for the Rationing Legal Section. In addition to reviewing the content of interpretations these units prepared digests of them for circulation among the staff, to field office attorneys, and to outside inquirers. When particularly significant rulings were issued, or, in connection with major regulations, without waiting for requests, the office issued press releases, sometimes in question and answer form, generalizing the interpretations for wide distribution; trade meetings were also used to convey interpretations more informally. 

In direct contrast with the publication of opinions and decisions, which started late but grew progressively complex, the business of making, clearing and publishing interpretations was voluminous and complicated from early in 1942 and became progressively routine. The devolution of the interpretative function in 1943 to branch counsels and field office attorneys, and the appearance of the OPA Service (the black books) and later of the Local Board Loose-Leaf Service (the green books), where interpretations were collected with each regulation, contributed to this development.

The mimeographed series Recent Price Interpretations began in January 1942 before the price control law was finally passed. Interpretations of the GMPR were excluded from this series and handled separately in question and answer press releases. After the 10th issue, and again after the 20th in the series, consolidations were prepared and published. 62

3. AGENCY POLICY, PROCEDURES, AND ORGANIZATION 

Large organizations having complex functions require elaborate internal communications for their direction and management. Organizational lines must be delineated, functions apportioned, and operating relationships defined in order to eliminate overlapping of activities and to achieve the highest degree of cooperative effort. This section of the bibliography is devoted primarily to the publications designed to explain the agency and its objectives to its staff and to instructions governing the performance of official duties. Both national and field instructions are included as well as statements of standards and criteria applying to regulatory actions, the granting of adjustments, etc.

The variety of such materials in the following pages illustrates both the number of kinds of problems on which instructions were necessary and the groping of a rapidly growing agency for adequate instruments of communication. The greatest advance occurred with the institution of the OPA Manual, item 3A.27, which contained in ten volumes of printed loose-leaf sheets, arranged in accordance with a decimal system, materials previously included in a dozen or more series of orders and instructions. 

The extent to which the OPA Manual dominated its field is well indicated by its place in this bibliography. In subsection A, marked "General," are gathered the items which applied to the agency as a whole, or at least to a number of its constituent parts. The first 35 or so, which are concerned with general administrative controls, are separated by side-headings into 4 chronological groups, and one need only glance over these to see that the appearance of the Manual coincides with the agency's arrival at adulthood. Very few general procedures, instructions, or policy statements were issued separately thereafter. The series of 

Administrative Orders, which had been the great instrument of control during the expansion of 1942 and 1943, ceased. From now on, whenever any Administrative Order needed clarification or revision, it was supposed to be incorporated in its new form in the Manual. On the other hand, the Staff Memoranda were continued for the issuance of brief or transitory notices, but this series was now put under the control of the editor of the Manual and so became virtually an adjunct thereto. 

At least two other loose-leaf compilations of importance had preceded the OPA Manual in the field of intra-agency communication (See above, 1B. 3). On August 1, 1942, the OPA Service was inaugurated, chiefly to present in convenient form the regulations and orders and to keep them up to date by supplying amendments, revisions, and new issuances. 

To its many subcribers outside of the organization this was all that the OPA Service provided. There were a great many sets, however, that went to lawyers and other officials within the agency, both in Washington 67

OPA Bibliography 

3A. General and in the field, and to those sets was added a considerable number of "confidential releases" containing procedural and instructional materials. 

Here the Administrative Orders, Operating Orders, Field Price Instruc tions, Local Board Administrative Letters, and many similar items were reprinted for convenient reference. After the establishment of the 

Manual the issuance of "confidential releases" ceased and the OPA Service confined itself to the official regulations and orders and matters. pertaining thereto. Naturally there were a few things on the borderline. 

The Procedural Regulations, for example, concerned both the public and the agency and continued to appear in both publications. 

On March 1, 1943, another instrument of communication made its appearance. Its name, the War Price and Rationing Board Loose-Leaf 

Service, was so formidable that it was almost universally called the "Local Board Service." In content it was a hybrid, carrying both regulations for the public to observe and procedures for the agency to follow. It confined itself to rationing at first and distributed not only the ration orders and their amendments but also great quantities of instructions as to forms and procedures. This was the one large field that the OPA Manual never took over. It set aside its Volume 11 for rationing but did not use it until after the demise of the Rationing Department as such. In 1947, when only sugar remained rationed and the 

Local Board Service had been discontinued, a few items were assigned to Volume 11 of the OPA Manual. 

During 1944 and most of 1945, therefore, when OPA was functioning as a fully developed organization, the Manual served, with relatively few exceptions, as the recognized means of intra-agency communication. 

But the processes of reconversion in late 1945 and the imminent breakup of the agency in late 1946 put severe strains on the communication system. To close 3,600 out of the 5,600 local boards, to reorganize subsequently without any boards at all, and then finally to liquidate the agency entirely, it was necessary to issue a considerable number of instructions very rapidly. As the entries below under "Reconversion and Liquidation" will show, this was done outside the regular channels of the OPA Manual, though in close collaboration with its editorial staff and with more or less explicit reliance on its legal authority. 

Publications closely related to those in section 3 are to be found elsewhere in the bibliography, notably among the Interpretations, in section 2B above; among the Economic, Technical, and Legal Studies, in section 

4 below; in section 5, especially subsection I, on Publicity Through 

Field Organizations; and in section 9D, on Employee Relations.

A. General 

Note. The side-headings in this subsection deserve a word of comment. The first four are chronological, with a view to bringing out the four main periods, 68

General (continued) 3A. each of about two years, in the life history of the organization. The years 1940 and 1941 mark its infancy and childhood. In 1942, with Congressional passage of the Emergency Price Control Act, OPA begins a period of adolescence covering two extraordinary years of growth. During 1944 and 1945 it lives a mature and robust adult life, but suffers in the second summer an operation removing one of its major organs, its Rationing Department. Without rationing it seems likely that no price control agency on a Nation-wide scale could long survive. At any rate, in 1946 the vital powers of OPA fail rapidly, and early in 1947 it is liquidated.

The later side-headings, such as the "Advisory Committees," and the "Training Programs," are obviously not chronological but topical. They represent auxiliary organizations, special programs, or service functions that affected the agency in an over-all manner. Naturally under each of them there could have been a further subdivision by periods if such refinement had seemed expedient. Instead it was judged sufficient under each heading to arrange the items in a general chronological order, though with occasional minor topical groupings that did not merit separate side-headings.

The Administrative Orders were frequently revised and supplements were issued in many cases, both to the originals and the revisions. Each order, revision and supplement bore a title. The mutations of subjects show the main lines of development of the agency, as reflected in the measures taken to build a functional organization and to make it effective in carrying out OPA policies. Orders providing for and defining the functions of offices, departments, divisions, branches, councils, meetings, conferences, committees, units and positions, appear in profusion. An Explanation of Accounting Operations in the National Office came early (May 8, 1942), as did various regulations bearing upon employee relations: personnel, salaries, promotion policy, leave regulations, per diem employment, building passes, and requisitioning employees from the typists' pool. A bit later (July 1942) employees were forbidden activities contrary to the Hatch Act, and the conditions for within-grade salary increases and for termination of employment were defined. 

Selective Service matters, the procedure in the giving of efficiency ratings and identification cards were stated in September 1942. Provisions relating to witness fees and court expenses were issued in November 1942 and July 1943. Later came orders relating to hours of work and rates of pay, the employee suggestion program, security of information, the elimination of possible conflicts between public duty and private interests of staff members, and restrictions upon the purchase by OPA in the open market of scarce articles for staff use. Matters relating to the mechanics of office operation included: an organization guide, communications and files, the issuance and field distribution of official orders, changes in telephone listings, relations between the national office and regional offices, simplified correspondence, numbering of forms, and notification of regional administrators of approaching field trips. 

There is regulation of printing, duplicating, and distribution service, of periodic reporting, of the naming of consultants, of administrative officers and analysts, of relations with other agencies, of meetings and conferences, and of the transfer or abolition of certain services.

27. OPA Manual. 

Looseleaf series, 12 vols., February 22, 1944-May 13, 1947.

Designed as a centralized means for the communication of agency instructions and procedures and for the official demarcation of organizational lines and functions. 

An exception was made, however, of the local War Price and Rationing Boards, for which was maintained a special looseleaf service (see below). The manual, at times referred to unofficially as the OPA Manual of Internal Procedures, was first issued in tentative hectographed form in December of 1943, but that was for the purposes of discussion only. It was intended that all administrative orders, operating orders, and other sets of internal procedures, instructions, policy statements, organization charts, and the like should as rapidly as possible be revised, brought up to date, and incorporated in the manual. For the quick issuance of more or less transitory information as to appointments, holidays, hours of work, and other details of current management, the series, Staff Memorandum, was still maintained. During the period of rapid liquidation in 1947, when it was not possible to wait for the issuance of printed material, certain sets of instructions went out by teletype or were mimeographed, and duly validated as extensions of the OPA Manual. 

The basic authority of the manual was understood to rest upon the last of the 

Administrative Orders, No. 90, effective February 15, 1944. This was issued February 9, 1944, by James G. Rogers, Jr., who was then Deputy Administrator of OPA and who had been authorized to act in certain circumstances for the OPA Administrator, at that time Chester Bowles. Subsequent scrutiny of the exact lines and terms of delegated authority led some to question the authentication of the manual. To allay misgivings, AO 90 was revised on July 6, 1945, with the personal signature of Chester Bowles, and was printed as the preface to the manual (NL 67; second revision, NL 111, August 2, 1946; third revision, NL 119, September 27, 1946).

According to this the several issues of the OPA Manual "are constituted an unnumbered serial supplement to Administrative Order No. 90, Revised." Responsibility for editing and publishing the work is placed upon the Director of the Office of Budget and Planning, who delegated the task to an editorial staff, headed by Mary Dale Buckner. The executive head of each organization unit is made responsible for currently maintaining those volumes or parts which pertain to the authority, structure, responsibility, operating relations, and operating procedures of his unit, and for conforming the operations of his unit to the manual. 

Volumes 1-4 deal with the organization as a whole. Vol. 1, Organization and 

Functions, not only describes the structure of OPA and the functions of its parts, but constitutes also a record of its organizational changes, together with a summary of the agency's legislative and delegated authority. Vol. 2, General Operating Pro cedures, deals with specific program operations involving 2 or more departments or offices, as for example the supervision of local boards. A supplement to Vol. 2 comprises reorganization and liquidation instructions. Vol. 3, National Office General 

Administrative Procedures, deals with matters, as for example travel authorization, 74

General (continued) 3A. usually affecting uniformly all parts of the national office. Vol. 4, Field Office 

General Administrative Procedures, contains instructions of general applicability devised in the national office for use in the field. 

Vols. 5-12 are assigned to the operations of the major departments or functional levels of OPA, as follows: 5, Price; 6, Accounting; 7, Board Management (at one time called Board Operations); 8, Administrative Management; 9, Enforcement; 

10, Clerical Staff; 12, Rent. Vol. 11 was originally designed for the Rationing Department, but remained unassigned because of the existence of another medium, the War Price and Rationing Board Loose-Leaf Service, popularly known as the Local Board Service. Toward the very end of the agency's career a few items were assigned to Vol. 11.

New material was distributed twice weekly for insertion in the manual, and as a covering memorandum a News Letter was prepared for each release. This listed the items covered, gave instructions for filing, and called attention to the salient features of the contents. The letters were numbered serially, and it was found convenient to identify each page of material by printing in the lower margin the number of its covering news letter (abbreviated as N. L. 47, N. L. 89, etc.). Presently the semi-weekly releases themselves were being referred to by these designations. When materials for Vols. 5-12 began to appear, additional sets of news letters were developed to cover them. The releases, together with the inclusive dates, the numerical designations, and the volumes in which the material was to be filed, are as follows: 

OPA Manual News Letter, N.L. 1-142, Feb. 22, 1944-March 31, 1947, Vols. 1-4. 

Price News Letter, P.N.L. 1-143, July 3, 1944-April 1, 1947, Vol. 5.

Accounting News Letter, A.N.L. 1-10, June 5, 1944-May 27, 1946, Vol. 6. 

Board Operations News Letter, B.N.L. 1-14, July 29, 1944–Aug. 17, 1945, Vol. 7. 

Price Board Management News Letter, B.N.L. 1-5, Feb. 5, 1946-May 7, 1946, Vol. 7.

1947, Vol. 8.

Enforcement News Letter, E.N.L. 1–113, Jan. 2, 1945-May 13, 1947, Vol. 9.

Sugar News Letter, National Office, S.N.L. (N.O.) 1, March 13, 1947, Vol. 11.

Citations from the OPA Manual are identifiable only when the section numbers are supplemented by the number of the release (i.e., news letter) as recorded at the extreme right of the lower margin of each page. A numbered series of Replenishment Memos was started to cover reprints of groups of earlier releases that were out of stock (R.M. 1, no date; R.M. 2, December 6, 1944, drafted but not issued).

The OPA Manual will be found with the files of the Records Branch of the Office of Administrative Services, at the National Archives.

32. Board Liquidation Instruction. 

Max McCullough, Deputy Administrator, to regional administrators. Series,

Nos. 1-14, October 29-November 13, 1946. 

Procedure for the liquidation of the remaining 1642 local boards, at that time known as Price Control Boards. Presents a time schedule for the successive steps from October 31 to November 20, discontinues the system of Price Board Management through which instructions and information have previously been channeled to the boards from the National Office, provides for appointment of regional and district liquidation officers, transfers the few remaining price control functions_to the District Offices, and specifies the continuance of rent control by Area Rent Offices and of sugar rationing by District Offices. Includes extensive informational material, reviewing in outline the history of the boards and praising their contribution to the anti-inflation program. Gives detailed directions for the dismissal of unneeded employees, for their placement as far as possible in other positions, for the disposition of records, including those especially asked for by the Bureau of Agricultural Economics, and for the handling of property and supplies. 

Owing to the pressure of time Board Liquidation Instruction No. 1 was sent out with the pages not yet numbered consecutively. On October 31, 1946, No. 2 was sent out by teletype, giving instructions to number consecutively the 44 sheets of No. 1, only a few of which were duplicated on the reverse side. These sheet numbers are referred to in the subsequent items of the series, most of them sent out by teletype, making additions or corrections in the original instructions. No. 3, issued 

November 1, 1946, gives a 5-p. model script for a suggested radio talk by the various 

District Directors, thanking the retiring board members and volunteers for their services, and urging that their efforts to prevent inflation shall now be carried on voluntarily by all citizens, merchants and customers alike. No. 6 issued November 

6, 1946, sends forms and instructions for a systematic reporting of the progress of board liquidation. No. 12, issued November 8, 1946, initiates a plan to transfer from

District to Regional Offices, about November 18, the responsibility for issuing sugar rations.

The series of Board Liquidation Instructions was not put out explicitly as a supplement to the OPA Manual, but is based on its authority. The Liquidation Order, on p. 3 of No. 1, sent out on November 1, 1946 by each Regional Administrator to his District Directors, authorizing them to close all Price Control Boards in their districts, cites the authority conferred upon Regional Administrators by Chapter 

1-106 of the OPA Manual. 

33. Reorganization Instruction. 

Max McCullough, Deputy Administrator, to regional administrators. Series,

Nos. 1-56, November 12, 1946-January 9, 1947. 

Procedure for the partial liquidation of the organization in accordance with the 

President's announcement of November 9, 1946, by which most of the price control programs were discontinued. Contains instructions for eliminating the Price Department and closing the district offices at a program level. To carry on the control of rents, the rationing and price control of sugar and certain syrups, and the price control of rice, the following structure is provided for: The National Office, 76

General (continued) 3A. 

the 9 Regional Offices, the Area Rent Offices, a series of Sugar Branch Offices in the locations of the previous District Offices, and 25 Enforcement Branch Offices. 

Gives organization charts for all levels of the new structure, lists of the authorized positions, and detailed directions for the dismissal of unneeded employees, for the disposition of records, and for the handling of property and supplies. 

Owing to the pressure of time Reorganization Instruction No. 1 was sent out by carrier with the 184 p. not yet numbered consecutively. On November 15, 1946, No. 2 was sent out by teletype, assigning page numbers and listing for each page the code number which it already carried, together with a brief statement of the contents of the page. Pages 179-184 consisted of the four explanatory telegrams and teletypes sent out on November 12, 1946, announcing to the Regional Administrators the projected reorganization and the plans for the series of instructions. Later numbers in the series, many of them sent by teletype, carried additions, corrections, and changes, frequently in the form of replacement pages. 

Pages 185-187 contain a copy of General Order No. 75, issued November 25, 

1946, by Paul Porter, Administrator, and sent out by teletype as Reorganization Instruction No. 15. This validates the entire series by declaring it to be a supplement to vol. 2 of the OPA Manual.

Local Boards and Volunteer Assistants.

Beginning January 5, 1942, OPA was represented in some 7,000 or 

8,000 communities by Tire Rationing Boards, composed chiefly of citizens serving without compensation. The number was later reduced to about 5,600, provision was made for some paid employees, and the official name was changed in April 1942 to "War Price and Rationing Boards." In spite of this they continued throughout their history to be known by the unofficial but convenient term of "Local Boards."

Without them the agency could hardly have conducted its functions of consumer rationing and of price control at the retail level. On their significance, and on the special problems of volunteer assistants, see 

Emmette S. Redford, Field Administration of Wartime Rationing and 

Imogene H. Putnam, Volunteers in OPA, in this series.
