66. War Price and Rationing Board Loose-Leaf Service. 

Loose-leaf series, intended to be filed in 3 volumes, releases 1-273, March 1, 1943January 9, 1946. Title changed to Price Control Board Loose Leaf Service, Releases 274-351, January 12, 1946-November 1946. 

Designed as a centralized means of communication from the national office to the war price and rationing boards which were commonly referred to as local boards. The service was announced by Price Administrator Prentiss M. Brown on 

February 15, 1943, and Release No. 1, sent out on March 1, 1943, was accompanied by a 2-p. News Letter explaining the plan and scope of the work. Subsequent releases went out twice a week, each accompanied by a set of filing instructions. 

Most, though not all, were accompanied also by a News Letter calling attention to salient developments in the program. 

Each page of the service carries in the lower margin the date (in figures), the release number (inserted in parentheses after the date), and a page number (for the guidance of clerks in filing the successive releases). The paragraphs of the text are numbered, and each opening of two pages carries in the outer upper corners the inclusive numbers represented in the text of those pages. All index references are to paragraph numbers, not to page numbers. The paragraph numbers leave no unexplained gaps. Where gaps would occur, the fact is noted that the paragraphs in question are (at the time of that release) blank. 

The orginal function of the local boards had been to administer the rationing programs and in the Service the pages from 1 to 37,000 (with many gaps) are reserved for these programs: Gasoline after 1000, tires 4000, automobiles 7000, bicycles 10,000, sugar 13,000, coffee 16,000, processed foods 19,000, meat 20,000, fuel oil 22,000, shoes 29,000, typewriters 31,000, industrial users 33,000, institutional users 35,000, general 36,000. Retail price control, first established on a wide scale by the 

General Maximum Price Regulation of April 28, 1942, was a second main function of the local boards, and for this the service reserves the pages after 37,000. The pages after 50,000 contain instructions as to certain reports, whether on rationing or on price, required of the boards. Many other reports are dealt with under the programs in question.

For rationing programs the arrangement of the material follows a fairly consistent pattern. After the indexes comes a section giving the regulations (i.e., Ration 

Orders, with their amendments insofar as these touch the operations of the board); then a Guide, giving instructions; then on green pages, with "F" in front of each page number and paragraph number, a field manual containing the procedures required of the district offices. 

The price control activities of the boards came in 1944 to be centered in Price Panels, which were sometimes spoken of as being "the community Price Executive" for the territory covered by the board. For their guidance a "Manual of Price 

Panel Operation" is included in the service, Fages 38,503-38,556, Paragraphs 

10,502-10,659, inaugurated March 29, 1944, with Release No. 111. With this issue the service enters properly into the period of the mature organization. 

This service will be found in the files of the OPA Records Branch at the 

National Archives. 

Training, Professional and Supervisory.

Very early in OPA experience it became apparent that special efforts would be necessary to train new employees in basic fundamentals of the rationing and price and rent control jobs which were assigned to them. 

The earliest recorded training session of this sort was conducted in 

November 1941 by the Clearance and Coordination Section of the Divi tion of Field Operations. The typewritten report of Frank Bane, Director of the Division of Field Operations, submitted in April 1942 for 

OPA's First Quarterly Report also recounts that in January 1942, Lester 

K. Born of his staff visited the existing regional offices across the country to conduct similar training sessions. In May 1942, George Shipman was recruited from the Office of the Deputy Administrator for Price to head 81

OPA Bibliography 

3A. General (continued) a Training Branch in the Personnel Division. This branch, at recurrent intervals from June 1942 onward, undertook a systematic series of indoctrination sessions for recruits. 

The training programs fall naturally into three groups, the professional, the supervisory, and the clerical, and they are presented in that order here. The literature for professional training culminates in the 1943 

Manual of Price Control (No. 73 below), which soon went out of print. 

A few copies were retained during 1944 and 1945 for distribution only to ambassadors and other persons of similar rank and importance. The work was never reissued, because it obviously needed revision to bring it up to date and the manpower to accomplish such a revision was not available. Some of the later thinking of the agency on the same basic problems may be seen in the items listed below under "Standards for 

Price Determination" (Nos. 3B.21–31).

There followed other "schools," such as the one for statisticians and economic analysts which gave rise to the Case Book on Interpretation of Statistical Data. These and subsequent activities of the Training 

Branch are discussed in an unpublished manuscript by Egbert S. Wengert, Analysis of the Work of OPA's Training Branch, item 10B.11 in this bibliography.

The files of the Training Branch contain a sizeable number of publications, not listed here, developed to aid in the education of new employees. 

Many were prepared for field use or developed in the field for use in indoctrinating their own new recruits.

Sent to all price executives with covering memorandum from J. K. Galbraith entitled, "Procedure for maintenance of price action files." Lays the foundation for a system of documentary files designed to provide "an adequate basis for decisions on questions of policy, and for administrative action." 30. Introduction to OPA's General Standards for Setting Maximum Prices, by Reed Dickerson.

Pricing Standards Office. September 20, 1946. [46 p.] 

This is an issue in pamphlet form of the four basic chapters of the General Pricing Standards series, which were a part of Volume 5 of the OPA Manual. Chapter 

5-50 deals with "The Role of Price Control in the Stabilization Program," 5-51 with "Duties and Powers of the Office of Price Administration," and 5-52 with "Establishment, Increase, Reduction, and Withdrawal of Maximum Prices." Chapter 5-73, on "Meaning of OPA Terms," is a glossary providing concise definitions of words and phrases significant in price control operations. 

The pamphlet was designed principally for the use of economists, lawyers, and business specialists, particularly in field offices, who did not receive the full series. 

The introduction is dated August 22, 1946, but the material was issued in the OPA 

Manual on September 20, 1946, as No. 10 in the series of General Pricing Standards 

(released under Price News Letter No. 127). Chapter 5-52 was new at that time, but the other three chapters were revisions, having appeared, respectively, as No. 5 

of the series (P.N.L. 98), No. 7 (P.N.L. 103) and No. 8 (P.N.L. 117). 

The occasion for the pamphlet was the need for an authoritative statement which should take particular account of the changes in pricing standards resulting from the Price Control Extension Act of 1946. (This Act put an end to the hiatus in price control which had followed the expiration of the previous Act on June 30, 1946). 

The treatment is highly condensed and closely reasoned, with continual regard to the legislative basis of the standards and to their historical development through successive stages. 

31. OPA General Pricing Standards, by Reed Dickerson and Jerome A. Levinson. 

Pricing Standards Office, January 2, 1946-December 31, 1946. 

This is an issue (in separate, loose-leaf binder) of the series appearing also in 

OPA Manual, Volume 5, Chapters 5-50 through 5-73, called "General Standards for 

Setting Maximum Prices," of which the first chapter was issued on January 2, 1946, as Price News Letter 79. Later chapters carried, in addition to the identifying symbols of the OPA Manual and the usual "Price News Letter" serial number, a special serial number (“General Pricing Standards No. 2," and so on). The last chapter completed was G.P.S. No. 16, issued December 31, 1946 (P. N. L. 142). 

The series states in concise, integrated form OPA's basic standards for setting maximum prices, including a description of OPA's part in the over-all stabilization program, an inventory of OPA's powers and limitations, and an explanation of the administrative standards adopted by OPA to implement the more general standards provided by the stabilization laws or by executive order of the President. It explains the heterogeneous and uncoordinated policy statements (such as the Tentative Summary of Price Policy, Price Division Directors Memoranda, and miscellaneous general policy statements) in which OPA's basic price policies had previously been stated. The first three chapters provide general orientation; the last, a glossary of 

OPA terms. Other chapters cover specified topics in greater detail, (e.g., exports, transition-product standard, agricultural commodities, decontrol). Each chapter car- 92

ts ed

 ries two appendices: (A) relevant excerpts from the stabilization law, executive orders and directives, (B) citation of other source materials. 

The intended content of the uncompleted chapters is set forth in the mimeo graphed outline, "Topical Analysis of OPA's General Standards for Setting Maximum Prices" (November 1946).

Part III (revised, 26 p.) is an outline of the GMPR, and a discussion of "The 

Retailer's Job under the Maximum Price Regulation," and of "Wholesaling and 

Manufacturing under the General Maximum Price Regulation."

Part IV, "Plan of Organization and Action under General Price Control." Part V, "The Rent Control Program,” 12 p. 

Appendix to Part V issued by Rent Division, 54 p. Designations and maximum rent dates of 323 defense-rental areas, by State. 

Parts I-V are combined in a revision, entitled Price Control Handbook. Part 

III was revised June 6, 1942 and Part IV on June 25, 1942. The "Handbook" ap peared July 1, 1942, 22 p. "While the handbook is not to be considered confidential, neither is it intended for circulation outside of official channels." 

With some omissions, including the pamphlet on sources, the text is identical with the originals.

Explains the factors which account for the rise of 11% between the effective date of the Hold-the-Line Order in April 1943, and November 1944, in the price of clothing. 109. Review of Outstanding Regulations; Elimination of Nonessential Re quirements. ) December 14, 1942. 2 p. 

Memorandum from J. K. Galbraith to division directors, attention price executives. 

Expresses anxiety "to have a thoroughgoing review of the outstanding regulations of the OPA for the purpose of removing, as far as possible provisions which do not by way of practical accomplishment justify the annoyance they may cause to those who are subject to regulation." Asks every price executive to review his regulations with a view to eliminating all that have not justified themselves. Covers reporting, filing, record keeping, substantive directions and requirements in regulations, and may include, at discretion of the price executive and director, "the elimination of wholly unconsequential items or firms from price control." Attached is a 

1-p. memorandum from Ben W. Lewis to regional price executives_and_district price officers (January 20, 1943), subject, "Simplification of Price Regulations."

States that Lewis is responsible "for an over-all review of the regulations with a view generally to their revision along the lines indicated." Asks for specific suggestions from the field.

D. Rent 

1. Administrative and Other Practical Problems Involved in Rent Control. 

Rent Section, Price Division. June 27, 1941. 

Memorandum from Karl Borders, Chief of the Rent Section (through Assistant Administrator, Price Division) to the Administrator, OPACS. Discusses the geographic limitation of defense rental areas, specified percentage increases as a condition precedent to rent regulations, limitation of regulation to categories of rental housing accommodations, and the mechanics of assuring local authorities an opportunity to handle the problem before legal controls are imposed. Concludes with recommendations.

8. Processing of Cases Arising Under Section 5(a) (9) of the Rent Regula tion for Hotels and Rooming Houses. 

Office of the Deputy Administrator for Rent. August 30, 1946. 6 p. 

Memorandum from Ivan D. Carson, Deputy Administrator, to all regional rent executives and all area rent directors. States that, effective immediately, the national office will no longer pre-audit substantial hardship cases arising under Section 5 (a) (9) of the Rent Regulation for Hotels and Rooming Houses, except those already being processed in that office. Unusual cases, it says, may still be forwarded to the national office. The procedure to be followed by area offices in processing cases under Section 5(a) (9) is stated. Pertinent paragraphs of that section are quoted and various phrases used therein are defined in language more or less technical. "Requirements" and "Adjustment Policy" are explained rather fully.

5. Field Legal Instructions: General Instruction. 

[Legal Division] Series, Nos. 1-2, July 20, 1942 - July 31, 1943. 

Nos. 1, 2 (tentative and final drafts), 2r, 2(2d r), and Supplements 1 and 2 to 

2(2d r), "Basic Instructions for Attorneys and Legal Investigators in Regional,

State, District, and Defense-Rental Area Offices," show the legal staff in a regional office as headed by a regional attorney, with a regional price attorney, regional rationing attorney, and a regional investigator. The last-named had charge of compliance surveys and legal investigations, a function which the Legal Division inherited from the former Division of Field Operations on the latter's dissolution. 

The instructions evolve through succeeding issues. 

6. Medford Plan of Promoting Price Compliance. 

) October 8, 1942. 1 p. 

Memorandum from Harvey Pinney, [Senior Administrative Analyst] to Stanley 

Orear, [Acting Director, Organization and Planning], to cover a compilation of documents pertaining to the plan. Critically appraises the type of activity reported. 

The covered documents include a letter, dated October 2, 1942, from John W. Teele, State Price Officer (Massachusetts), to Stanley T. Orear, which covers copy of "Community Mobilization for War Economy" (the "Medford Plan"), and reports 100% compliance in Medford as a result of the program. Note on attached routing slip suggests that this plan may have been influential in the making of later plans for securing compliance. 

7. Field Legal Instructions-Enforcement Instruction. 

Series, Nos. 1-22, December 22, 1942 – August 8, 1944. 

Nos. 1-4 were issued by Brunson MacChesney, Assistant General Counsel. Later ones were by Thomas I. Emerson, Senior Associate General Counsel, with the exception of Nos. 11 and 12. George J. Burke, General Counsel issued No. 11, and 

No. 12 was over the signature of both Donald H. Wallace, Acting Deputy Administrator for Price, and Burke. No. 12 appeared also as Price Operating Instruction, Field, No. 6 and carries that title as well as that of the series here listed. Revisions, supplements and amendments were issued by Emerson under the abbreviated title of Enforcement Instruction, which also beginning with No. 13 (July 3, 1943) became the sole series title. For the period covered, these instructions contain the basic developing enforcement program of OPA. Evolution was rapid, and, especially after Emerson became a leading figure in it, the changes were extensive, as shown in the revisions of the instructions. Topics stressed are rent and rationing enforcement, enforcement reporting, licensing enforcement procedure, and suspension order, treble damage, and criminal proceedings. The Enforcement Department issued (October 14, 1943) Field Enforcement Instruction No. 15, which superseded Field Legal

Instruction, General Instruction No. 2 (2d Revision) on "Reporting on Field Legal Operations"; also Field Legal Instructions, Enforcement Instruction No. 2 on “En forcement Reporting."

12. The Compliance Program. 

Office of the Administrator. May 17, 1944. 5 p.

Memorandum from Chester Bowles to deputy and regional administrators. Outlines the program for setting up compliance committees to promote enforcement or compliance. The basic work is directed to be organized through the program and enforcement staffs (no compliance staff to be organized). The compliance committees were to function through meetings of those committees, separately and jointly with those of the trade, through the use of educational or instructional material, and in cooperation with the program and enforcement staffs.

102. Facts About the OPA Administrator's Claim. 

Department of Information. August 1944. 2 p.

This claim is stated to be that arising under the Emergency Price Control Act of 1942 allowing an overcharged buyer to sue for three times the amount of the overcharge, or $50, whichever is greater, and amended to permit OPA to bring suit under the law if the buyer does not sue within 30 days. Such an OPA suit deals with what is called the "Administrator's Claim." States that this authority was given 

OPA in response to a popular demand for securing compliance with ceiling prices. 

Traces the procedure by which such a claim is presented. 

103. Retroactive Effect of Prices Established by the Office of Price Administration Under MPR 88 and MPR 188. 

Litigation Division. August 12, 1944. 7 p. 

Memorandum from Fleming James, Jr., Director Litigation Division, to David B. 

Love, regional litigation attorney, Dallas Regional Office. Discusses the conditions under which treble damage suits should be brought against sellers of goods at overceiling prices. Thinks "retroactive" not an accurate word to use, as the offense was, in some instances, committed before OPA fixed a price. Presents considerable legal argument.

H. Budget and Personnel 

The nature of the operations carried on by the personnel and budget offices gave rise to few published materials. Perhaps the most important exceptions to this statement are the instructional and procedural series listed under 3A above, of which the Administrative Orders, the OPA Manual, and the Reorganization Instructions are good examples. Being management offices, they were concerned primarily with the agency's internal problems. Considerations of personnel and budget entered so generally into all management problems that these offices contributed substantially to many of the materials listed throughout this section, although few of them could be placed in a category so narrow as suggested by the terms "personnel" and "budget.”

Even the items listed below are not publications in the sense that they were intended to have wide distribution. The appropriation estimates submitted at least once a year provide the agency's official statement of its objectives, program, and needs, and are an invaluable source of many kinds of information. Since the regular annual estimates were rather formal in nature and were necessarily prepared long in advance of their appraisal by Congress, a fuller appreciation of the considerations which went into the determination of OPA's scale of operations can be had if the estimates are studied in conjunction with the legislative hearings, appropriations committee reports, and the floor debates in Congress. 

Because the operations of the personnel and budget offices involved policy matters which were the concern of only a few top management 153

OPA Bibliography 3H. Budget and Personnel (continued) 

officials, few reports were prepared for wide dissemination. Monthly employment reports were prepared for the U. S. Civil Service Commission on Standard Form 3257 and for the Senate Committee on Executive Expenditures (Byrd Committee) which at the time this bibliography went to press were in the operating files of the Division of Liquidation of the Department of Commerce. 

The records of the personnel office sent to the National Archives include a great variety of memoranda on personnel problems of broad significance such as turnover, minority groups, etc. Those of the budget office include materials for both the national office and field offices on which were based the employment reports listed below, as well as the working papers used in the preparation of appropriation estimates, and quarterly allotment requests and approvals for the national office departments and the field offices. 

1. Appropriation Estimates and Justifications. 

Twenty-four volumes of looseleaf notebooks, listed below, covering the period from October 1941 to June 1947 and containing mimeographed, multilithed, dittoed, and photostatic tables, charts, and text material prepared for formal presentation to the Bureau of the Budget and to the Congress, setting forth in considerable detail the expenditures proposed for each program or organizational unit and information as to the needs for such expenditures.

Prior to July 1, 1942, the agency's financial requirements were provided from emergency funds at the disposal of the President of the United States and its expenditure program was reviewed only by the Bureau of the Budget. For this reason, because the agency was then small, and because its needs could be reviewed at frequent intervals, the materials prepared in this early period were both less formal and less comprehensive. In subsequent years the form in which the estimates and justifications were presented varied considerably in accordance with directions issued by the Estimates Division of the Bureau of the Budget and the expressed wishes of the Appropriations Committees of the House and Senate. 

In the case of supplemental estimates especially, the press of events sometimes precluded comprehensive documentation of a request, with the result that the materials listed below do not cover all supplemental and amended appropriation requests which were actually submitted to the Congress. Conversely, the list contains two estimates which were prepared but never submitted. The first of these was an appropriation estimate to cover the period from February 1, 1942, to June 30, 1942, prepared shortly after the OPA was given a statutory basis by the passage of the 

Emergency Price Control Act. With the decision to continue providing the agency's financial requirements out of emergency funds for the remainder of the 1942 fiscal year, its submission became unnecessary. The other instance occurred in the third quarter of the fiscal year 1943, when plans to request a deficiency appropriation for the remainder of that year were finally abandoned after the estimates had been prepared. 

Federal budgetary procedure requires that each appropriation estimate be reviewed and approved by the Bureau of the Budget before it is transmitted to the Congress as the recommendation of the President. Revisions made in the estimates by the 

Bureau of the Budget, often extensive in the case of OPA, obliged the agency in many instances to prepare a completely new set of estimates and justifications for presentation to the Appropriations Committees of the Congress. In the listing below, when separate presentations were prepared in connection with the appropriation requested for any particular year, this fact is indicated by the phrase "Bureau of the Budget Submission" or "Congressional Submission," as the case may be. 4. ECONOMIC, TECHNICAL, AND LEGAL STUDIES 

In every period a significantly large portion of the work done by OPA employees consisted of making studies, economic, legal, accounting, etc., and of taking action upon the basis of such studies. Price regulations, to name but one example, were nearly always preceded by extensive economic and accounting investigations, the results of which were apparent in the text of the regulations and summarized in the accompanying statements of considerations. Publications which might properly be classified as technical studies are therefore to be found listed in nearly every section of this bibliography. Attention is directed to the products of economic and legal research included among the policy statements and instructions in the previous sections, the statistical studies relating to forms listed in Section 9, and the informational materials prepared for the public or OPA field officials summarized in Section 5. Many of these latter present the products of OPA research in a concise and useful form. 

In addition many of the speeches and statements grouped in Section 7, particularly the statements and exhibits to Congress, differ little, except in manner of presentation, from studies contained here. 

Most of the studies made by the OPA staff were for a particular occasion and because of a limited number of interested readers remained in typewritten form. This is true particularly of the economic studies made by price and rationing branches in support of their regulatory actions. It is also true of the bulk of the legal studies made by the Legal 

Department's Research Branch. These latter took the form of a numbered series of interpretative memoranda, many of them of considerable length, upon points of law arising in the course of the development of regulations or in the conduct of litigation. Studies made by the Research 

Division, on the other hand, were generally intended for a wider audience, both in the particular operating division concerned and throughout the policy echelons of the agency, and for that reason were more frequently duplicated. Consequently, publications of the Research Division bulk large in this collection.

Prominent among the Research Division's contributions to the literature of OPA are five sets of publications in series, as distinguished from serial publications. They are the Price Analysis Series, the Price Policy 

Series, the Price Control Reports, the War Profits Studies, and the For eign Information Series. The first three of these were closely related in content, authorship, and time of preparation, 1942-43. The first consists largely of a series of analyses of statistical information, price indices and the like; the second deals with the methodology of price control, of which the essays on The Pricing of Joint Products, item 4D.8, and on Economic 

Criteria of Fair and Reasonable Profits, item 4D.6, are representative. 157

OPA Bibliography 44. General Economic Studies (continued) 

These theoretical discussions were intended to aid the top officials in the Price Department in deciding particular policy issues in a way consistent with a reasoned approach to the basic economic problems involved. 

Approximately a dozen items included in the Price Control Reports series indicate for the information of the Administrator, his top aides, and other higher Government officials, a running history of the price controls actions taken and of their effectiveness.

Research on the experience of foreign governments with economic mobilization, price control and rationing began in the Price Stabilization Division in the summer of 1940. The usefulness of the studies then produced led to the preservation of this staff as a Foreign Information Unit in the Division of Research. The Foreign Information series consists of many of the publications of this unit which were duplicated to make them easily available to top OPA officials and other Government agencies interested in foreign trade and foreign economic controls. The unit with its files was eventually transferred to the Foreign Economic Administration.

70. Statement by Paul A. Porter, Price Administrator, before the Interstate

Commerce Commission, Ex Parte 148 “reopened” (and Ex Parte 162). 

Office of the Administrator. 1946. 11 p. plus 3 exhibits. 

Stresses that the effect of the drastic rate increases sought by the railroads, in his judgment, would be seriously detrimental to the stabilization program. Does not urge that no rate increase be allowed. Recognizes rights of railroads to reasonably remunerative rates. Without that, their inefficiency would be injurious to the whole economy. Suggests that rate action be aimed at securing during the coming year an adequate and efficient transportation system. Thinks just rates can be based only on a full hearing. Considerable rate increases would force price increases, he says, which would become general. Says a coming witness will testify that railroads do not urgently need a raise. 170

23. Preliminary Report on Survey of Cost Accounting in Industry. 

Accounting Department. April 8, 1946. 27 p. 

A study, covering approximately 150 industries, of: (1) The extent to which cost accounting systems exist; (2) The type of cost accounting systems in use; (3) The availability of prime, manufacturing and total costs in existing cost records and reports. Prepared by Martin L. Black, C.P.A. and Harold B. Eversole, C.P.A., Consultants, from information available within the Accounting Department. 

Attached is a covering memorandum from Paul M. Green, Deputy Administrator for Accounting, to Paul A. Porter, Administrator (April 10, 1946) which states the report "is a preliminary one but it does emphasize the difficulties that would be involved in attempting to determine a total unit product cost for a given product in all of the companies in any industry." 

24. A Report on Cost Accounting in Industry. 

Accounting Department. June 30, 1946. 72 p. 

A report on cost systems in industry, unique in accounting history in that for the "first time information has been collected to show the extent to which cost accounting data are actually available." Prepared by Martin L. Black, Jr., C.P.A. and Harold B. Eversole, C.P.A., Consultants.

This is a final report on the study of cost accounting in approximately 150 industries and industrial groups on which a preliminary report was made on April 8, 1946. This final report contains, in additon to the information in the preliminary report, references to competition, historical pricing, tendencies under price control, and some elaboration of cost accounting details for most of the industries covered.

20. Summary of "Demobilization of Wartime Economic Controls" by J. M. 

Clark.

Office of the Economic Advisor. February 26, 1945. 13 p. 

Prepared as a research study under the sponsorship of the Committee for Economic Development. Relates to the "gradual relaxation and removal" of special wartime economic controls in general. Forecasts a probable tapering off of war effort toward the end and considerable reconversion to civilian production. After the close of the war the bulk of reconversion is scheduled, including return of most men and women from the armed services and the general reorganizing for peace production. Then would come the period of catching up with deferred demand for civilian durable goods, followed by that of long-run adjustment. Summarizes aims, methods, objectives, goals, future plans, lingering war controls, persisting difficulties, deficit spending in the long pull, and conclusion. Attached is a 1-p. covering note from the economic advisor.

33. Canadian War Finance, by A. F. W. Plumptre, Consultant.

Defense Finance Section, OPACS. April 1, 1941. 273 p. Foreword by Leon 

Henderson is dated May 15, 1941.

Broad analysis of Canada's war effort to show the manner in which the real burden of the war program has been borne by the Canadian economy-to what extent by increased employment of men and resources and increasing the national income, and to what extent by diverting men and resources from usual peacetime channels into the war effort. Covers the period from September 1939 to the end of 1940. (This report was prepared during the period of NDAC, but was not ready for distribution until after the inauguration of OPACS.)

73. Relation Between Wages and the Cost of Living Index in Wartime 

Britain.

Foreign Information Unit. March 14, 1942. 3 p. 

Says average wages rose 20% from the outbreak of the war until April 1941, and that cost of living index rose 27% over the same period. Since April 1941, the the government's policy is said to have been to stabilize the cost of living index by means of subsidies and this is reported to have been effective in controlling wages without industrial friction.

Concludes with a set of principles to be used as a guide to a price control program in the "present emergency." 5 charts, 3 tables. Exists also in House hearings on price control, 1941, p. 146–156. A 13-p. edition without appendix exists.

living. Concludes with a discussion of the aftermath of deflation which follows all periods of inflation. 28 p. of charts (not included in the pagination). Exists also in House hearings on price control, 1941, p. 204–224. 

5. Character of Government Control of Prices During the World War. 

) n.d. 21 p. plus 5-p. appendix.

Reviews the course of prices during the first World War, the organization, authority and timing of government price control, methods of control, the information necessary for the inauguration of price control, procedure for determining maximum prices, the "bulk line" cost method of establishing maximum prices, and the removal of government price controls. ) [1941?] 20 p. Reviews conditions of the first World War and those of the first year of this one, with the 1941 price rise, and concludes with a warning against extended price increases. 14 charts. Exists also in House hearings on price control, 1941, p. 237256. 

6a. The Control of Rents. 

[Rent Section, Price Division, OPACS] [About July 1941] 19 p. 

Argument for, and history of, the Federal control of rents in wartime. Describes the unprecedented need for rental housing in shipbuilding centers, aircraft centers, ordnance plant vicinities, military establishments and centers of varied industrial production. States there has been steadily increasing demand for crude petroleum above prewar levels. Figures for 1943 are given. 15. The Effects of the Pace Bill. 

Division of Research. March 25, 1943. 15 p.

It states that the direct results of the bill would be to necessitate high maximum prices for flours, corn, sugar, cotton textiles, and many other products; that indirect results would be the raising of prices for feeds other than corn, meat, dairy products and poultry; also an increase of parity prices of all farm commodities by 2%, an estimated increase of 10% in the retail cost of food, and an estimated increase in the cost of feeding our armed forces and supplying our allies of three-quarters of a billion dollars annually; that these increases would involve raises in wages which would naturally lead to high prices paid by farmers, and, in turn, raise further the prices of farm products.

27. Analysis of Price Control Bill Passed by the House. 

) April 26, 1946. 8 p.

Appraisal of the House-passed version of the price control renewal act. Rejects claims that this bill would stimulate maximum production while staving off inflation. Would require immediate removal of price ceilings covering more than one-half the goods in our economy. Remaining ceilings, it is stated, would be materially raised. Experience shows hoarding would result, wages would be pushed up, followed by price increases, and inflation would be on the way. Discusses eight amendments, any one of which would endanger public confidence in the stability of prices, and which together amount to repeal of price control.

5. RELATIONS WITH THE PUBLIC AND THE TRADE 

The press releases issued by the OPA and its predecessor agencies were the chief medium by which it sought to explain its programs and activities to the public. The different series of such releases are contained in the record files of the Information Department rather than in this bibliographical collection and reference to them will supplement the other types of publications listed in this section. With the file of press releases is a card index containing the number of the release, the date, and a brief summary of its contents. There are in the collection eight series of releases, each series identified by a letter symbol; within each series the releases were numbered in the order of their issuances. The T stands for "Trade," N for "Negroes," and W for "Women." The basic series are as follows:

PR release series. This series was the output of the divisions which made up the 

National Defense Advisory Commission including the Price Stabilization Division and the Consumer Division which were the predecessors of OPACS. The file is complete from No. 1, June 3, 1940, to No. 3510, January 15, 1941.

PM release series. These press releases were issued by various war agencies through the Office for Emergency Management. The first was dated December 21, 1940; the last in this file December 30, 1942. OPA issuances through this series apparently stopped with No. 3677, June 17, 1942. This file is incomplete.

T release series.-This series was the companion to the PM series being issued for a number of agencies first by OEM, then by OWI. These releases were considered to be of more special interest to the trade press than the PM series which was for the general press. About half of the items in this incomplete file running from No. 2, October 4, 1941, to No. 821, September 2, 1942, originated in OPA.

OPA series. This series for daily newspapers succeeded the PM series but was limited to OPA issuances. The file runs from No. 1, June 15, 1942, to No. 6978, April 28, 1947.

OPA-T series.-The counterpart of the OPA series, being intended for the technical and trade press. The file is complete from the first issuance on June 15, 1942 to No. 5205, May 12, 1947.

The press releases in the PR, PM, and T series issued prior to February 11, 1942 by OPA and its predecessor agencies pertaining to price control are indexed and digested in Federal Price Control, item 6D.2 in this bibliography.

There were also three series more limited in number and scope: 

N release series.-The file of these releases issued by OPA through OEM and 

OWI is quite incomplete. It begins with No. 38, October 3, 1941. The later issues are undated.

W releases. A series started by the Consumer Division of OPA and continued by the Information Department for the editors of women's pages of daily newspapers. The incomplete file begins with No. 7, December 1, 1941 and ends with No. 

213, December 10, 1943.

OEM-OPA (Consumer Division).-This series of weekly releases listed best buys in fruits and vegetables. There were several releases each week from December 12, 1941 to December 25, 1942 for different areas of the country. 207

B. Information to Consumers, Price Control 

1. Memorandum (to Consumers). 

Consumer Division. n.d. 1 p. 

From Harriet Elliott. Expresses interest in holding down the cost of living. Suggests that consumers support pending action by Congress. 

2. Consumer Prices. 

Consumer Division. November 15, 1940-June 1, 1942. 24 issues, appearing every two weeks. (Nos. 1-8 issued under NDAC, No. 9 under OEM, Nos.

10-18 under OPACS, and Nos. 19-24 under OPA). 

Part of the consumer protection program of the Consumer Division, which sought to minimize the effect of defense purchases upon the supply of consumer goods. 212

Information to Consumers, Price (continued) 5B. 

Question of food is stressed. Expressed optimism regarding the food supply (November 1940). This series was designed to help consumers keep abreast of supplies and prices, particularly relating to food. Reports of food prices are based upon data collected (at the request of the Consumer Division) by the U. S. Bureau of 

Labor Statistics on the prices of certain foods in large cities, semi-monthly, and upon other reports of that Bureau and other agencies. Numerous varieties of consumer goods and services were given special treatment at opportune times. Some of them were nylon hosiery (December 21, 1940), meat (January 13, 1941), fish (January 27, 1941), rents (February 10, 1941), "enriched" bread and flour (February 27, 1941), substitutes for aluminum cooking utensils (March 14, 1941). Beginning with No. 9, April 7, 1941, the issues were enlarged, and beginning with No. 

10, April 30, 1941, the magazine type of arrangement was adopted with several articles upon significant topics in each issue. Soon coal, fuel oil and gasoline, and work clothing received attention, followed by refrigerators, electric power, coffee, olive oil substitutes, consumer information centers, women's coats, woolen blankets, milk, scrap, the price control law, sugar rationing, cloth, and pork chops. 

Attached to issue No. 1 is A Guide to the Use of Consumer Prices (November 

15, 1940) 3 p., which is in_the_nature_of_a substantial covering memorandum, originating in the Consumer Division, NDAC.

E. Information to Trade and Press

The effectiveness of OPA's rationing, price and rent control programs depended in substantial measure upon the voluntary cooperation of those most directly concerned with them, principally the business community. This, in turn, required that formal legal methods of giving notice of regulatory actions be supplemented by less formal explanations of why the actions were taken, and what in general they required, giving answers to questions most likely to be raised. For this purpose, the chief instrument was, of course, the agency's series of press releases. Such releases, or a waiver by the Information Department stating that none was necessary, were accordingly required by agency rule to accompany the issuance of every formal regulatory action. Although all of them 223

OPA Bibliography 

5E.  were made available to the general press, many were expected to be of interest primarily to trade journals and were, for that reason, usually written with their readers particularly in mind (the T and OPA-T 

Series). To aid in the distribution of such trade releases, three serial issuances were eventually established, Facts for the Apparel Trade, Food 

Facts of Interest to the Trade, Facts for the Consumer Durables Trade, items 27, 33, and 38, below. Each contained in a single weekly issuance all office press releases of that week of interest to these industries. 

Perhaps the second most significant channel used in reaching businessmen with information designed to inspire their compliance with OPA rules lay through the field offices. A section below, I., is devoted to the informational materials developed for the use of field officials in bringing the OPA story to their local communities. Still another device resorted to was the explanatory article written by an OPA official for a particular trade journal and printed by it over his signature. These are not here classed as OPA publications. In addition to all these there were innumerable pamphlets, handbooks, question and answer sheets, and the like, prepared for a particular occasion and for a specific industry audience. It is mainly these which are listed here. Because of the temporary character of many of these documents and their origin in operating branches as well as in the Information Department, no central file of such publications was ever kept. The listing here is admittedly far from exhaustive.

50. Price Control and Teacher's Purchasing Power in 1944-45.

Department of Information. September 1945. 2 p. plus two charts. "To Educational Journals." States that increases in teachers' salaries between 

1939 and 1943 had lagged considerably behind increases in cost of living, and that although there was an increase in their salaries of about 5.5 per cent between the school years of 1943-1944 and 1944-45, teachers in the period since 1939 had suffered a "real salary cut" of about $47 (1944-45 dollars) per teacher below the 1939-40 level. Meanwhile, it says, the cost of living had risen 27%.

OPA Bibliography interested groups and the public generally, either directly or through the local press and other mass media of communication. 71. Meat Supply Situation. 

Office of the Administrator. March 22, 1945. 3 p. 

Memorandum from Chester Bowles to regional administrators and district directors. Points out that though the slaughter of federally inspected beef is 17% above a year before, the Army, Navy and other procurement agencies (Lend Lease, etc.) were getting over 50% of such beef. Also that number of beef cattle in feed lots is near all time high. Discusses further misconceptions regarding hogs and all meats.

6. REPORTS ON AGENCY ACTIVITIES A. Periodic Progress Reports 

There is in the Federal service a strong tradition in support of periodic progress reports; OPA was no exception. Almost with the beginning of the National Defense Advisory Commission, each of its constituent divisions was required to submit a weekly report of its activities to the Executive Secretary. A limited number of these divisional progress reports were then bound together and distributed to members of the commission and other high Government officials. They give a weekly bird'seye view of the progress of war mobilization. 

A similar pattern of weekly progress reports was instituted with the formation of OPACS. Each of the divisions submitted to the Administrator's office a typewritten report of one or two pages in length. These were assembled into a single mimeographed document. A collection of these weekly OPACS and OPA progress reports, together with many of the typewritten reports from which they originated, extending well into 1942, is in the agency's record files deposited in the National Archives. 

As the agency grew, reports aiming to keep the Administrator and his chief aides informed regarding divisional activities were no longer sufficient. They could not be detailed enough to give the heads of the major departments-price, rent, and rationing-the information they and their field office counterparts needed. As a result each department developed a reporting system adapted to its needs. Initially most reports were required weekly, although some, especially from field officers, were as infrequent as monthly. Ultimately most reports were placed on a biweekly basis since preparation of more frequent reports seemed to consume time more urgently required for other activities.

In general progress reports from organizational units below the divisional level were submitted in typescript only. The divisional report both in the national office and in the regional offices was, however, characteristically mimeographed. In form it was frequently merely a collection of the reports of subordinate units with perhaps an introductory statement prepared in the divisional executive's office. Similarly regional office reports were composites of the reports of district program executives and of the section chiefs within the division in the regional office. The duplicated reports of regional executives were often circulated to all other regions for their information as well as sent to the national office. 

Under the pressure of other business these reports often tended to become formal outlines of actions contemplated or taken, containing barely enough information to satisfy the requirement that there be a report. Those from the field offices were generally more informative, as regional officials sought by every means at their command to impress 271

OPA Bibliography 6B. Minutes and Transcripts of Meetings their problems and urgent needs upon their national office colleagues. 

Occasionally one finds a choice bit as some regional executive "lets down his hair" with a blast. Where the task was taken seriously the reports are candid and revealing, especially on problems of field delegation. 

The Enforcement Department in particular maintained an elaborate system of periodic reports. In addition to the customary field narrative report there were various statistical reports of investigations made, violations found, sanctions imposed, etc. The national office report was also frequently used as a vehicle for the transmission of important statements of office policy or of program changes to the field. 

Files of periodic progress reports are much too bulky, and even a list of originating divisions would be too lengthy, for inclusion in this bibliography. The OPA record files of each department, Price, Enforcement, Rationing, etc., in the National Archives, however, contain relatively complete sets of the mimeographed divisional and regional progress reports. 

B. Minutes and Transcripts of Meetings 

All extant transcripts of OPA meetings held in or sponsored by the national office were brought together by the Records Branch in a single collection for transfer to the National Archives. Some were mimeographed; most were typescripts from stenographic notes; most of them also were unedited and reflect among other things the state of the stenographic art during wartime. They were originally arranged in one chronological series, but in the process of transfer an attempt was made to classify them into major categories. 

Unlike the War Production Board, whose structure and method of operation involved numerous inter-agency and inter-divisional committees, each leaving minutes for the record, OPA's organization called for few operating committees, and hardly any that regularly kept minutes of their meetings. Three exceptions may be noted: (1) The Price Administration 

Committee was an inter-agency sounding board for Henderson, established by the executive order creating OPACS, which met from April 1941 to March 1942. Transcripts of its meetings were taken, and summaries of these were prepared and circulated by one of Henderson's assistants. The summaries have been printed under the title Minutes of the 

Price Administration Committee (item No. 6B.1 in this bibliography); 

the transcripts are filed with other transcripts in OPA records and are a first-class source on the development of early policy at a top civilian level. Notwithstanding the notation on p. iv of the published Minutes, a complete set of the transcripts has been located and filed. (2) The 

Policy Committee, consisting of the Assistant Administrators (later Directors of the Price Divisions), a few price executives, the top price lawyers, Henderson's economic advisor, and from time to time others, was established early in 1942 under the chairmanship of Price Deputy 272

6. Reports on Agency Activities Minutes and Transcripts of Meetings (continued) 6B. 

J. K. Galbraith to formulate the over-all price freeze known as the 

GMPR. For a time it was almost a governing body for the price divisions; it considered and decided major price control issues as they rose. 

Its corporate authority declined after June of that year, but its members were at all times key officials for price policy. Minutes of its meetings from March 17, 1942 to June 9, 1943 were kept, and duplicated (item 6B.4 in this bibliography). These too are an authoritative and revealing source for the study of price policy during the period covered. (3) In 

1945 a network of so-called Coordinating Committees, each including representatives of a commodity program division, and the Enforcement and Information Departments, was established in the national office and in the field offices, to bring about a better coordination of mutually interdependent activities. The committees were instructed to meet regularly and to keep minutes but few of them were duplicated. A brief discussion of their work will be found in Virgil B. Zimmermann, Problems in Price 

Control: National Office Organization and Management (item No. 6D.1 

in this bibliography).

Separate mention should also be made of the transcripts of some early meetings Henderson addressed, not always in OPA. A notable example is his session with the National War Labor Board on February 6, 1942, at which he reviewed stabilization developments and problems of the previous year and presented a forecast for the months ahead. Not included because not duplicated are a fairly lengthy series of minutes of Bowles' staff meetings, and a series of transcripts of the Administrator's press conferences.

Transcripts of testimony of OPA officials before congressional committees are excluded as available elsewhere; these include legislative, appropriation and special investigating committees.

Apart from these, the transcripts cover two main categories of meetings-those with advisory committees, and intra-agency conferences. 

The advisory committees included the informal industry panels, industry advisory committees, the Labor Policy Committee, the Consumer Advisory Committee, and a few others intermittently or ad hoc. The labor and consumer committees met fairly regularly four or five times a year with someone from the Administrator's immediate staff and reviewed agency activities and problems broadly. 

The transcripts of industry committee meetings make up by far the largest part of all transcripts in the collection; they probably amount to some 200 linear feet, the equivalent of two dozen 4-drawer file cabinets. 

Ultimately, over 600 industry committees were formally established under the terms of Procedural Regulation No. 13. A few never met; many more met only once or twice, at the time a regulation was issued; but a substantial number met frequently and were prolific for the record. 273

OPA Bibliography 6B. Minutes and Transcripts of Meetings (continued) 

Industry committees were established and extensively consulted from the beginning, early in 1941, and transcripts of their meetings became the common practice. Their discussions usually centered on the specific problems and regulations in their commodity areas. As the agency's organization crystallized the committees' contacts were channeled through the sections (later branches) having jurisdiction over their commodities; their meetings were ordinarily attended by the respective price executives. 

After the issuance of Procedural Regulation No. 13 and the establishment of the Office of Industry Advisory Committees with procedural and coordinating functions in mid-1943, that office expressed concern lest the existence of purportedly verbatim and actually unedited transcripts should prove a source of embarrassment; by that time, too, stenographic help was at a premium. Consequently summary minutes were suggested as the preferred practice, with price executives retaining the authority, nevertheless, to arrange for transcripts in their discretion in particular cases. As it turned out, summaries pleased no one and proved no less difficult to prepare. Transcripts continued to be obtained in most cases. 

They were ordinarily supplied in 4 copies, one each for the committee chairman or secretary, the commodity branch, the Office of Industry Advisory Committees, and the files of the Conference Service Unit that made physical arrangements for meetings. In the interests of candid discussion, committee members were asked not to publish or release their copy. 

Transcripts were taken at many but by no means all general conferences of agency personnel. One type commonly reported was the training session. At the inception of each major program it was customary for the national office division chiefs concerned to summon their regional office counterparts for a series of explanatory conferences. Since these men in turn were responsible for training and supervising district office personnel in the program, a conference record was a useful addition to whatever informational materials were prepared. Where time permitted in the development of a program such conferences might be held before the regulation was fully crystallized, and field advice thus be brought to bear on the resolution of anticipated problems. This was done, for example, in the planning for clothes rationing (which never materialized) in July 1942, and in January 1943 in connection with community food pricing plans. Galbraith's Chicago conference with regional price executives in

July 1942 to review the development of price policy was a notable reported instance where training and consultation were joint objectives. 

Periodic and less ambitious conferences of this sort, usually but not always held in Washington, were a regular method of consultation between the Administrator or his senior deputy and the regional administrators; the price deputy and the regional price executives; the rationing and rent deputies and their regional executives; the personnel, budget, board operations and administrative services chiefs and their regional 274

6. Reports on Agency Activities Minutes and Transcripts of Meetings (continued) 6B. 

representatives; the commodity division and branch chiefs and their regional representatives, and so on. All this was part of the scheme of multiple lines of communication and control by which the needs of technical and administrative supervision were accommodated. Only the regional administrators' meetings were consistently reported, though transcripts of the others were frequently prepared. 

Training conferences were a necessity not only in connection with new programs, where the program division took the initiative, but also for new personnel in established programs. Most of these meetings were held by or under the auspices of a Training Branch in the Personnel Division. Publications prepared by it or relating to its activities are grouped in Section 3A.67-93, above. 

1. Minutes of the Price Administration Committee, 1941–1942. 

Policy Analysis Branch. 1947. 65 p. 

Historical Reports on War Administration, Miscellaneous Publication No. 2. 

There is an index and a table of contents. The 2-p. foreword gives a brief historical sketch of the committee and its policies. The minutes cover the period from the first meeting on April 14, 1941 to the last one on March 4, 1942. The minutes of each meeting include a list of those present and a summary of the proceedings, including the remarks of speakers. The basic policies and proceedings of OPACS were discussed in these meetings, and the record refers to such subjects as the steel price schedule, coal freeze order, automobiles, farm machinery, zinc concentrates, textiles, copper prices, agricultural prices, cotton yarn, fats, oils, drugs, rubber, fuel oil, lead hides, and nitrogen. In spite of the note on p. iv, a complete set of the verbatim transcripts has been found and deposited in the National Archives. 

2. Confidential Transcript of Meeting on Preliminary Financial Report Forms. 

Division of Accounting, Analysis and Review. December 31, 1941. 

Meeting held December 16, 1941, in New York City, between Controllers Institute of America and Office of Price Administration. Ten representatives of the former participated and Messrs. Barnett, Foster, Hyming, Kleinman, Smith and Taitel, for

OPA. One representative each for the Securities and Exchange Commission and the 

Bureau of the Budget also participated. The transcript is by Wallace Woodbury. The financial report form aimed "to give the Office of Price Administration the data from which they can determine the trends of profits, and more important-what the profit status of industry was at any time." Extensive discussion of difficulties in securing from industry the information wanted. 

3. Meetings of (Special) Committee for Retail Price Consideration. 

March 13-16, 1942.

Three reports of meetings have been traced-held on March 13 and probably on the 15th and 16th. This committee did the spade work on a system of price control devised to keep down the cost of living. At their meeting on March 13 they decided upon the issue of a "60-day freeze on factory, wholesalers' and retailers' prices of an extensive list of non-luxury consumers' goods." The meeting also discussed seven questions stemming from the pertinent problem of price control. At a meeting apparently held on March 15, 1942, the "discussion centered about the submitted list of proposed commodities for control under the retail freeze order planned." After considerable discussion of what the list should contain, it was decided to concentrate on the meaning of a "select list," and "essential items."

At a meeting held "March 16, 1942," there was discussion of the "order drafted" and of the "pricing of new items." No report has been found of a later meeting called for "Thursday." 

4. Meetings of Policy Committee. 

The first 33 reports of meetings held were unnumbered. Later in the period from 

May 16, 1942, to June 9, 1943, 35 numbered reports were issued. This committee fell 275

OPA Bibliography 6B. Minutes and Transcripts of Meetings (continued) 

heir to problems considered by the Committee for Retail Price Consideration. Reports of its meetings, especially the earlier ones which were frequent and had an atmosphere of urgency, suggest a hewing out of the rough outlines of a policy of price control. Such a policy was, in fact, adopted in the form of the General Maximum 

Price Regulation, and its subsequent modification by the application of price ceilings to separate commodities or groups of commodities. The committee was a forum for vital discussions and the men on it included several of the leaders of OPA. The committee gradually became less active and meetings were not held regularly. The reports were confidential. Dated April 28, 1942, is a memorandum from the Policy 

Committee to all price executives, discussing the need for organizing OPA relationships with organized business, industry, and trade groups. 3 p. Also accompanying the reports is a memorandum from the Subcommittee on Standards of Price Control Policy. It deals with "a more complete form of price control through standardization and simplification, grading and labeling of commodities."

C. Reports to Congress Series, Nos. 1-22. Periods ending April 30, 1942–May 31, 1947. 

Quarterly_reports to Congress filed under the requirements of section 301 of the 

Emergency Price Control Act. 

Nos. 1-3 were submitted by Leon Henderson, Administrator; Nos. 4 and 5 by 

Prentiss M. Brown, Administrator; Nos. 6-15 by Chester Bowles, Administrator; 

Nos. 16-18 by Paul A. Porter, Administrator; Nos. 19 and 20 by Major General 

Philip B. Fleming, Administrator, Office of Temporary Controls (reporting on the period of Paul A. Porter's administration ending September 30, 1946); and Nos. 21 and 22 by Major General Fleming (reporting on the administration of Max McCullough as Commissioner of Price Administration, OTC, and Earl W. Clark, Liquidation Officer for OTC, acting as Commissioner.)

These reports are, in general, the official record of accomplishment by the Office of Price Administration throughout its life. Especially important is the first one, which contains a valuable historical survey of the measures for price control taken by the Federal Government between the outbreak of war in September, 1939 and 

April 30, 1942. It includes chapters on War and the Defense Program, the Nation at War, the President's Program and the General Maximum Price Regulation, the 

Rent Control Program, the Rationing Program, the Office and How It Works: 

Organization-Procedures-Enforcement. 

The 2d report analyzes the effects of OPA measures during the first three months' 

operations in chapters entitled as follows: Cost-of-Living Stabilization, First Three Months of the Program, the Price Control Program, Special Problems of Price Control, Explaining and Enforcing Price Control, the Rent Control Problem, the Rationing Program, General Organization and Administration. 

Later issues were much less extensive, and tended to fall into a pattern of periodic reports upon price control, rent control, and rationing. With the 5th report, submitted by Administrator Brown, there is a chapter on Enforcement, which was stressed under his successor, Chester Bowles. The 7th report had chapters on Trans portation and Utility Rates, and War Price and Rationing Boards. 

As rationing increased in scope it received additional space and emphasis in the reports, with separate treatment for the various fields in which it was applied. At the same time, the price control program was treated in segments relating to the different groups of commodities controlled. A chapter on the Emergency Court of 

Appeals (decisions relating to OPA) appeared for the first time in the 12th report. 

With the 17th quarterly report (for the period ending March 31, 1946) the chapter on rationing is limited to the rationing of sugar. 

From then on the reports contain an atmosphere of perturbation at the relatively unfavorable status of OPA programs. The 19th report (to September 30, 1946) records the passage of the Price Control Extension Act of 1946 and includes chapters on Price Decontrol and Price Increases. The 20th report covers the demise of price control, the decontrol and reorganization program, price increases, and a report on the continuing rent and sugar programs. The 21st report (to March 31, 1947) deals with the progress of liquidation and the functions which were transferred to 278

4. OPA Highlights. 

Division of Research. 

Series began as "Price Action Highlights," No. 1, December 26, 1942, to No. 18, week ending April 24, 1943.

With the week ending May 1, 1943, the series was issued under the title of "OPA Highlights," which was itself unnumbered, but eventually grouped together four separately numbered series entitled, "Price Action Highlights," "Rationing Highlights," "Economic Highlights," and "Rent Control Highlights.' 

The first issue of "OPA Highlights" continued the "Price Action Highlight" series with No. 19 and included the first of the "Rationing Highlights" series. "Economic Highlights" was first included with "OPA Highlights" for the week ending 

May 15, 1943 and "Rent Control Highlights" started with the week ending June 5, 1943. 

"OPA Highlights" continued the four series as follows: 

"Price Action Highlights" through No. 199, Nov. 22, 1946; "Rationing Highlights" through No. 121, January 5, 1946; "Economic Highlights" through No. 5, November 20, 1943; and "Rent Control Highlights" through No. 12, October 21, 1944.

This series presents in condensed form all important OPA actions in the field of price, rent, and rationing, and information on economic conditions. 

The price series announces and explains major price actions, and pricing methods, grouped under the following and other subjects: price adjustments, reconversion pricing, individual adjustments, "hold-the-line" actions, dollar-and-cent prices, decontrolled items, extension of control, price decreases, protests and appeals, subsidies, maintenance of industry practices, actions taken to comply with new legislation. 

The rationing series briefly reports important developments in the programs, such as extension of controls, changes in rationing allowances, removals from the ration list, differential rationing, liberalization of requirements, adjustments in procedure, ration banking, enforcement activities.

The rent series announces and explains adjustments, changes in defense rental areas, extension of control, court decisions, "hold-the-line" actions, new procedures and adjustments.

The economic series contains brief facts on war and consumer expenditures, inventories, gross national product, gross national income, income payments, savings, salaries and wages, prices, treasury finance, and corporate profit. "For staff use only."

7. SPEECHES AND PREPARED STATEMENTS 

OPA officials were frequently called upon to make speeches at trade association meetings, to conventions and other groups, and over radio. 

Usually such talks were made as a result of invitations addressed to the office; many, if not most, of these invitations had to be declined because of the pressure upon officials' time. They were accepted when they afforded an opportunity to announce or explain a major office policy and when it was desirable to make a special effort to explain and elicit the cooperation of an industry with respect to a specific action which had been or would soon be taken. Many speeches were made by minor officials at trade association or industry meetings as a part of their routine duties of keeping the trade informed regarding OPA actions and of stimulating voluntary compliance.

Of special interest are items 49 and 218 below which are the scripts of the popular weekly mid-day radio talks given by Administrators Bowles and Porter and regularly carried by several hundred stations. 

Typescripts of nearly all speeches were cleared in advance by the Information Department. They were duplicated only when the points to be made were expected to be of considerable interest to the general press or when copies were desired for distribution to an industry or to office personnel for their information. The items listed here do not constitute an exhaustive list of those which were duplicated. They do, however, include most of the more significant ones and a representative sample of the others.

B. Statements to Congress and Congressional Committees 

Members of the OPA staff, especially those in top positions, were frequently called upon to testify before Congressional committees with respect to various aspects of agency policy and operations. Their testimony often included prepared statements which were either read to or filed with the committee. These statements usually also appeared in the printed volumes of committee hearings as well as in the mimeographed or printed form in which they were submitted. In a few cases testimony given extempore was duplicated and distributed to the OPA staff for its enlightenment.

Listed here are three categories of OPA communications to Congress : statements of specific individuals, exhibits consisting of charts or poster presentations reproduced in pamphlet form, and letters to Congressmen. 

Although there were literally many thousands of these latter, only a few, of unusual interest, were duplicated for distribution to other members of Congress or to the OPA staff. By reason of their elaborate content, statements or briefs filed with Congressional committees in the name of the agency rather than of any individual are not listed here. 308
