8. STATISTICAL, REPORTING, AND OTHER FORMS 

OPA's forms, though ordinarily printed or otherwise duplicated, were too numerous for practicable listings in this bibliography. The rationing forms alone would probably fill two four-drawer file cabinets. The most complete collection of OPA forms will be found in the office records in the National Archives, built up by OPA's Records Branch around the collection originally maintained in the files of what was successively known as the Questionnaire Branch, the Statistical Standards Office, the 

Statistical Standards Branch, and the Reporting and Statistical Review 

Section of the OPA Secretary's Office. Included there also is a duplicate set of the OPA forms (but not including NDAC or OPACS forms) in use to the end of 1942 submitted to the so-called Byrd Committee in connection with the legislative consideration of the Federal Reports Act of 1942. 

Another group of forms, not reporting forms, but used in rationing, consisted of the rationing currency itself. These were books or sheets or strips of coupons or stamps, at first on plain, later on safety paper, and in the later years serially numbered; and certificates and check forms. 

The incorporation of safety features was a noticeable trend. Through the cooperation of the Library of Congress, sets of ration currency together with a brief explanatory pamphlet, Rationing in World War II (item no. 6D.15 in this bibliography), were deposited in 1947 in a good many libraries throughout the country. 

Relatively little of the vast amount of detailed information needed for the planning, installation and operation of rationing and price and rent controls existed in any one place or in usable form at the time these programs were undertaken. Accordingly much of the time and concern of officials and employees were spent in attempting to make good the need. Forms were used wherever the prospective volume or frequency of usage warranted their design and duplication. In general, apart from the ration currency, they fell into two categories, depending on the nature of the users-public reporting forms and intra-office administrative forms. 

The use of public reporting forms depended on Sec. 202(a) of the 

Emergency Price Control Act which gave the Administrator broad discretion and a subpena power "to make such studies and investigations and to obtain such information as he deems necessary or proper to assist him. . ."; and on similar authority in the Second War Powers Act in connection with rationing. The forms were supposed to be, and at least after mid-1942 ordinarily were, cleared with the Bureau of the Budget; this is indicated by a notation in the upper corner of the expiration date of the Bureau's approval. In general, this clearance, until perhaps 1945, had the effect of slowing the issuance, narrowing somewhat the scope, and improving the technical design, of forms. 323

OPA Bibliography 

Public reporting forms were of varied sorts. Those used in the greatest quantities were the forms on which consumers made application for the four war ration books, for "A" gasoline books, for fuel oil, etc. The most complicated of these was probably the original fuel oil application form issued in Octber 1942. Supplemental ration applications, e.g., for "B" and "C" gasoline (later "mileage") rations, for home canning sugar, for extra shoes, for tires and tubes-accounted for many more forms. 

Rationing forms used by the trade and others, not household consumers, included initial and periodic inventory and disposition reports, institutional and industrial user applications, dealers' "bail-out" applications, and ration currency "flow-back" and ration banking reports. The forms used in connection with specific rationing programs are described in several of the manuscripts dealing with commodity programs, listed in section 10 of this bibliography, e.g., items 10BB.1, 2, and 10EE.3. Two general trends may be noted. As changes were made in the light of experience, forms tended to become simpler. The best example of this was the fuel oil application form; another was the rubber footwear certificate, which began as two letter-size sheets in three parts and ended as one check-size form. Also, they tended to become standardized, especially in the arrangement of common items. 

The basic rent form under the housing regulation was the landlord's registration form, one for every rented dwelling space under control in the country; the original was filed in the area rent office, the landlord and tenant each receiving a copy. A separate form was used for hotels and rooming houses under the hotel regulation. Both forms showed the computation of the maximum rent and described the nature of the accommodations on the base date. Other rent forms included complaint forms for tenants, application forms for rent adjustments and eviction certificates for landlords, and survey forms used by OPA to collect data on occupancy ratios, trends in rental charges and income, expense factors, net profits and the like. 

Price forms were of three main sorts, survey forms, registration or filing forms, and application forms. OPA conducted at least one survey in the affected industry in connection with nearly every one of the approximately 600 maximum price regulations issued, and many more in connection with later challenges of their validity or petitions for their amendment. The forms usually called for operating statements and balance sheets at successive time intervals, for product identifications and proportionate sales of various products, for base period and current prices, costs, margins and the like in detailed breakdowns, and for a variety of information on business practices such as discounts, terms, freight allowances, geographical distribution, proportions of sales to wholesalers, chains and independent retailers, etc. Where resources permitted and the complexity of the forms warranted it, the forms were 324

8. Statistical, Reporting, and Other Forms often completed by OPA staff accountants after field inspection of the books of responding firms. Registration or filing forms were used to record and establish ceilings where the number of firms or transactions was too voluminous to permit their individual consideration. Of special interest were the "pricing chart" forms, prescribed by MPR 580 and other consumer goods regulations, showing individually experienced margins on many categories of merchandise; the retailers' reports of new goods pricing under section 3 of the GMPR and the similar provisions of MPR 165 applicable to service establishments; and the food store registration forms. Forms were developed in the summer and fall of 

1942 for a gigantic registration of all retail establishments under the GMPR, but the plans were ultimately abandoned, largely under Budget Bureau pressure. Application forms were prescribed in connection with procedures for upward adjustments of established ceilings and for the establishment of ceilings on new goods, under the varying terms of many regulations. Many early OPA regulations required firms in the industries affected to report periodically, sometimes on prescribed forms, their sales, production, inventories, prices and similar data, both for OPA's information and in the interests of compliance before there was a statutory basis for enforcement. These reporting requirements proved generally of disappointing value and were gradually abandoned, except where, as in the case of premium payments on non-ferrous metals, they served a more specific purpose also.

Among the OPA forms best known in the business community were the so-called Form A and Form B, designed by the Financial Reporting Division of the Accounting Department and circulated by it to thousands of firms in all lines of business, to bring in current annual and quarterly data, respectively, on the financial results of their operations. Here too a striking simplification took place in later revisions, made in consultation with the American Institute of Accountants. The immediate purpose of the forms was a continuing up-to-date thermometer reading on the economic health of industries under price control; but the detailed breakdowns enabled a variety of special analyses to be made for more specific purposes. In particular, the breakdown of "cost of goods sold" and of general overhead provided much more detailed figures than are ordinarily available in the public reports of corporations (except for railroads and utilities where standard accounting classifications are prescribed) or in income tax returns. The functions and records of the Financial Reporting Division were transferred from OPA to the Federal Trade Commission early in 1947, in accordance with Executive Order No. 9809. 

Data from the Form A and Form B reports have been tabulated and analyzed by OPA's Research Division and published in part in its series of War Profit Studies (see item 4C.10 in this Bibliography). The Finan cial Reporting Division also published a cumulative listing of tabulations 325

OPA Bibliography completed and of individual firms showing reports received (items Nos. 

3F.15 and 18 in this bibliography). A discussion of some of the problems arising in the preparation and clearance of public reporting forms used by the Price Department will be found in Virgil B. Zimmermann, Prob lems in Price Control: National Office Organization and Management, chapter 3 (OPA series, Historical Records of War Administration); see also Joseph M. Selove, A History of the Review and Clearance of Sur veys and Reporting Requirements in the OPA, item No. 10B.13, below; and the references given by W. J. Wilson, The Beginnings of OPA (item 6D.17 in this bibliography), p. 98, note 10.

The Enforcement Department developed elaborate forms, sometimes amounting to worksheets, for the use of its investigators in compliance surveys, as a means of facilitating and controlling their work. Some of these forms provided space for the signature of a representative of the firm investigated, if he was willing to sign, in order to eliminate dispute over matters of fact developed in the investigation. The necessity of clearing these forms with the Bureau of the Budget remained a controversial point to the end.

Internal administrative forms were also varied and numerous. In one group may be put the clearance sheets accompanying all official regulatory actions, designed to show the signatures or initials, and dates, of approval by all officials required to review them. A much larger group consisted of budgetary, fiscal, personnel and administrative service forms, covering every type of administrative action: appointments, transfers, promotions, terminations, travel, payrolls, bond and tax deductions, allotment advices, requisitions for printing, equipment, supplies and space. Many such forms were taken over or adapted from standardized government procedures, rather than devised by OPA. These were, however, supplemented by a great many special housekeeping forms over which there was little central control. An individual commodity branch or section, or occasionally even a unit, if it avoided crossing jurisdictional lines—and sometimes when it did not—could devise and get duplicated any form it thought might help it to keep track of or dispose of its workload. Another large group of forms used in the program and the housekeeping phases of operations may be designated as internal reporting forms, designed to enable central offices to keep informed, to plan and to control. In this group fall the elaborate system of reports of proposed and pending price actions in the commodity branches in the national office, instituted by the Executive Office for Price; the reports required of field offices of their exercise of delegated authority to make price and rent adjustments, to interpret regulations, to issue ration currency, to hire people, to rent space and procure equipment, to spend money and to control local board operations. In the category of field office report forms, special mention should be made of the periodic employment and fiscal reports, of the 326

8. Statistical, Reporting, and Other Forms Standardization of Forms 8A. 

board management reports in 1946, and of the enforcement reports which brought into the national office on IBM cards the essential facts about every pending enforcement case.

Successive efforts were made, beginning in the fall of 1942, and at intervals to the end, to review and eliminate reporting requirements that had not proved their value. This was true both of forms circulated to business firms and of reports required of field offices and of operating units in the national office. There were continuing objections to the burden on respondents; and too voluminous or numerous reports were self-defeating-time and staff were lacking either to prepare or to analyze them all. Nevertheless new requirements were continually introduced; the appetite of conscientious regulators for information about what they were doing was insatiable. 

Until late in 1942 there was no standard system of numbering OPA forms except those specifically related to an official price schedule. For these the Federal Register Liaison Attorney devised a system which used for the first part of the form number the price schedule number increased by 100. Thus, Form 102:1 denoted the first form used with 

Price Schedule No. 2; 108:3, the third form used with Price Schedule

No. 8; and so on. Many early forms in fact bore no identifying symbol; others had a designation consisting of letter symbol and serial number, such as R for a rationing form, P & D, a Printing and Distribution Branch form, and so on. T designated a form prescribed for applicants for price adjustment under Temporary Procedural Regulation No. 2. 

The numbering system ultimately adopted gave each form a compound symbol; the first part was the budget code symbol of the originating office or division, and the second was a serial identifying the sequence of forms issued by that office. Thus OPA Form 611-196 was the 196th form adopted by the Office of the Deputy Administrator for Price. The budget code symbols assigned to organization units will be found in the OPA Manual. Both public reporting forms and forms for internal administrative use were numbered in the same sequence. When forms were revised they retained their previous numbers, but an R was usually added at the end, with the date of revision. In other cases a notation such as (Rev. 10-44) was placed below, showing the month and year of revision.

A study of OPA forms is a laborious task, but it provides one of the best means of obtaining a concrete understanding of the agency's methods, and of the types of information on which the conduct of its programs rested.

8. Opinions of the Attorney General With Respect to Government Protection Under Section 302 (i) of the Second Revenue Act of 1940. 

Price Stabilization Division. [1940 or 1941] 20 p. 

Opinions rendered November 25 and 30, 1940, by the Attorney General at request of the Assistant Secretary of War and the Secretary of War, respectively. Related to the payment to the Government of an appraised value of an emergency plant at the end of 5 years or the earlier termination of the "present emergency,' or the con' eyance of the facility to the Government. A Senate committee was informed that 329

OPA Bibliography 

9A. Legislation under contracts entered into, contractors "would not be permitted to recapture the whole or a substantial part of the cost of their emergency facilities during the emergency or national defense program period by charging the Government abnormal prices and then at the end of the period be the owners of such facilities freed of any claim or interest of the Government." Says disposition of a facility of the sort discussed was a matter for joint action by the Secretary of War and NDAC. In the second opinion the Attorney General suggests a redraft of a supplemental agreement, which he believes will protect the interests of the United States in the facilities under discussion, and states that when the Secretary of War finds that such a proposed supplemental agreement, redrafted as suggested, will adequately protect the pertinent interests of the United States, "and that finding is concurred in by the Advisory Commission to the Council of National Defense," the contractor might be furnished a Certificate of Government Protection under the provisions of subsection 

(i) of section 302 of the Second Revenue Act of 1940.

Subjects ranged from housing, through income tax blanks, cultural opportunities, entertainment, health, war items, relations to the agency, war savings bonds, employee suggestion system, stamp collecting, churches, vacations, etc. Messages from the Administrator are occasionally folded in. These became rather frequent in Vol. IV and presented Mr. Bowles' current views of OPA problems of interest to employees. Administrator Porter carried on the custom of issuing such messages. 336

Porter, was dated March 18, 1946. Beginning with that issue it became the Administrator's Letter to Employees. There are a number of gaps in the dated issues. 16. Letter to All OPA Employees from Max McCullough. 

Office of the Administrator. [read Commissioner] May 1, 1947. 4 p. 

A letter of thanks for faithful service. Traces the larger aspects of the development of OPA, including its spirit and purposes. Divides its work into 3 main phases -missionary campaign to get converted to war production and get the cost of living stabilized, to maintain price stability and capacity production, and finally, reconversion and decontrol. Expresses opinion that controls were removed too soon. Analyzes reasons for failure of OPA to retain control until danger of inflation was over.

10. APPENDIX: UNPUBLISHED OPA HISTORICAL REPORTS ON WAR ADMINISTRATION 

In 1943, as a part of the Government-wide program sponsored by President Franklin D. Roosevelt to provide an adequate record of the war administration, OPA appointed a Historical Records Officer. His office endeavored for nearly two years to persuade other segments of the national office to organize their record files so that they would be available for future research, and assisted them in the process. In addition a chronological outline was drawn up to serve as a guide to history writers. In 1945 the functions of records management and historical analysis were separated. A History Branch was established which drew up plans for a series of comprehensive volumes covering the gamut of OPA experience and activities. The Rationing Department, too, appointed a historical staff to make detailed program studies; and with the end of rationing several of its executives prepared summaries of their experiences and problems. 

Throughout the office, other manuscripts of historical significance were produced: terminal reports of departing officials, individually volunteered accounts of administrative experience, dissertations written by former staff members. Several of these, including "A Letter to the OPA 

Historian" by J. Kenneth Galbraith, who had been in charge of price activities from early 1941 to mid-1943, were deposited with the Historical 

Records Section of the Bureau of the Budget. 

With the elimination of price controls in the fall of 1946, the Policy Analysis Branch emerged, superseding the History Branch. It was enlarged temporarily until it included about 30 professional employees, most of whom had had lengthy experience in the agency. With considerable assistance from outside sources this group prepared a series of eighteen volumes for publication as an OPA historical records series. 

The choice of subjects depended, of course, initially upon a judgment as to the most significant aspects of the agency's experience, but it was influenced also by the range of experience of the individuals available as authors. Thus there are important gaps, such as sugar rationing and rent control after its initial phases. This group also produced a number of studies which were not published, a frequent reason being that the services of the author were lost to the agency before the draft could be brought to publishable form.

In anticipation of liquidation, officials in both national and field offices were asked to prepare narratives or chronologies of their segments of agency activities. In this way most of the commodity histories were secured. Manuscripts prepared in field offices usually covered particular organization units. Many of them were the products of considerable research and demonstrate a careful analysis of agency problems. The 341

OPA Bibliography 10A. Accounting voluminous histories produced in the regional offices in Cleveland, Dallas, and Region IX were mimeographed in a limited number of copies. Copies of these have been deposited in the Library of Congress. 

While many of these unpublished studies did not get beyond draft form, they will provide future students of OPA with valuable source material and with references to other OPA records. For that reason they have been collected and are listed here. Because of their preliminary form they must be used with some caution. As in the case of other materials included in the bibliography the numbers here assigned are an index to their location in the OPA files in the National Archives.

By Joseph A. Kershaw.

Earlier, longer version of his published A History of Ration Banking (item No.

By Procter Shelley. 65 p. 

Description of distribution plans, methods used, experience with various procedures. 

3. Rationing in the Second World War. 

By Paul M. O'Leary. 66 p. 

The broad phases of external and internal administration and major policy prob lems by the Deputy Administrator for Rationing from March 1942-October 

1943. Report written for the Bureau of the Budget in October 1944, and partially printed in the American Political Science Review for December 1945 (Vol. 

XXXIX, No. 6). 

BB. Rationing: Automotive 1. Automobile Rationing. 

By Margaret L. Stecker. 440 p.

Thorough and informative account of the automobile rationing program. Thirteen chapters include descriptions of the planning, administrative organization, coverage of the order, allocations and quotas, dealer relief, eligibility, release of frozen cars, inventory control. Critical analysis and appraisal of each phase of operations. 

2. Battery Rationing.

By Victor A. Thompson. 12 p. 

Background of scarcity, outline of proposed ration plan, never put in effect.

3. Gasoline Rationing. 

By members of gasoline rationing staff. 310 p. 

Seventeen-chapter volume covering all major phases of subject. Chapters vary greatly in length and thoroughness of treatment. 

4. Tire Rationing. 

By Evelyn Meyer, Paul Cody, others. 681 p., 3 vols.

Thorough descriptions of many phases of tire rationing, including quotas, eligibility, inspections, regulations, relations with other departments. 

CC. Rationing: Food and Soap 1. Institutional User Rationing. 

135 p. 

Substantial but unfinished manuscript covering in six chapters the planning and operation of procedures for supplying rationed food to restaurants and others serving food. 370

2. Plan for Rationing Soap. 

54 p., 4 chapters and appendix.

Rationing: Fuel 10DD. 

Contents: introduction; the soap business; the rationing plan; conclusion. Materials were prepared by A. Allen Thompson, formerly in charge of the plans for developing a rationing program; manuscript was put in narrative form and edited by Judith Russell. The rationing of soap never materialized. 

DD. Rationing: Fuel 1. Development of Fuel Oil Rationing. 

By Joel Dean and L. C. Vass. 640 p. 

Detailed and personal account of planning, installation, and administration of fuel oil rationing during 1942 and 1943. Written for the Bureau of the Budget in

By Joel Dean. Approx. 200 p.

Description of planning and operation of coal and woodfuel rationing in Washington, Oregon, Idaho. Includes highlights of a unique enterprise. Written by the chief of the branch which ran the program from Seattle. 

4. Stove Rationing. 

By Louis W. Koenig. 532 P., 2 vols.

Exhaustive account of all major phases of stove rationing. Eleven chapters include explanations of the regulations, eligibility, field organization. 

EE. Rationing: Miscellaneous Products 1. Clothes Rationing in Australia.

Explanation of fundamentals of Australia's clothes rationing program, including coverage, point system, basic ration, extra rations, ration currency, trade matters. 

2. Plan for Rationing Clothing. 

By Laurence E. Tilley. 37 p.

Description of planning operation with explanation of salient points of an unused rationing program. 

3. Rubber Footwear Rationing.

By Luella C. Zettler. 269 p. 

Detailed and thorough description account of the rubber footwear rationing program. Nine chapters include explanations of the planning, launching and operating of the program from 1942 to 1945. Complete (nine-page) topical outline facilitates use of the volume. 

4. Shoe Rationing. 

By Perham Nahl. 197 p.

Chronological account of the administrative problems, and highlights of shoe rationing, with thorough treatments of forms and form design.
